**"O my people! Remember Allah’s favours upon you"** calls for remembrance with the heart and tongue. Musa begins with what Allah has done for them rather than presenting the task without its background of mercy. Their past deliverance gives a reason for present trust.

**"when He raised prophets from among you"** names the spiritual gift first. Prophets repeatedly arose among them to call people toward Allah and warn of punishment. The wording says prophets were raised from among the people, not that every member of the community was a prophet.

**"made you sovereign"** recalls their release from Pharaoh's domination and their control over their own affairs. Muluk, kings, can describe the rule enjoyed by a people through its rulers. It is also explained more broadly as the independence of a person with a home, household and help, rather than only someone possessing a royal throne.

**"and gave you what He had never given anyone in the world"** refers to exceptional favours among the people of their time. These include both spiritual distinction and material gifts: revelation, leadership, the parting of the sea and the provisions given in the wilderness. Manna and quails are named, while another gloss describes quails and honey.

### Why begin the command with a reminder of blessings?

The people had seen Pharaoh and his army drowned and had been delivered from slavery. The historical explanation describes them as becoming masters of Egypt and then being called to recover the ancestral land in Syria. Allah had already demonstrated power over an enemy far stronger than themselves.

Musa's approach therefore brings the coming obligation into continuity with what they know. They are not being asked to trust an unknown power after receiving no help. The Lord who delivered them also commands the next step.

The wider story will show refusal followed by wandering, and the promise will later be fulfilled under new leadership. Those consequences belong to the later verses. Here the emphasis is on the favour that should have made obedience a grateful response rather than a burden considered in isolation.

### What was exceptional about the succession of prophets?

The explanation traces prophetic guidance through the family of Ibrahim (Abraham). Among the Children of Israel, prophets continued to arise, one following another, until 'Isa (Jesus), the last prophet from that community. The blessing was not merely possession of an old memory. It included repeated living calls to guidance.

A report through A'mash, recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim, gives a thousand prophets in the period from Musa to 'Isa. The account describes the Children of Israel as having received an unusually large number. The figure is retained as reported, not independently verified through an additional chronology.

After 'Isa, Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ, the son of 'Abdullah, from the descendants of Isma'il (Ishmael), Ibrahim's son. He is described as the final and most honoured Prophet. The earlier community's distinction therefore does not mean prophethood or divine favour could never reach another community afterward.

### In what sense could an entire people be kings?

A nation cannot consist entirely of monarchs any more than it can consist entirely of prophets. One explanation therefore uses ordinary collective speech. The rule of a dynasty or people is attributed to the whole group, even though one ruler or a small number actually administers it.

The discussion gives the Umayyads and Abbasids as examples, followed by Ghaznavis, Ghauris, Mughals and the British in India. In each case, people commonly name a rule through its associated people or house. The expression need not mean that every person individually occupied a throne.

An additional political observation is drawn from this. The ruler's authority may be understood as that of the community through its chosen representative. The account describes the people as entitled collectively to appoint and remove their leader. That is the argument made from the collective wording, not a separate constitutional code supplied by the verse.

A second explanation gives malik a wider everyday sense. Someone with property, a home and assistance may live with a kind of household independence. After subjection, possessing those things could make each family seem sovereign within its own life.

Abdur-Razzaq reports Ibn 'Abbas explaining the expression through a servant, wife and house. Al-Hakim's Mustadrak records a wording mentioning a wife and servant, and the qualification that the exceptional favour concerned the people of their own time. Al-Hakim calls its chain sahih according to the standards of the Two Sahihs and notes that they did not collect it.

Qatadah says they were the first people to take servants. A further hadith describes someone who begins the day bodily healthy, secure with his family and supplied with that day's provision as having what amounts to the world's riches gathered for him. The point is that security and sufficiency can be a great form of wealth without a royal title.

### Does their distinction exclude the later Muslim community?

The favour is explained relative to contemporary peoples, including Greeks and Copts. The Qur'an elsewhere describes the Children of Israel receiving scripture, judgment, prophethood and good provision, and being preferred above the nations (45:16).

When they later asked for an object of worship like those of another people, Musa rebuked their ignorance and reminded them of Allah's preference toward them (7:138-140). Distinction should have led to fidelity, not imitation of idolatry.

The Muslim ummah, the community of the final Prophet ﷺ, is also described as favoured. The passage cites its appointment as a just community bearing witness over humanity (2:143) and its description as the best community raised for people (3:110). It refers to widely transmitted reports about that honour without providing additional reports to reproduce here.

The discussion also speaks of that community's more complete law, greater extent of rule, resources and lasting public honour. These are the comparisons made in its account of the communities. They do not require reading Musa's words as a claim about every later people in every age. A blessing unmatched in one period can be followed by a greater blessing in another.

### What responsibility accompanies being a bearer of revelation?

Allah may choose a people to carry His message to others, just as He chooses a person to receive revelation. The Children of Israel held that responsibility in an earlier age. After the final Prophet ﷺ, his followers carry it.

Honour is joined to a test. The explanation connects a community's public distinction with showing the truth of the guidance it bears, but does not make that benefit unconditional. The community must prove its faith and willingness to obey when patience is tried.

The coming refusal therefore matters precisely because the people have received so much. The gifts are not a licence to decline every costly duty. They are reasons to respond faithfully when the command arrives.

### In short

- Musa recalls prophetic guidance, freedom and exceptional provision before asking his people to undertake a difficult command.
- Sovereignty includes collective rule and the security of an independent household, not only individual kingship.
- The exceptional favour concerns the people of their time and does not exclude later favour to another community.
- Carrying revelation brings responsibility. Gratitude must be shown through obedience when faith is tested.

21.text:
Musa (Moses) now states the command for which he has prepared his people: "O my people! Enter the Holy Land which Allah has destined for you ˹to enter˺." The promise of the land is joined to a duty to enter rather than retreat in fear. Turning back would bring loss instead of the promised success.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O my people! Enter the Holy Land"** commands entry into the purified land. The accounts identify Jerusalem and its surroundings, while other explanations extend the description across the region of Syria. The immediate task is to confront the occupying enemy under the command given through Musa.

**"which Allah has destined for you ˹to enter˺."** Allah has assigned or promised it to them. One explanation describes it as the inheritance promised through their father Isra'il to those among them who believe. Another connects the bequest with Ibrahim (Abraham). A further gloss emphasises that Allah has commanded them to enter it.

**"And do not turn back or else you will become losers.”"** forbids retreat from the duty because of fear. The loss concerns the intended success in this life and their standing in the next. A gloss also mentions the loss of the quails and honey among their provisions.

### Which place is meant?

The names supplied include Baytul-Maqdis, Jerusalem, and the associated names Quds and Eliah. Other explanations mention Ariha, situated between the Jordan and Jerusalem. It is described as an ancient city with reports of great size. One such account gives a thousand districts, each with a thousand gardens. Those numbers are part of the reported description, not independent measurements.

Other identifications include Damascus and Palestine or parts of Jordan. Qatadah calls the whole land of Syria holy. The explanations can therefore describe either the wider region or a particular place within it, rather than necessarily contradicting one another.

The land is called holy because of its association with Allah's prophets. Ka'b al-Ahbar says he read in a revealed book, perhaps the Torah, that Syria was a special treasure containing servants especially dear to Allah. Another narration describes Ibrahim standing on a mountain in Lebanon and being shown the land within his sight as holy. These are reported accounts attached to the explanation, not additional geographical claims established independently here.

### How does the command fit their earlier history?

The account describes Ya'qub (Jacob) and his household leaving their earlier home for Egypt during the time of Yusuf (Joseph). Their descendants remained there until Musa led them out. A powerful people had meanwhile taken control of the land to which they were now directed.

Musa promised victory if they obeyed Allah and entered to confront that enemy. The promise did not mean they could refuse the commanded action and still demand the result. The command and assurance belong together in this particular prophetic episode, not as a new instruction concerning contemporary territorial conflict.

### In short

- Allah's promise is joined to the command to enter, not to permission to remain inactive.
- The Holy Land is explained through Jerusalem and the wider Syrian region associated with the prophets.
- Fearful retreat from the command would turn the opportunity into loss.

22.text:
The people answer the command by making their obedience depend on the disappearance of the difficulty: "There is an enormously powerful people there, so we will never ˹be able to˺ enter it until they leave." Musa's (Moses') assurance of victory does not persuade them. They will enter only after the enemy has already gone, without undertaking the struggle required of them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They replied, “O Moses!"** introduces the response of the Children of Israel to their own prophet. It is the answer of people who have received the command and understand that it requires action from them.

**"There is an enormously powerful people there"** describes inhabitants of great bodily size, strength and ferocity. The accounts call them Amalkites and associate them with the remaining people of 'Ad. A brief gloss describes them as violent killers.

**"so we will never ˹be able to˺ enter it until they leave."** expresses refusal through a claim of inability. Their attention is fixed on the enemy's visible strength rather than Allah's promise. They will not enter while those people remain.

**"If they do, then we will enter!”"** offers compliance only after the decisive obstacle has been removed for them. It is not acceptance of the command as given. The command required them to advance despite the enemy's presence.

### What did the reconnaissance party report?

Reports associated with Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Abi Talhah describe Musa advancing with his people toward Syria and Baytul-Maqdis. After crossing the Jordan, they stopped at Ariha. The twelve chiefs were sent ahead to investigate the people, local conditions and the ground on which the confrontation would take place.

Near the city's gate, an Amalkite man seized the twelve and brought them before the king. The court discussed killing them or punishing them in another way. It finally chose to release them, hoping that their experience would spread terror among their people and prevent an attack.

The chiefs returned and reported the enemy's power to Musa. His confidence was not shaken because he had already received Allah's promise of victory. But he recognised that an alarming public account could make the people retreat before the command was attempted.

He therefore told the chiefs not to spread their report among the people. Ten privately told friends, and the news soon became public. Only two, Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yu'qina, kept the instruction and confined their report to Musa. Their faithful response is developed in the next verse.

### What happened when the news spread?

The people became distraught and protested against the journey. They said it would have been better to drown in the Nile with Pharaoh's people than to be delivered there only to die at the hands of these powerful inhabitants. Their language turned an earlier rescue into a grievance against the next obligation.

The refusal in the verse expresses that reaction. They treated the enemy's strength as decisive even though they had recently witnessed deliverance from Egypt. They wanted the benefit of entry without the test through which they had been commanded to obtain it.

The passage's criticism concerns this disobedient response in the narrated event. It does not turn every descendant of the community into a person responsible for those words. Its lesson is the danger of allowing fear to overthrow a commitment already accepted.

### Should the exaggerated giant stories be accepted?

The discussion expressly rejects the extravagant Israelite tales attached to this episode. Some name the man who seized the chiefs as 'Awj ibn 'Unuq and give him fantastic proportions and powers. Those exaggerations are described as unsupported by reason or the revealed law, a collection of fabrications rather than reliable explanation.

The retained account is more limited. It describes the Amalkites as people of unusual size and strength, associated with the people of 'Ad, and reports one man overpowering the scouts. It does not endorse the additional towering measurements and marvels found in the rejected tales.

That distinction matters. Retelling a story associated with scripture does not require accepting every later embellishment. The reservation belongs beside the story so that a reader can distinguish the reported core from the material expressly dismissed.

### What makes the response a breach rather than simple caution?

Reconnaissance itself was not the problem. Musa had sent the chiefs to learn the conditions. The breach came when their fear overruled the command and assurance he had conveyed. Information meant to prepare the people for obedience became an excuse for abandoning it.

The two faithful chiefs would urge a concrete step rather than denial of the danger. Their example shows that the alternative was not pretending no strong enemy existed. It was to place that danger under the authority of Allah's promise.

### In short

- The people refused to enter while the powerful inhabitants remained, making obedience conditional on effortless safety.
- The scouts' report spread fear after most of them disregarded Musa's instruction to keep it private.
- The exaggerated tales about a giant are explicitly rejected, while the limited account of a formidable enemy is retained.
- The failure was not gathering information, but letting fear cancel a command whose promised outcome came from Allah.

23.text:
Two men answer fear with trust and a practical step: "Surprise them through the gate. If you do, you will certainly prevail." Allah describes them as blessed and God-fearing. Unlike the people refusing Musa's (Moses') command, they urge obedience to the promise he has conveyed and reliance on Allah for its fulfilment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Two God-fearing men"** is principally explained as two men who feared Allah and the consequence of disobeying Him. They are identified as Yuwsha' son of Nun, Joshua, and Kalib son of Yufna, Caleb. Other forms supplied are Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yu'qina, or Caleb ben Jephunneh.

**"who had been blessed by Allah"** means He had granted them righteousness, faith and the ability to remain obedient. The description makes their firmness a divine favour rather than proof that they possessed independent moral power.

**"said, “Surprise them through the gate."** They call for a decisive advance into the city instead of remaining outside in fear. The gate of Baytul-Maqdis is the immediate objective. Their counsel turns confidence into action.

**"If you do, you will certainly prevail."** They assure the people that the promised victory will follow obedience. One explanation connects their confidence with assessing the inhabitants as physically impressive but weak in courage. Another grounds it in complete trust in Allah's promise received through Musa.

**"Put your trust in Allah if you are ˹truly˺ believers.”"** makes reliance part of faith. Preparation and the commanded advance are to be undertaken, while the outcome is entrusted to Allah. Trust does not mean waiting for the city to empty itself before acting.

### Who were the two men?

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Atiyyah, As-Suddi and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas are among those identifying them as Joshua and Caleb. In the reconnaissance account, they were the two chiefs who kept Musa's instruction and did not frighten the people with their report. They told Musa what they had seen but did not spread it among everyone else.

There are other explanations of the wording. One reading takes the expression as indicating men who were feared or respected among their people. A gloss describes them as men who themselves feared the violent inhabitants but were granted certainty. Another says they were two men from those inhabitants who feared Musa and received faith in Allah's oneness.

These alternatives should not erase the principal account of the faithful scouts, nor should that account make the others disappear. They reflect different explanations of who feared whom and of the men's position among the people.

### Why mention both fear and blessing?

One explanation notices that the object of fear is not explicitly named in the phrase. The omission points toward the One who ultimately deserves fear: Allah, the absolute Lord. No created being can independently give benefit or bring harm against His will.

The mention of blessing is equally important. All twelve chiefs had outward faculties, understanding and the company of a prophet. Yet only two remained firm in the reported test. Possessing intelligence and opportunity did not make guidance automatic.

The lesson is not that effort is unnecessary. Deed and effort are conditions of seeking the gift. But success in right guidance remains Allah's favour. An intelligent or capable person should therefore ask Him for guidance rather than become proud of personal resources.

### How do courage and reliance work together?

The two do not ask their people to ignore what has been learned. They propose going forward despite it, because the command comes with a promise. Faith, preparation and reliance form one response rather than competing choices.

Their statement about victory may include insight into the enemy's weakness of heart, or rest entirely on confidence in revelation. In both explanations, the practical counsel is the same: begin the commanded action and trust Allah, instead of allowing fear to make obedience impossible in advance.

### In short

- The two blessed men urge a concrete advance under Allah's promise, not passive waiting.
- Their principal identification is Joshua and Caleb, the faithful scouts, with other interpretations also reported.
- Right guidance is Allah's gift, even where people possess similar abilities and opportunities.
- Faith joins preparation and obedience with reliance on Allah for the result.

24.text:
The Children of Israel repeat their refusal more harshly: "O Moses! ˹Still˺ we will never enter as long as they remain there." They then tell Musa (Moses) and his Lord to fight while they stay where they are. Advice from the two faithful men has not overcome their resistance. The moment that required commitment instead reveals their determination not to act.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Yet˺ they said, “O Moses! ˹Still˺ we will never enter as long as they remain there."** renews the same condition despite the command and the promised victory. The enemy must leave first. The people will not participate in bringing about the outcome they want.

**"So go—both you and your Lord—and fight"** is an offensive refusal to support their prophet. One explanation understands the intended sense as telling Musa to fight with Allah's help while they withhold theirs. Another gloss takes the address to his master as a reference to Harun (Aaron), with Allah helping the two as He had helped against Pharaoh.

**"we are staying right here!”"** leaves no ambiguity about their own choice. They intend to remain away from the fight. The words became proverbial as an example of abandoning a leader at the moment his followers were required to stand with him.

### Is the statement explained as outright disbelief?

The discussion distinguishes insolent refusal from deliberate mockery of Allah. If the words were intended as mockery, it says, they would be open kufr, disbelief. Yet Musa's continuing presence with them and his later prayers for them in the wilderness are taken as reasons not to assume that intention.

On the explanation preferred there, they mean that Musa should act with his Lord's help because they themselves will not help. That remains deeply hurtful and disobedient without requiring the additional conclusion that the sentence was spoken as a theological denial or jest. The distinction preserves the severity of the breach while attending to the subsequent account.

### How did the Companions answer a similar moment at Badr?

The contrast is drawn with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ consulting his Companions before Badr. They had missed the caravan led by Abu Sufyan, while an armed Quraysh force of roughly nine hundred to a thousand approached. The Muslims faced a serious confrontation rather than the easier outcome they had first expected.

Abu Bakr spoke well, and other emigrants did likewise. The Prophet ﷺ continued asking for advice because he wanted to hear from the Ansar, who formed the majority. Sa'd bin Mu'adh recognised that and pledged that they would follow even if he entered the sea. They would not refuse battle, and he hoped their conduct would give the Prophet ﷺ satisfaction. The Prophet ﷺ was pleased and encouraged to proceed.

Anas relates another version recorded by Abu Bakr bin Marduwyah, and also by Ahmad, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban. After 'Umar spoke, the Prophet ﷺ again sought their view. The Ansar understood that he was addressing them and declared that they would not repeat the refusal made to Musa. They would follow even to Bark Al-Ghimad near Makkah.

### What did Al-Miqdad say?

Al-Bukhari records 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud recalling Al-Miqdad's response at Badr. He told the Prophet ﷺ that they would not tell him to go with his Lord while they stayed behind. Instead, he should proceed and they would be with him.

The fuller account names him Miqdad ibn al-Aswad and describes him promising to defend the Prophet ﷺ from the front and rear and on both sides. The Prophet ﷺ had been praying before Allah as the powerful enemy approached. Miqdad's pledge delighted him and strengthened the Companions' resolve.

Ibn Mas'ud later expressed his wish that he had enjoyed the honour of making that declaration. The contrast makes the duty clear without a new abstract rule: one community refused its prophet at the test, while these Companions pledged their presence and support.

### In short

- The people insist on remaining inactive until the enemy leaves, despite the command and counsel they have received.
- The offensive words are explained as disobedient refusal, while the discussion distinguishes that from an intention of blasphemous mockery.
- The Companions' pledges before Badr provide the opposite example: they would accompany and defend the Prophet ﷺ rather than leave him to act alone.
- A pledge of obedience is tested when support becomes costly, not only when agreement is easy.

25.text:
Musa (Moses) turns to Allah after his people's repeated refusal: "My Lord! I have no control over anyone except myself and my brother." He cannot compel their hearts to accept the command they have rejected. His prayer asks Allah to distinguish him and Harun (Aaron) from the people whose choice has made the intended advance impossible.

The words express both the limit of his authority over others and his own continued commitment. He does not join their refusal or abandon the command as unworthy. He places the separation between obedience and rebellion before the Lord who can judge it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses pleaded, “My Lord!"** introduces his appeal to the One who sent him. The account describes him as angry and deeply hurt by the refusal. He brings that pain to Allah instead of surrendering his own faithfulness.

**"I have no control over anyone except myself and my brother."** He can answer for his own obedience and is certain of his brother's support. He cannot make the rest of the people carry out what they have refused. This is not a denial that he conveyed the command clearly, but recognition of their refusal to act upon it.

**"So set us apart from the rebellious people.”"** asks for a distinction between the obedient and those who contravene Allah's command. Ibn 'Abbas explains ifruq as judging between the two sides, and Ad-Dahhak gives the same sense. Another explanation takes it as separation. The prayer asks that each receive the treatment appropriate to its conduct.

### Why is their refusal especially painful?

Musa had faced great hardship to bring them out of ignorance and subjection. They had seen Pharaoh's magicians accept the truth after the contest at his court. They had witnessed the proud ruler and his forces overcome, his wealth left behind and his power destroyed through drowning, while they themselves crossed safely.

The account describes Allah giving them the country and wealth over which Pharaoh had boasted, without a battle for those possessions. Their deliverance was therefore not merely something they had heard about from distant ancestors. They had seen it.

Against that background, their refusal to enter under a promise of victory was a bitter rejection of both divine favour and prophetic labour (5:21-22). Musa's steadfastness appears in the restraint of his appeal. He continues seeking Allah's judgment rather than allowing their ingratitude to overturn his own purpose.

### Why mention only Harun when two chiefs had also remained faithful?

Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yu'qina had supported the command and counselled their people. Their absence from this prayer is not explained as proof that their earlier counsel was false.

The explanation instead points to the certainty Musa had concerning his brother, who was himself a prophet under divine protection. The two chiefs, though righteous, did not have that same protected status. After repeated betrayal, Musa named the obedience about which he was certain: his own and Harun's.

His words therefore describe the limit of what he could reliably undertake at that moment. They do not require erasing the virtue already attributed to the two men.

### What judgment is he asking for?

Ibn 'Abbas explains the prayer as asking that the people's deserved consequence be assigned to them, and that Musa and his brother receive what was appropriate for their own conduct. They should not be treated as participants in a refusal they had opposed.

The next verse gives Allah's response through a period of exclusion and wandering. The prayer itself stops at entrusting the division to Him. Musa does not invent a punishment or claim independent power to impose whatever he pleases.

### In short

- Musa acknowledges that he cannot force a rebellious people into obedience.
- He remains certain of his own commitment and that of his prophet brother Harun.
- The prayer asks Allah to judge or separate the obedient from those who have refused His command.
- Pain caused by betrayal becomes an appeal to Allah, not abandonment of Musa's own responsibility.

26.text:
Allah answers Musa's (Moses') prayer with a consequence matching the refusal: "Then this land is forbidden to them for forty years, during which they will wander through the land." The people who had insisted on staying where they were would not reach the destination offered to them. Their confinement would occur in open country rather than behind a prison wall.

Musa is then told not to grieve over the rebellious people. Their punishment is not an injustice done to people who kept the covenant. It is the result of their own refusal, though the compassionate prophet would still feel pain at their hardship.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah replied, “Then this land is forbidden to them for forty years"** excludes the Children of Israel from entering the Holy Land during the stated period. The explanation understands this not merely as an instruction they might choose to ignore, but as an enforced inability to reach it. They could not obtain the destination while persisting in the refusal that had brought the sentence.

**"during which they will wander through the land."** They move without finding the way out, bewildered in the wilderness called At-Tih. Their attempts to go forward to Baytul-Maqdis or return to Egypt bring them back to where they began. Movement alone does not free them from Allah's judgment.

**"So do not grieve for the rebellious people.”"** comforts Musa. Prophets are naturally distressed by the suffering of those they guide. He is told not to be overcome by sorrow over a sentence their own disobedience has deserved.

### How can open land become a place of confinement?

The account emphasises that Allah does not need guards, iron gates or chains. The earth, atmosphere and every direction belong to His creation and obey His command. A people can therefore be unable to escape even where no visible barrier surrounds them.

Reports describe them travelling through the day only to find themselves at the starting place by evening. Others describe the same result after earnest travel through the night. Their freedom to walk did not amount to freedom to reach the goal they had rejected.

The reported dimensions vary. Muqatil gives thirty farsakhs in length and nine in width. With a farsakh taken as three miles, that account gives ninety by twenty-seven miles. Another report gives thirty by eighteen miles. A gloss describes a space of seven parasangs, while another attributes roughly nine parasangs, described there as thirty miles, to Ibn 'Abbas.

These measurements are the differing accounts supplied, not a single surveyed map. The population is also reported as about six hundred thousand. The central point is the same in each version: a very large people remained confined in a relatively limited open area for forty years.

### Why does the punishment fit the refusal?

They had told Musa that they would sit where they were instead of joining the commanded struggle. The explanation sees their detention in that very region as a consequence proportionate to those words. They were denied the entry whose conditions they had refused.

This did not annul Allah's promise concerning the land. It meant that the particular generation rejecting the opportunity would not receive it as though it had obeyed. The later fulfilment came through the people who remained and the generation raised during the interval.

The historical reports differ over how completely the older generation passed away. One account says those aged twenty or above died during the forty years. A report from Ibn 'Abbas recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim mentions those above forty. Other summaries say the disobedient generation disappeared, while some allow survivors. These differences should not be hidden behind a single unsupported age threshold.

One account dates the forty years from 1440 to 1400 before the common era. Those are the dates of that narration's presentation, not an independently established chronology here. The verse itself supplies the duration.

### Were there still blessings in the wilderness?

Yes. Punishment did not mean the absence of all mercy. Musa and Harun remained with the people, along with the faithful Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yu'qina. The wilderness was a place of hardship for the rebels but also a setting of divine gifts through those righteous people.

Clouds shaded them from the sun and followed their movement. A stone provided water when Musa struck it with his staff, with twelve streams for their needs. Manna and quails supplied food. Another account describes a pillar or tower of light that enabled activity during the dark hours.

The account also places the revelation of the Torah, the establishment of its law and the erection of the Tabernacle of the Covenant within this period. Detention did not stop the work of guidance.

These gifts are explained through the barakah, blessing, associated with the prophets' presence. A further possibility is that the people repented after witnessing the consequences of their conduct, and that some of the gifts came in response to that repentance. The possibility is offered as such, not asserted as a fully narrated event.

### What happened to Musa and Harun?

Both died during the wandering according to the reports supplied. One account places Harun's death first, followed by Musa's after either six months or a year. Their presence in the same place as the punished people did not make their own standing identical to theirs. The account describes their circumstances as mercy for them, though chastisement for the others.

A hadith relates that, as death approached, Musa asked Allah to bring him within a stone's throw of the Holy Land. His request was granted. He did not personally lead the later conquest described in these accounts.

Yusha', also called Yuwsha' son of Nun, Joshua, was then appointed as a prophet to guide the Children of Israel. One gloss places his becoming a prophet sometime after his fortieth year. When the period of wandering ended, he led those remaining toward the land.

### How did the later conquest fulfil the promise?

The people advanced under Yusha' and laid siege to Jerusalem. The account describes victory on a Friday afternoon. As sunset approached, Yusha' feared the beginning of the Sabbath before the task was completed. He addressed the sun as something under command, just as he himself was under command, and asked Allah to hold its setting.

Allah delayed the sunset until the conquest was achieved. One account gives an hour. Ahmad bin Hanbal records in his Musnad a hadith stating that the sun was not held back for any human being except Joshua on his march toward the Holy House. The event is thus narrated as Allah's act in answer to the prophet, not as independent control of the sun by a creature.

The wealth found after entry is described as extraordinary. But the people were not entitled to keep the spoils in that dispensation. They gathered them for a fire to consume, and the fire would not take them. Yusha' concluded that something had been withheld.

He called the twelve tribal leaders to pledge. One man's hand remained attached to his, identifying the theft. The man brought out a golden cow's head whose eyes were precious stones and whose teeth were pearls. Once it was returned to the gathered spoils, the fire consumed them. Ibn Abi Hatim records this account from Ibn 'Abbas, and the discussion notes supporting evidence in the Sahih.

The account also recalls the instruction to enter the gate bowing and saying hittah, asking that sins be removed. Some instead entered dragging themselves along and substituted words about a seed in a hair. That later act of disobedience is mentioned in connection with the fuller account in Surah Al-Baqarah. Victory did not remove the obligation to obey the instructions attached to it.

### What changed in the generation raised in hardship?

The parents had feared that an invasion would bring defeat and leave their children as plunder. The explanation notices that those children, after growing up, became the generation that entered and conquered. Conditions feared as a threat to their future became a means of developing strength.

Desert life demanded effort, realism, simplicity and courage. The account contrasts this with the settled habits of the earlier community in Egypt. It treats difficult circumstances as capable of bringing out capacities that prolonged ease and dependence had left unused.

The point is not that suffering is pleasant or that every hardship automatically reforms everyone. It is the explanation of this generational change in the narrated event. A community weakened by its accustomed life can be confronted with circumstances through which a different kind of character is formed.

### How does the story challenge claims of automatic favour?

The people had seen Pharaoh and his soldiers overwhelmed, yet refused an enemy described as possessing less than a tenth of Egypt's former strength. Musa, a messenger to whom Allah spoke, was among them and had conveyed a promise of victory. Their refusal therefore exposed the distance between receiving a blessing and faithfully responding to it.

The account uses this history to challenge the claim that being Allah's children and beloved ones guarantees privilege. Disobedience has consequences even for a community with a great religious inheritance. The warning concerns that breach, while the prophets, faithful men and later generation remain distinguished from those responsible for it.

Musa's consolation completes the judgment. His compassion is recognised, but he is not asked to treat the sentence as wrong. Allah's promise was ultimately fulfilled, and the people's refusal was neither ignored nor made stronger than that promise.

### In short

- Refusal to enter brought forty years of wandering and exclusion, without the need for visible prison walls.
- Mercy continued through the prophets' presence, provision and guidance even within the period of punishment.
- The reports differ over some measurements, ages and chronology. Their shared account places the later entry under Joshua after Musa and Harun had died.
- The later conquest fulfilled Allah's promise, while the stories of the spoils and the gate show that victory did not cancel obedience.
- Religious inheritance is not immunity from consequences. The final consolation asks Musa to trust Allah's just judgment despite his sorrow.

27.text:
The story begins with two offerings and two different responses to Allah's judgment: "Abel’s offering was accepted while Cain’s was not." The rejected brother turns his disappointment into a threat against the accepted one. His brother answers by identifying the real issue: acceptance depends on devotion to Allah, not on removing someone else's blessing.

The passage follows the account of people who refused a commanded struggle. It now condemns the opposite error, unjust violence. Neither shrinking from a rightful obligation nor attacking an innocent person is faithfulness. The two stories distinguish obedience from both cowardice and aggression.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Relate to them in truth ˹O Prophet˺ the story of Adam’s two sons"** commands Muhammad ﷺ to convey the account faithfully. The immediate warning is directed toward envious wrongdoers among the People of the Book, while its instruction reaches the wider community. The majority identification is Adam's own sons, Habil, Abel, and Qabil, Cain, rather than two later descendants called sons of Adam in a general sense.

**"how each offered a sacrifice"** describes an offering made to seek nearness to Allah. Qurban means something through which nearness is sought. In religious usage it can mean a sacrificial offering. Here Habil offers from his flock and Qabil from his produce.

**"Abel’s offering was accepted while Cain’s was not."** distinguishes the outcome according to their inward condition. The accounts describe a heavenly fire consuming Habil's offering while leaving Qabil's untouched. The acceptance of one does not itself wrong the other.

**"So Cain threatened, “I will kill you!”"** shows envy becoming an intention to destroy. Instead of asking how to correct his own worship, he treats the accepted brother as the cause of his disgrace.

**"His brother replied, “Allah only accepts ˹the offering˺ of the sincerely devout"** points to taqwa, being mindful of Allah, obeying His commands and avoiding what He forbids. Ikhlas, sincerity, requires truthful speech, action and a heart directed toward Him. Habil does not answer anger with another threat. He states the principle through which his brother could seek reform.

### What occasion led to the offerings?

The reported background describes Adam and Hawwa', Eve, having twins, a boy and a girl, with each pregnancy. At the beginning of human life there were no unrelated families from which spouses could be found. A special ruling permitted marriage between a boy and a girl born in different pregnancies, while forbidding marriage between the twins of the same pregnancy.

Qabil wanted to marry his own twin sister, described as more beautiful than the sister born with Habil. Adam refused the demand under the ruling then given. To settle the dispute, he directed them to offer sacrifices, with acceptance identifying the one entitled to the marriage. His confidence was that Allah would confirm the rightful outcome, not that an offering could change a forbidden marriage into a permitted one.

Habil, who kept sheep and goats, presented a fine lamb. Qabil, a farmer, brought grain or green crops. Fire consumed the former offering and left the latter. The account from Ibn 'Abbas recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim is described as having a chain better than good. The special marriage arrangement belongs to the initial circumstances described and is not a permission concerning later sibling marriage.

A further gloss says Qabil concealed his envy until Adam left on pilgrimage, then confronted his brother. The Qur'anic passage itself centres the offering, threat and answer rather than narrating every surrounding detail.

### Why insist that the story be told in truth?

Truthful narration must not be altered through invention, misleading omissions or changes that distort its meaning. A small adjustment in wording can give a very different impression of an event. Religious history is therefore not material for decorative storytelling unconcerned with accuracy.

The same emphasis appears in the true account concerning 'Isa (Jesus) in Al 'Imran (3:62), the narrative of the youths in Al-Kahf (18:13), and the statement concerning 'Isa son of Maryam in Surah Maryam (19:34). Al-Haqq means the truth, and joining that word to these narratives underscores their purpose and reliability.

The Prophet ﷺ had not received human instruction in these ancient events. His truthful account is presented as evidence that he receives revelation. At the same time, the Qur'an's purpose is not to supply an uninterrupted chronicle. It selects the part of a history that conveys guidance, moral warning and the basis of religious duties.

### What is the cure for the envy shown here?

Habil directs Qabil away from attacking another person's favour and toward examining himself. The rejected offering calls for repentance and corrected conduct. Destroying the accepted brother would not make the rejected offering acceptable.

Whatever blessing a person receives comes from Allah. Envy that seeks to take it away becomes resistance to His giving. The person may be allowed to act within this world's test, but that temporary ability is not divine approval of the act.

The lesson concerns the envy displayed here, not a rule that every worldly deprivation proves a person's wickedness. Qabil's fault has been identified in the story: he is warned about sincerity and devotion, yet chooses hostility instead of reform.

### Why did the righteous fear for the acceptance of their deeds?

'Amir ibn 'Abdullah wept near death despite a life of worship because he did not know whether his deeds had been accepted. The verse's condition remained before him. Long activity in worship was not a reason to become careless about the heart with which it was offered.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said certainty that one deed had been accepted would be worth more to him than a world turned to gold. Abu Ad-Darda', in a report recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim, valued the acceptance of a single salah, prayer, above all worldly possessions.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz counselled someone by letter to hold fast to taqwa, connecting acceptance, mercy and reward with it. He observed that many urge it upon others while few practise it. Al-Murtada similarly taught that a deed accepted through taqwa cannot be dismissed as insignificant, however small it seems.

These examples turn the verse toward self-examination. The proper response is not to count one's deeds proudly or resent another's acceptance, but to seek sincerity in what one offers.

### In short

- The true account warns against envy, injustice and the attempt to destroy another person's blessing.
- The two offerings are distinguished by sincerity and taqwa, not merely by their outward presentation.
- Habil answers the threat with a principle calling his brother to reform himself.
- Truthful historical narration requires care, while the Qur'an selects events for guidance rather than entertainment.
- Even a small accepted deed is precious. Concern for acceptance should produce humility, not rivalry.

28.text:
Habil, Abel, refuses to turn his brother's threat into a mutual contest of murder: "If you raise your hand to kill me, I will not raise mine to kill you". His reason is fear of Allah, not lack of strength. He will not escape another person's wrongdoing by taking the same wrongdoing upon himself.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you raise your hand to kill me"** acknowledges the threat directly. Habil knows that Qabil, Cain, intends to kill him without right. His reply does not pretend the danger is imaginary.

**"I will not raise mine to kill you"** rejects answering the threatened evil with the same evil. He chooses patience rather than becoming a willing participant in wrongful bloodshed. One gloss explicitly supplies the qualification of killing wrongfully in both halves of the statement.

**"because I fear Allah—the Lord of all worlds"** gives the controlling reason. Allah is Lord over every created being, and His judgment matters more to Habil than prevailing over his brother. Fear restrains the act even where physical strength might make it possible.

### Was Habil simply unable to defend himself?

'Abdullah bin 'Amr says that Habil was the stronger brother. What held back his hand was fear of Allah. The account therefore presents moral restraint, not mere helplessness disguised as virtue.

Habil's accepted offering had already shown his devotion. The threat now tests whether that devotion governs his response under danger. He refuses to become like the person threatening him and chooses endurance rather than murderous rivalry.

### Why does intention matter in mutual violence?

A hadith in the Two Sahihs says that when two Muslims confront one another with swords, both the killer and the one killed face the Fire. Asked why the victim shared the warning, the Prophet ﷺ explained that he too had intended to kill his opponent.

The warning concerns two willing participants intent on one another's destruction. It does not erase the distinction between an innocent victim and an aggressor. Habil preserves that distinction by refusing the murderous intention his brother embraces.

One explanation draws a strong practical lesson for conflict among Muslims: refusing retaliatory killing can stop the sequence of attack and counterattack through which a whole society is drawn into bloodshed. It applies Habil's example even to the threat of assassination. Another gloss focuses specifically on refusing wrongful killing. These emphases should be kept visible rather than expanded into a complete ruling on every circumstance of self-defence.

### How was this example recalled during civil turmoil?

Ahmad records Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas speaking at the beginning of the calamity surrounding 'Uthman. He testified that the Prophet ﷺ had warned of fitnah, a time of trial and civil disorder. In it, remaining seated was better than standing, standing better than walking, and walking better than rushing into the conflict.

When asked about a person entering one's home and reaching out to kill, the Prophet ﷺ directed the questioner toward the example of the righteous son of Adam. The report teaches withdrawal from the murderous turmoil being described rather than eagerness to become one of its actors.

At-Tirmidhi records the report and calls it hasan, good. He also notes related reports from Abu Musa and Abu Waqid, as well as Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Bakr, Khabbab bin Al-Aratt and Abu Hurayrah. Their mention locates the warning within transmitted counsel concerning fitnah.

### In short

- Habil rejects wrongful killing because he fears Allah, not because he lacks strength.
- The intention to kill matters: two willing murderers do not become morally different merely because only one succeeds.
- His example is invoked in counsel against joining civil bloodshed and escalating revenge.
- The explanations supplied concern wrongful violence and fitnah, not a complete treatment of every self-defence question.

29.text:
Habil, Abel, tells his brother where the responsibility will lie if the threat is carried out: "I want to let you bear your sin against me along with your other sins". He will not join in the wrongful intention. Qabil, Cain, must answer for the crime he chooses and the sins already upon him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"I want to let you bear your sin against me along with your other sins"** is principally explained as the sin of murdering Habil added to Qabil's earlier wrongdoing. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi and Qatadah give that sense, recorded by Ibn Jarir. The expression does not require treating the innocent brother as having committed the murder.

**"then you will be one of those destined to the Fire."** warns of the consequence of unjust killing before the deed is carried out. The warning concerns accountability before Allah, not simply an earthly struggle between two brothers.

**"And that is the reward of the wrongdoers.”"** identifies the Fire as the recompense of those who transgress. One explanation reads this closing statement as Allah's declaration confirming the warning. The term wrongdoers describes people who cross His limits.

### What choice is Habil making?

He does not want to take on the crime himself by killing his brother. His words express the decision to remain free of the wrongful bloodshed Qabil is planning. If Qabil persists, the responsibility for that act will belong to him.

The principal explanation therefore connects the sin against Habil with his being killed, alongside the murderer's existing sins. Another brief gloss joins the language of the sin against the victim and the guilt of shedding his blood. These forms all centre the responsibility created by the aggressor's own act.

A further explanation develops the contrast between mutual violence and patience. Where both intend destruction, both incur guilt. Where one remains patient and prayerful, the aggressor carries the burden while the victim avoids the retaliatory sin he might otherwise have committed. That is an additional moral explanation of the contrast, not a reason to replace the principal gloss with an unrestricted transfer of all personal sins.

### Why speak about the Hereafter at this moment?

The full reward of deeds belongs to the next life, even though acceptance may sometimes be shown here, as it was through the offerings. Qabil's envy has fixed his attention on an immediate humiliation. Habil redirects him to the much greater consequence of acting upon it.

The accepted brother is described in the broader account as receiving forgiveness and Paradise, while the murderer loses in both lives. Outward success in an attack is therefore not the measure of who has truly gained. The warning still addresses Qabil before the murder, giving him reason to abandon it.

### In short

- The main explanation is that Qabil would carry the sin of murdering his brother in addition to his previous sins.
- Habil refuses to acquire the same guilt through wrongful retaliation.
- The warning places the threatened act before Allah's judgment and the reality of the Fire.
- A victim's patience and an aggressor's outward success must not be confused with moral defeat and victory.

30.text:
The warning does not stop Qabil, Cain, from persuading himself to commit the crime: "Yet Cain convinced himself to kill his brother". His soul makes the wrong seem acceptable, and he kills Habil, Abel. What he imagines as a solution to his grievance makes him a loser in this life and the next.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Yet Cain convinced himself to kill his brother"** describes an inward process of permission and persuasion. His evil-prompting self makes the act appear manageable or justified, despite the counsel he has heard. The murder is not presented as a conclusion forced upon him by his brother's conduct.

**"so he killed him"** marks the move from intention to action. Envy has passed through excuses into irreversible harm. The warning about Allah's judgment was heard before the deed, but Qabil chose not to submit to it.

**"becoming a loser"** concerns both worldly and final loss. Killing does not obtain divine acceptance or remove the guilt of the rejected response. It brings punishment and establishes an evil example whose effects extend beyond this one victim.

### What happened to his conscience?

Habil's words caused hesitation because Qabil could recognise that killing his brother had no just basis. Envy nevertheless remained. He supplied excuses until the resistance within him was silenced and the decision seemed defensible to himself.

The moral explanation treats this questioning of conscience as part of the test Allah places before a person. Success lies in responding honestly to the warning, not in finding language that allows the intended evil to proceed. Rationalising a deed does not change its standing before Allah.

A blessing given to another person remains Allah's gift. Trying to erase it through violence is not a way of correcting an injustice done to oneself. The temporary freedom to act in this world must not be mistaken for approval of the act.

### What do the reports say about the murder?

The narrated details describe Qabil not knowing how to kill. One report, recorded by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, says Shaytan demonstrated with an animal and stones after Qabil tried twisting his brother's neck. Qabil then imitated the act against Habil.

Another report, through 'Abdullah bin Wahb from 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam from his father, describes Shaytan directly instructing him to use a stone. Ibn Abi Hatim records it. These are reported details attached to the verse, not details stated in the verse itself or supplied with a new authenticity grade here.

That account continues with Shaytan telling Hawwa', Eve, what had happened. She asks what killing means and learns that Habil will no longer eat, drink or move. She weeps, and Adam repeatedly asks what is wrong. The report ends with a saying about the women inheriting weeping while Adam and his sons are apart from that practice. The statement is preserved as part of that narration, not turned into a general command about grief or an independently established description of all men and women.

### How can one murder create a continuing burden?

Ahmad records 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud reporting the Prophet ﷺ that every unjust killing leaves a share of responsibility upon Adam's first murderous son, because he was the first to establish the practice. The hadith is also recorded by the group of collectors mentioned in the account except Abu Dawud.

Ibn Jarir records 'Abdullah bin 'Amr expressing the same consequence: Qabil carries a burden from the bloodshed that follows his precedent until the Resurrection. This does not reduce the responsibility of later murderers. Their imitation is still their own choice and their own sin.

A person's loss can therefore extend beyond what he immediately sees. The act that creates a pattern of evil carries consequences beyond its first occasion. Here the evil precedent is added to the murder of his own brother.

### In short

- Qabil's soul made wrongful killing seem acceptable after he had already heard clear warning.
- Silencing conscience with excuses is failure in the test, not a change in the moral character of the deed.
- The reported details of Shaytan's involvement remain distinguished from the verse's own concise account.
- The first murderer bears a continuing share from the precedent he established, without relieving later killers of their guilt.

31.text:
After the murder, Qabil, Cain, cannot even resolve what to do with his brother's body: "Then Allah sent a crow digging ˹a grave˺ in the ground ˹for a dead crow˺". He learns burial by watching a bird. His attempt to overpower another person ends in humiliation at his own ignorance and regret over what he has brought upon himself.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then Allah sent a crow digging ˹a grave˺ in the ground ˹for a dead crow˺"** describes the lesson Allah placed before him. The bird scratches and turns the earth, using its beak and feet, and covers a dead bird with soil.

**"in order to show him how to bury the corpse of his brother."** The action demonstrates how to conceal and cover Habil's body. Some glosses emphasise the exposed condition of the corpse. Qabil had not known how to bury it, and the demonstration supplies that missing knowledge.

**"He cried, “Alas! Have I ˹even˺ failed to be like this crow and bury the corpse of my brother?”"** expresses shame at falling below a bird in this practical task. The brother he chose to kill has become a responsibility he does not know how to discharge.

**"So he became regretful"** describes the sorrow that follows his loss. Al-Hasan Al-Basri explains it as Allah making him feel regret after the ruin he had earned. Other glosses identify the immediate object of the regret more narrowly, as his inability to cover the body or his having carried it around.

### What did he see the crow do?

As-Suddi reports from the Companions that Qabil first left the body on the ground without knowing how to bury it. Allah sent two crows, which fought until one killed the other. The surviving bird dug and covered the dead one, showing the action Qabil needed to perform.

'Ali bin Abi Talhah reports from Ibn 'Abbas a version in which a crow comes to another crow's body and covers it with soil. That version does not require the preceding fight. Both accounts explain the same teaching through the burial of a bird.

Another gloss says Habil was the first of Adam's children to die on earth and that Qabil carried him on his back before learning what to do. After observing the crow, he dug a hole and covered his brother. These details explain the practical helplessness behind his cry.

### Does regret here necessarily mean repentance from murder?

Not every distress over consequences is the same as repentance for the wrong itself. One explanation expressly says he regretted being unable to cover the body, not the act of killing. Another says his remorse concerned the burden of carrying it.

The broader explanation describes the sorrow following his loss without specifying that his murder was forgiven. The verse therefore should not be made to certify a completed repentance beyond what the supplied accounts say. It shows the miserable end to the act he had persuaded himself was worthwhile.

### Why is the crow's lesson humiliating?

Qabil had acted as though his desire entitled him to remove his brother. He then discovers that a bird knows something about dealing with death that he does not. Human ability becomes no safeguard against disgrace when emotion governs action without restraint.

The lesson also turns back toward the earlier stage of intention. Had he put away the evil wish before acting, he would not have faced the shame of covering a body. Burying an evil intention is not the same as merely hiding evidence after a crime. The body may be hidden from sight, but the deed remains known to Allah.

### What punishment is described beyond this immediate regret?

A prophetic hadith warns that transgression and cutting family ties are especially liable to punishment hastened in this world as well as what remains in the Hereafter. Qabil's act combined both: he unjustly attacked a person and destroyed his own brother.

A further report through Mujahid says Qabil's lower leg became stuck to his thigh and that he lay neglected until dying in distress. This is presented as a transmitted account of his worldly misery, without adding a grade not supplied with it.

The warning does not depend on reproducing that condition in every later offender. The narrative already shows that the act intended to satisfy envy produced helplessness, shame and loss. It gives reason to stop an evil design before it becomes a deed whose effects cannot be undone by concealment.

### In short

- Allah taught burial through a crow, exposing the murderer's helplessness after his act of aggression.
- The reports differ over the birds' preceding fight and what Qabil did with the body before burial.
- His regret is not automatically a declaration of accepted repentance. Some explanations connect it specifically with the difficulty of covering the corpse.
- Transgression and broken family bonds bring grave consequences. An evil intention should be rejected before it becomes lasting harm.

32.text:
The killing of Adam's son leads into a solemn statement about the sanctity of every life: "and whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity." The opposite comparison is equally severe. Whoever unjustly kills one person attacks the principle by which every person is protected.

The verse states what Allah ordained for the Children of Israel, then rebukes those who continued transgressing after receiving clear guidance. Knowledge of a sacred law is not enough when conduct contradicts it. Respect for life must govern what people permit themselves to do.

### Phrase by phrase

**"That is why We ordained for the Children of Israel"** connects the ordinance with Qabil's wrongful killing of Habil, Cain and Abel. Allah legislated and made the command known to the Children of Israel. A brief explanation places it in the Torah.

**"that whoever takes a life"** concerns the killing of a human being without a valid justification. The wording gives the life of one person immense weight. An innocent person cannot be treated as expendable merely because the number killed is small.

**"unless as a punishment for murder or mischief in the land"** distinguishes wrongful killing from the legal exceptions named. The explanations include retribution for murder and punishment for grave corruption, such as armed attacks, waylaying, treason or waging war. Some classical glosses also name unbelief, idolatry or fornication within their discussion of corruption. These are explanations within a legal framework, not permission for an individual to declare another person guilty and attack them.

**"it will be as if they killed all of humanity"** expresses the violation of life's sanctity. The protection that applies to this person is not a different principle from the one protecting everyone else. Treating one protected life as lawful to destroy breaks that common protection.

**"and whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity."** includes refraining from killing someone whose life Allah has made sacred and recognising that prohibition. It also includes protecting a person from oppression. The lives of others are safe from a person who honours the principle rather than making arbitrary exceptions for personal desire.

**"˹Although˺ Our messengers already came to them with clear proofs"** recalls Al-Bayyinat, evident signs and proofs. The messengers brought commands, prohibitions and miracles. The people were not left without knowledge of what Allah required.

**"many of them still transgressed afterwards through the land"** condemns exceeding the limits despite that instruction. The explanations mention killing, disbelief, associating partners with Allah and opposition to the messengers. The verse says many, not every member of the community.

### How can one killing be compared with killing everyone?

Ibn 'Abbas explains the comparison through violating or protecting the sanctity of a soul. The issue is not that one body numerically becomes all bodies. It is that the killer disregards a protection shared by every innocent life.

In a report through 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, Ibn 'Abbas explains saving life as not killing a person whose blood Allah has forbidden. Mujahid similarly says that the lives of people are safe from someone who refrains from killing them. Sa'id bin Jubayr frames the same principle through the blood of a Muslim: regarding one such life as forbidden or permitted reflects the attitude taken toward protected life generally.

Another report from Mujahid explains the comparison through the gravity of punishment. Intentional murder of a believing soul brings the warning of the Fire, Allah's anger, curse and tremendous punishment, described as the same threatened consequence as if all had been killed. A brief gloss likewise connects wrongful premeditated killing with Hell and sparing a life with Paradise.

These explanations emphasise sanctity and accountability rather than turning the verse into a calculation that makes further crimes unimportant. The first killing is already a grave violation. No numerical argument can make it a small matter.

### How did 'Uthman apply the warning during the siege?

Abu Hurayrah relates entering upon 'Uthman while he was besieged and offering to fight in his defence. 'Uthman asked whether he wished to kill all the people, including him. When Abu Hurayrah said no, 'Uthman invoked the principle that killing one person was as killing all.

He then allowed Abu Hurayrah to leave, praying that he would receive reward and remain free of the burden. Abu Hurayrah withdrew without fighting. The report is transmitted through Abu Salih by Al-A'mash and others.

The incident shows how seriously 'Uthman treated the danger of bloodshed around him. It is an account of his response in that siege, not a complete ruling governing every case of lawful defence.

### Why does a single attack threaten the wider society?

Respect for life is built through a long history of people recognising one another's protection. Violence breaks more than the immediate victim's security. It gives others reason to fear that the same principle will no longer protect them either.

The explanation extends this social concern to attacks on honour and property as well as life. One such incident should not be dismissed as irrelevant to everyone else. It indicates a breach in the safety on which all depend.

Those who establish violence as a practice do grave harm to the community. Once the habit of mutual respect has been broken, restoring it can take a long time. Protecting one threatened person therefore upholds something whose benefit reaches beyond that person alone.

### What contradiction is exposed in the people's conduct?

The account recalls Jewish groups in Al-Madinah, including Banu Qurayzah, An-Nadir and Qaynuqa', joining their respective allies among Aws and Khazraj in the wars of the period of ignorance. Afterward they would ransom captives and pay compensation for those killed.

Their concern for ransom did not excuse their earlier participation in killing and expulsion. Surah Al-Baqarah rebukes accepting one part of the scripture while acting against another: the same covenant that concerned captives had forbidden shedding one another's blood and driving people from their homes (2:84-85).

This is the force of the final reproach here. Clear signs and inherited knowledge should have restrained transgression. Religious concern displayed after the damage cannot make deliberate disregard of the earlier prohibition into obedience.

### In short

- Unjustly killing one person violates the shared sanctity on which every protected life depends.
- Saving life includes refusing forbidden bloodshed and protecting people from oppression.
- The named legal exceptions are not a licence for private accusation or violence.
- A single attack harms the wider community's security, while protecting one person upholds a principle that benefits everyone.
- Clear guidance increases responsibility. Selective observance cannot excuse violating the very covenant one claims to honour.

33.text:
The protection of life in the preceding verse is followed by penalties for organised violence: "those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread mischief in the land". The passage concerns armed attacks that destroy public safety through killing, plunder and terror. It sets out grave legal consequences, then reminds offenders that earthly disgrace does not make the Hereafter disappear.

These are punishments administered through legal authority, not instructions for private vengeance. Their explanation requires distinctions between different offences, kinds of punishment and rights. The following verse also supplies an important exception for repentance before capture.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger"** describes muharabah, the forcible destruction of peace and security. The immediate victims are human beings, but the attackers openly challenge the law of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ through their armed power.

**"and spread mischief in the land"** includes terrorising travellers, killing and seizing property. The legal discussion concerns an armed group or an individual operating through force, not every ordinary theft or act of pickpocketing. The wider expression of corruption also includes attacks on people's honour and safety.

**"is death, crucifixion, cutting off their hands and feet on opposite sides, or exile from the land."** names four penalties. The word aw, or, is understood in two principal ways. One gives the ruler a choice appropriate to the case. The other assigns a particular punishment to each kind of offence. These positions must remain distinct.

**"This ˹penalty˺ is a disgrace for them in this world"** identifies the public humiliation and punishment attached to the crime. Violent power does not become honour merely because it frightens other people.

**"and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter"** adds the warning of the Fire. How this relates to repentance and to punishment as expiation is discussed through different explanations and hadith reports below.

### What does waging war mean here?

Harb is explained through taking or wresting away, and is set against salm, peace and security. Muharabah therefore concerns more than a fight between two individuals. It is the use of force to overturn public safety and impose the attackers' will upon others.

Muqatalah refers to fighting, whether or not it ends in death and whether or not looting accompanies it. Muharabah emphasises armed intimidation and the destruction of peace. The legal examples include highway robbery, violent rebellion and group attacks upon life, property and honour.

The distinction does not mean a single murder or theft is harmless. Such crimes have their own rules. Here the focus is the additional public danger created when offenders rely on armed strength to defy the law and make people unsafe.

The fighting is called war against Allah and His Messenger because an Islamic government is charged with enforcing their law. Force used to break that law openly challenges the authority it represents. The expression does not suggest that human weapons can physically harm Allah.

### Which events are connected with the revelation?

Al-Bukhari and Muslim record Anas bin Malik's account of eight men from 'Ukl who came to the Prophet ﷺ and pledged Islam. Other versions name 'Ukl or 'Uraynah, and another description calls them the 'Arniyyun. They became ill because Al-Madinah's conditions did not suit them.

The Prophet ﷺ sent them with a shepherd and camels, allowing them to drink the animals' milk and urine. The account says that they recovered, then killed the shepherd and drove off the camels. This is a narrated historical treatment, not medical advice to reproduce it.

They were pursued and captured. Muslim's wording describes the cutting of their hands and feet, the branding of their eyes with heated iron and their being left in the sun until they died. Another version places them in the Harrah area and says their request for water was refused.

A further narration from Anas describes them as cattle people rather than farmers. After going out with the herd, they killed the shepherd in al-Harrah and stole the animals. Its wording describes their eyes being gouged and their remaining in that condition until death. Qatadah says he had been told the verse concerned them. Muslim records this narration through Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and 'Abd al-A'la from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah.

Other accounts connect the ruling with attacks on people travelling to embrace Islam. One names Hilal Ibn 'Uwaymir's people, who killed travellers from Banu Kinanah and took their belongings. Another report from Ibn 'Abbas describes Abu Burdah Aslami breaking a peace agreement with the Prophet ﷺ by robbing people on their way to Madinah. These are differing reported settings, not details to merge into a single event without explanation.

### Is the ruling limited to those particular people?

'Ikrimah and Al-Hasan Al-Basri are reported by Ibn Jarir as connecting these verses with idolaters. They explain that repentance before capture protects those people from the specified penalty, but does not allow a Muslim who commits murder and violent corruption to erase liability simply by joining the unbelievers.

Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i also record an account from Ibn 'Abbas through 'Ikrimah concerning idolaters. The supplied wording of that report still speaks of liability for committed crimes. It should not be made to say that every private claim disappears through a change of religious affiliation.

The broader legal explanation treats the verse as general, covering whoever commits the described acts rather than only members of one tribe or religious group. The discussion of repentance in the next verse must then be read together with the distinction between public penalties and the rights of victims.

### Why distinguish three kinds of punishment?

In the Shariah, the revealed law, not every penalty belongs to the same category. A crime can wrong another person while also disobeying Allah. Both rights are involved, but the legal treatment depends on which is considered predominant.

Hudud, the plural of hadd, are fixed penalties in which Allah's right is treated as predominant. Qisas means proportionate retaliation, in which the injured person's right is predominant. Ta'zir refers to penalties whose particular form or measure is left to the relevant judicial or governing authority rather than fixed in the same way by revelation.

Confusing these categories leads to mistaken conclusions about pardon, discretion and proof. A power that a judge possesses in one category cannot simply be assumed in another.

For ta'zir, the authority considers the offence and the circumstances of place and time. The penalty can be lighter or heavier, and pardon may be appropriate. A government may also regulate judicial discretion within the bounds of the law rather than leave every decision entirely to an individual judge.

The fixed penalties are different. In the account given here, a ruler cannot arbitrarily increase, reduce or abolish a hadd once its conditions have been met. A change in time or place does not itself authorise rewriting it.

### Which fixed penalties are named?

The legal classification presented here lists five hudud: those concerning robbery, theft, unlawful sexual intercourse, false accusation of such intercourse, and drinking wine. The first four are described as expressly stated in the Qur'an. The fifth is explained through ijma, the consensus of the Companions, concerning wine.

This is the classification used in this legal discussion, not a reason to treat every kind of criminal penalty as one of these five. Qisas and ta'zir remain distinct categories.

Intercession is also treated differently. A relevant recommendation may be heard in a discretionary matter, but intervention to set aside an established hadd is prohibited. The Prophet ﷺ strongly forbade such intercession in Allah's fixed penalties.

Repentance can remove the sin before Allah without automatically cancelling the established worldly penalty. The exception for highway robbery, when repentance occurs before capture, is especially significant because it differs from the general rule stated here.

### How does strict punishment relate to strict proof?

The account joins the severity of hudud to exacting requirements for establishing the crime. If a required condition is missing, or a legally relevant doubt remains in the proof, the hadd is not applied. The principle is that doubt averts fixed penalties.

That does not necessarily end every legal consequence. A case that does not qualify for a hadd may still warrant a discretionary penalty under the authority's assessment. The absence of the fixed penalty and the absence of any proven wrongdoing are not identical propositions.

The discussion illustrates this with three trustworthy witnesses to unlawful intercourse where the required fourth witness is absent. It says the fixed penalty would not be imposed, while describing a discretionary corporal penalty as possible. This is the particular legal account supplied, not a complete treatment of all evidentiary and accusation rules.
