For the faithful there are glad tidings here. A person who does not turn back is reckoned with the friends, the people of love and faith. The order of the wording matters. Allah's love is affirmed first, then the servants' love, showing that a servant does not love until Allah loves him. Wasiti said that the Fire was nullified when Allah mentioned His love for them in the words describing a people whom He loves and who love Him.

### Which trial did this verse announce?

Most explanations treat the verse as a prophecy of the trial of apostasy and as good news for the group that would overcome it. Its germs had already spread toward the end of the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime. After his death it became an epidemic across the Arabian Peninsula.

Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab, the liar, was the first to claim prophethood alongside the Prophet ﷺ. He was bold enough to send the Prophet's ﷺ emissaries back with a threat that he would have killed them had the rule protecting envoys not forbidden it. The Prophet ﷺ did not live to wage jihad against him.

Aswad al-'Ansi, chief of the Mudhhaj tribe in Yaman, also announced prophethood. The Prophet ﷺ ordered his appointed governor of Yaman to fight him. He was killed, and the Prophet ﷺ died the day after that night. News of his death reached the Companions at the end of Rabi' al-Awwal.

Tulayhah ibn Khuwaylid, chief of Banu Asad, made a similar claim. Groups from these three tribes had turned away during the Prophet's ﷺ final illness. The news of his death released the storm. Across Arabia, seven tribes in various regions rose against the faith and its governing authority, withholding the zakah that Islamic law required them to pay to Abu Bakr As-Siddiq, the caliph of that time. Refusing the alms tax was not treated as a private opinion about wealth. It amounted to a refusal of the authority of the law itself.

### How did Abu Bakr respond?

Responsibility for the community fell on Abu Bakr at a moment of shock and rebellion together. 'A'ishah describes her father's grief after the Prophet's ﷺ death as something that would have crumbled lofty mountains into dust had it been laid upon them. Allah gave him patience and fortitude, and he prevailed.

Rebellion could be met only by force, but the situation was dangerous. He consulted the Companions, and none initially approved a hard line. The fear was that internal warfare would leave the young community exposed to outside powers.

Allah then strengthened his heart and settled him on jihad. He delivered an eloquent khutbah, a sermon, that opened the Companions' hearts to the same course. His words are reported as saying that whoever turns back after becoming Muslim and rejects the Prophet's ﷺ injunctions and the law of Islam must be fought.

He added that even if all jinn and human beings, and all the trees and rocks of the world, came against him and he had no comrade, he would still place his own neck on the stake and carry out that jihad alone. He then mounted his horse and began to move.

The Companions came forward, made Siddiq al-Akbar sit down again and quickly drew up a battle plan with fronts assigned and departure times set. Khalid ibn al-Walid was sent to Yamamah against Musaylimah, who had grown powerful in his area. The fighting was hard, but Musaylimah was ultimately killed at the hands of Wahshi, and his people repented and returned to Islam.

Khalid also went against Tulayhah ibn Khuwaylid, who escaped to another region. Allah later gave him the ability to repent, and he came back into Islam. Word that Aswad al-'Ansi was dead and that his followers had given up reached Madinah near the close of Rabi' al-Awwal, which was the first month of Abu Bakr's caliphate.

That was the first news of victory to reach him in those circumstances. From then on the Companions were given clearer victories on every front against the tribes that had refused zakah.

### Whom does the verse identify?

'Ali, Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah are reported as saying that the verse was revealed about Abu Bakr As-Siddiq. On that reading he was the first of the promised people who would rise to defend Islam at Allah's command.

That does not exclude others. Elders who pointed to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari or other Companions are not really in contradiction. Al-Hakim al-Naysaburi records in his Sahih that the Prophet ﷺ said of the promised people that they are people like him, pointing to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

The soundest and safest position is that all these honoured people are included, and with them every Muslim until the Day of Resurrection who confronts disbelief and apostasy according to the Qur'an's commands. The description is of qualities, not of a single closed group in one year.

The historical demonstration then confirms the promise of the verse that follows. The qualities listed were visibly present in Abu Bakr and the Companions with him: Allah's love for them, their love for Him, gentleness with Muslims and firmness against the enemies of faith, and jihad in Allah's way without fear of blame.

### What is the personal test in all this?

The most critical moment in a person's life is when sacrifice is required to remain resolutely on the path of Islam. Such occasions arise so that a person may clearly confirm or reject his faith.

Allah wants that proof not only in comfortable conditions but when a person must restrain his emotions or face danger to his life and property. Only by passing that test does he become entitled to be counted among Allah's faithful servants.

Proof at such a moment validates a person's earlier deeds. Failing it renders them valueless. The test in this world is a test of intention, and intention is proved by disregarding danger and taking the first step toward Allah. His help then comes.

Someone who does not prove his intention and does not take that step is a transgressor in Allah's sight and cannot expect help given without his own part. The verse's promise is therefore not a reason for passivity. It is a reason for confidence in Allah while doing what He has commanded.

### In short

- Islam is protected by Allah. Apostasy by some people does not endanger the religion, and He raises others in their place.
- The replacement people love Allah and are loved by Him, and that love is pursued by following the Sunnah in every part of life.
- They are gentle with believers and firm against the enemies of faith, and their loyalty is for Allah rather than for personal rights.
- They strive without fearing blame, including blame from their own people, and they do not humiliate themselves by seeking trials they cannot bear.
- The trial of apostasy after the Prophet's ﷺ death, and Abu Bakr's response to it, are reported as the fulfilment of this promise, which also extends to every later Muslim who confronts disbelief.

55.text:
After forbidding one kind of alliance, the verse names the alliance that is real: "Your only guardians are Allah, His Messenger, and fellow believers". Every other bond is perishable. Loyalty to the Messenger ﷺ is not separate from loyalty to Allah, and the believers described here are marked by prayer, alms and humility.

The positive statement answers the preceding prohibition. A person is not left with a rule about what to avoid. He is told where genuine protection and companionship are found.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Your only guardians are Allah, His Messenger"** identifies the real friend, protector and guide of a Muslim in every condition. Allah alone can be that friend at all times. Fidelity to the Prophet ﷺ is connected with Allah and not separated from Him.

**"and fellow believers"** adds the sincere companions of a believer. One explanation describes this as the protection, help and intimate companionship available to a believer, in contrast to what was forbidden earlier.

**"who establish prayer and pay alms-tax"** describes them by two obligations. They fulfil salah punctually, observing its etiquettes and conditions, and give zakah from their wealth. Prayer is among the most important pillars of Islam because it worships Allah alone without partners, while zakah is the right of other people and help extended to the needy and poor.

**"with humility"** translates the word for bowing. Its interpretation is discussed below, and the difference matters for understanding the character of these guardians.

### What does the final word mean?

Some leading explanations take it as the technical bowing that is a pillar of prayer. On that reading the phrase follows the mention of prayer in order to distinguish Muslim prayer from the prayer of others, since Jews and Christians also pray but their prayer has no bowing of that kind.

Most explanations instead take the word in its lexical sense of bowing as modesty and humility. Abu Hayyan in Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit and Al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf adopt that meaning, and Tafsir Mazhari and Tafsir Bayan al-Qur'an follow it. These people do not become proud of their good deeds. Their natural disposition is modesty.

A third discussion rejects a literal reading in which alms are handed over during the bowing of prayer. It observes that, if that were the meaning, giving alms while bowing would be the best way to give them, and no scholar from whom rulings are taken says so. It therefore explains the phrase as attending prayer in congregation in the mosques and spending in charity on the various needs of Muslims.

Another gloss reads it as humility or as performing voluntary prayers. The readings are not mutually exclusive in their moral point: the guardians described are people of regular worship who are not arrogant about it.

### What is reported about 'Abdullah Ibn Salam?

When 'Abdullah Ibn Salam said that his own people had shunned him, this verse was revealed. Another account names him and his companions, including Asad, Usayd and Tha'labah Ibn Qays, and describes them as shunned by the Jews.

The context explains the comfort in the wording. Someone cut off from his former community is told where his real protection lies. The believers named in the explanation include Abu Bakr and his companions, described as establishing the five daily prayers, giving the poor due from their wealth and bowing in congregation with the Prophet ﷺ.

### What is reported about 'Ali and the ring?

Some narrations say this sentence was revealed about 'Ali. He is described as praying, and when a needy person asked him for something while he was bowing, he took a ring from his finger and passed it to him rather than delaying until the prayer ended.

That eagerness toward good is described as pleasing to Allah and as being praised by this wording. The chain of authority for the narration is a debated matter among scholars and hadith specialists, and the material records that debate rather than settling it silently.

Even if the narration is accepted, its meaning is not that guardianship belongs to one person alone. It shows that those deserving the close friendship of Muslims are ordinary Muslims who fulfil prayer and zakah particularly and regularly, and that 'Ali is especially deserving among them.

Two prophetic reports support that standing. One says that whoever counts the Prophet ﷺ as a friend should count 'Ali as a friend, recorded by Ahmad. Another asks Allah to befriend whoever befriends him and to treat as an enemy whoever shows him enmity.

The explanation suggests he may have been given this honour because a future trial was unveiled to him, and he knew that people would nurse enmity toward him and even rise in rebellion, as happened with the Khawarij.

### Does the wording apply only to him?

No. Even if the verse is connected with that event, its wording is general. It includes all the Companions and all Muslims, and is not a specific command about one individual.

When Imam Baqar was asked whether the words about the believers in this verse mean 'Ali, he answered that 'Ali too is included under the believers and falls within the verse's scope. That answer preserves his honour without narrowing the text.

The point matters for how the verse is used. It establishes where a believer's loyalty belongs, not a restriction of guardianship to a single person.

### What does an inward reading add?

Abu Sa'id Khurraz describes how Allah takes a servant as a friend. He opens for him the door of remembrance. When the servant takes pleasure in remembrance, He opens the door of nearness, raises him to the sitting place of intimacy and seats him on the throne of tawhid, affirming Allah's oneness.

The veils are then lifted from him. He is placed in the house of being alone with Allah, and majesty and tremendousness are disclosed to him. When the servant's sight falls upon that majesty, he remains without himself, becoming a servant in annihilation, falling under Allah's protection and rid of his soul's claims.

The first kindness is described as keeping the servant in remembrance, so that he turns from his own work to Allah's work, from remembering himself to remembering Allah, and from love of himself to love of Allah. Once he is at rest in that remembrance and love, Allah brings him near.

The marks of nearness are the sweetness of obedience, dislike of disobedience, withdrawal from people and pleasure in seclusion. The servant becomes a stranger to himself, one with Allah, consumed within himself, having reached his Patron.

The same passage carries a longing prayer of the Pir of the Tariqah, asking to be delivered from the trouble of Eve and Adam, freed from the bonds of existence and nonexistence, and to take ease with the Beloved in the sitting place of intimacy. It ends by asking how long there will be talk of Adam's attributes and creation, and of the world's time and eternity.

That inward language does not cancel the outward description of the verse. It explains what the guardianship of Allah feels like in a heart that has been turned away from everything else. Remembrance, obedience and humility are its visible marks.

### In short

- Real guardianship belongs to Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and sincere believers, not to alliances forbidden earlier.
- Those believers are marked by regular prayer, zakah and humility rather than pride in their deeds.
- The final word is read as ritual bowing, as modesty, or as congregational prayer and charitable spending.
- The reports about Ibn Salam's shunning and about 'Ali's ring are preserved with the debate over the latter's chain, and the wording remains general.
- The inward description of remembrance and nearness explains the character of a person whose loyalty is truly Allah's.

56.text:
The conclusion is short and decisive: "then it is certainly Allah’s party that will prevail." Whoever takes Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers as protectors joins a side that cannot be defeated. The promise is not conditional on numbers, resources or the strength of the opposing alliance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever allies themselves with Allah, His Messenger, and fellow believers,"** describes the choice set against the forbidden alliance. One explanation adds that this means seeking their help and support. Another describes it as accepting the allegiance of Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the faithful believers.

**"then it is certainly Allah’s party that will prevail"** states the outcome. The party of Allah is described as His soldiers, namely Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions, victorious over their enemies. Another explanation says that whoever affiliates with Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers will be helped and assisted, and that they are the victors because of that help.

The wording is explained as placing the party of Allah where an implied statement about them would stand, since they belong to His party and are His followers. The sense is that victory belongs to them because Allah supports them, not because of anything in their own strength.

### What else does the Qur'an say about this party?

A related passage records Allah's decree that He and His messengers will be victorious, and describes Allah as all powerful and almighty. It then says that no people who believe in Allah and the Last Day will be found befriending those who oppose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, even if those are their fathers, sons, brothers or kindred.

For such believers, faith has been written in their hearts and they have been strengthened with a proof from Allah Himself. They will be admitted to gardens beneath which rivers flow, dwelling there forever, with Allah pleased with them and they with Him. They are Allah's party, and it is His party that will be successful.

That passage joins the outward promise of victory with the inward condition of the heart. Loyalty to Allah is tested most sharply where family ties pull the other way. Success in this life and the next belongs to those who accept the allegiance described here.

### How was this fulfilled in history?

The events after these verses were revealed confirmed the statement. The Companions overcame the powers that threatened them. Internal revolts rose against Abu Bakr, and Allah gave him mastery over every one of them. The great powers of that age arrayed their threatening force against 'Umar al-Faruq, and Allah wiped them from the earth. The account adds that as long as these injunctions were dutifully observed by the caliphs and the Muslims after them, including refraining from close bonds of friendship with non-Muslims, they remained victorious in the struggle of life.

That is a historical claim about a particular period, not a formula guaranteeing success to any group that adopts the label. The condition attached to it is obedience, not merely identification.

### What kind of people prevail?

The description of the faithful here is inward as well as outward. If a person does not fulfil the requirements of faith after embracing it, he has turned away from the religion in Allah's sight. The truly faithful are those whose whole being is pervaded by faith until their relation with Allah reaches the level of love.

Fulfilling the objectives of Islam should be so dear to them that their hearts hold only sympathy and kindness toward their brothers in faith. Their powers and talents are never turned against other Muslims.

Islamic life is purposeful and therefore a life of struggle. A Muslim's mission is to convey Allah's religion to His servants, guiding people away from the path leading to the Fire and toward the path leading to Paradise. Carrying out that task brings difficulties and humiliation.

Two groups then emerge: those whose hearts are set on this world and those whose focus is the Hereafter, with a continuing struggle between them. The test is that a person relies completely on Allah in every difficulty, caring for no one except Allah, and continues his spiritual journey until the day he stands accountable.

Such people centre their attention on Allah. They are steadfast in prayer, give zakah and deal with others on the basis of mutual goodwill. Their bowing before Allah shows that there is no egoism or arrogance in their worldly affairs. They adopt humility and do what Allah desires on every occasion.

The account concludes that when people of this type gather in considerable numbers in any place, they are destined to become dominant in that region. Victory is described as the natural outcome of that character, not as a prize for whoever merely claims the name.

### In short

- Alliance with Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers places a person in the party that prevails.
- Victory comes from Allah's support rather than from numbers or resources.
- The related passage ties that success to refusing alliances that oppose faith, even with close relatives.
- Historical fulfilment is reported in the victories of Abu Bakr and 'Umar al-Faruq, conditioned on continued obedience.
- The prevailing people are marked by love of Allah, humility, prayer, alms and goodwill toward other Muslims.

57.text:
The earlier prohibition of intimate alliance is restated with its reason made explicit: "Do not seek the guardianship of those given the Scripture before you and the disbelievers who have made your faith a mockery and amusement." The identifying mark is not another person's religion as such. It is treating the faith of the believers as a joke.

The verse closes by tying this instruction to taqwa. Reverence for Allah is what makes a person unwilling to place his closest loyalty where his religion is ridiculed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Do not seek the guardianship of those given the Scripture before you"** addresses those who believe in Allah and follow His Messenger ﷺ. The guardianship meant here is close friendship, seeking their assistance and support, not ordinary fair dealing with them.

**"and the disbelievers who have made your faith a mockery and amusement."** adds the idolaters and other unbelievers. The wording is read in two ways in the recitation, one treating the word for disbelievers as governed by the preceding phrase and the other as a predicate. Both convey the same prohibition.

The meaning of the word here is explained as idolaters. Ibn Jarir records that in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud the phrase reads as those who commit shirk, associating partners with Allah. Another verse commands shunning the evil of idols (22:30), which shows how the category is identified.

**"And be mindful of Allah if you are ˹truly˺ believers"** joins the command to faith itself. Fear Allah and do not take the enemies of your religion as intimate friends, if you truly believe in the law and religion they mocked.

### Why are two groups named?

Abu Hayyan observes in al-Bahr al-Muhit that the People of the Book were already covered by the general word for disbelievers. Their separate mention is explained by something else. Although they were nearer to Islam than other unbelievers, experience showed that very few of them embraced it.

A survey of those who accepted Islam during and after the age of prophethood is said to show that most came from the common polytheists rather than from the People of the Book. The number from the latter group was much smaller.

The reason given is pride in belonging to a divine faith and scripture. That proud partisanship made acceptance of the truth harder for them, and mockery of Muslims was the attitude they displayed most. When mockery hardens into wickedness, worse things can follow, as the next verse illustrates.

This is an explanation of a historical pattern, not a claim about every individual in those communities. The verse's own test is conduct toward the faith, not ancestry.

### What was the reported occasion?

Ibn 'Abbas says that Rifa'ah ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Harith displayed faith in Islam while being hypocrites, and that some Muslim men showed affection toward them. This verse was revealed about that situation.

The concern is therefore practical. Close affection for people who privately opposed the faith gave them access to the community's confidence. The instruction protects the believers rather than expressing contempt for anyone's person.

### How does this relate to the earlier ruling?

The prohibition restates the instruction given earlier in the chapter, in verse 51, about intimate friendship. Scholars say the two rulings agree and that the later wording adds the reason of mockery. That ruling distinguished deep alliance from justice, kindness and fair dealing, and this verse repeats it with the additional reason of mockery.

A related verse forbids believers taking disbelievers as intimate allies in preference to believers, and warns that whoever does so will not be helped by Allah in any way, except where danger from them is genuinely feared. That exception concerns protecting oneself from harm, not adopting their loyalties or approving their ridicule.

The closing command to be mindful of Allah keeps the matter where it belongs. The issue is a person's reverence for his Lord, not merely social strategy.

### In short

- Intimate guardianship is forbidden with those who turn the faith into mockery, whether People of the Book or idolaters.
- The separate mention of the People of the Book is explained by their closeness to Islam and their historical reluctance to accept it.
- The reported occasion concerned hypocrites who received affection from some Muslims.
- Fear of genuine danger is recognised elsewhere, but it does not make ridicule of the faith a basis for loyalty.
- The command is grounded in taqwa rather than in hostility toward people as such.

58.text:
The mockery is given a concrete example: "When you call to prayer, they mock it in amusement." The adhan announces the greatest act of worship, and it is treated as a joke. The verse explains why: "This is because they are a people without understanding".

### Phrase by phrase

**"When you call to prayer"** refers to the adhan, the call to prayer, and the iqamah, the announcement that prayer is beginning. One explanation says the call is made through both.

**"they mock it in amusement."** They treat it as a joke and a falsehood. The prayer itself is also described as the object of their mockery, with laughing and jesting among themselves.

**"This is because they are a people without understanding"** gives the cause. They understand neither Allah's command nor His oneness nor His religion, and they do not grasp the meaning of worshipping Him or the sacred laws He has made. Their failure is not ignorance of shirk, associating partners with Allah, as a word. It is failure to say or grasp anything true about the worship of the One Allah. The earlier ruling in verse 51 named the alliance that is forbidden, and this verse shows the conduct that identifies it.

### What was said about the call to prayer?

Al-Kalbi relates that when the caller appointed by the Messenger ﷺ made the adhan and the Muslims stood to pray, some Jews mocked them with words wishing that they would never stand, never pray and never bow. That mockery is given as the occasion of the verse.

As-Suddi reports a man among the helpers of Madinah who, on hearing the caller testify that Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah, said that the liar should be burnt. One night his servant brought fire into the house while the family slept. A spark set the house alight and it burned down with the man and his family inside.

Tafsir Mazhari, referring to Ibn Abi Hatim, reports a similar account of a Christian in Madinah who used the same words whenever he heard that testimony, until the remark became the cause of his whole family burning to ashes. Another brief account describes a Jewish man poking fun at Bilal's call to prayer, and says Allah burned him.

These reports differ about the man's identity and community. They are preserved as differing accounts of the same warning rather than merged into one version. Their point is that contempt for the call to prayer is a serious matter, not that any individual may take punishment into his own hands.

Other explanations describe a different objection. Some heard the call, resented it and said that the Prophet ﷺ had innovated something unheard of among earlier nations. They argued that if there had been good in it, previous prophets would have had a better right to it, and asked where he had obtained this cry resembling the cry of camels, calling it an ugly sound.

The Qur'an answers that kind of contempt by asking who is better in speech than one who calls to his Lord, does right and says that he is among those who submit (41:33). The call to prayer is thus placed among the best of speech rather than among inventions to be scorned.

### Why is Satan connected with the call?

An agreed hadith describes Satan fleeing when the call to prayer is made, passing wind so that he will not hear it, returning when it ends, fleeing again at the iqamah and returning afterward to interfere with the worshipper's thoughts.

He is described as making a person remember this and that, things not previously on his mind, until the worshipper loses track of how much he has prayed. Whoever cannot remember is told to make two prostrations before the greeting of peace.

Az-Zuhri notes that Allah mentioned the adhan in His book. The hadith and the verse together show that the call is a real event in the spiritual life, resisted by those who hate it and disrupted even for the sincere.

### What kind of understanding is missing?

Qadi Thanaullah of Panipat explains in Tafsir Mazhari that Allah calls them devoid of understanding although their intelligence in worldly matters was well known. A person can be sharp in certain work while his mind does not operate at all in another direction.

The Qur'an describes people who know the outward matters of the present life while being heedless of the Hereafter (30:7). That is the deficiency named here. Technical cleverness and comprehension of worship are different capacities, and the second can be entirely absent in someone admired for the first.

### In short

- The adhan and iqamah announce the greatest act of worship, and mocking them exposes a lack of understanding.
- Reports differ over the identity of the man who cursed the caller, and the differing accounts are preserved.
- The objection that the call was an innovation is answered by the praise of one who calls to his Lord and does right.
- Satan is described as fleeing the call and returning to disturb the worshipper's attention.
- Worldly intelligence does not compensate for heedlessness of the Hereafter.

59.text:
The believers are told how to answer the contempt: "Do you resent us only because we believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before". The question exposes the emptiness of the objection. Nothing blameworthy is being alleged except faith itself.

The verse adds a second clause about most of the addressees being rebellious. Its grammatical connection is explained below, and the difference it makes is important.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book!"** directs the Messenger ﷺ to address those who mocked the religion from among the People of the Scripture. The reply is not left to impulse. It is given to him.

**"Do you resent us only because we believe in Allah"** asks whether they find any fault beyond belief in Allah alone, without partners. The wording implies that this is no ground for blame at all.

**"and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before"** includes the Qur'an and the earlier scriptures and messengers. The believers do not deny the previous revelations. They accept them all.

**"while most of you are rebellious?”"** is connected in one explanation to the statement of belief. The meaning is that the believers also hold that most of the addressees have rebelled and strayed from the straight path. Another reading treats it as completing the description of what is resented: their refusal of the faith is itself described as wickedness.

### What prompted this reply?

Ibn 'Abbas reports that a group of Jews asked the Messenger ﷺ which messengers he believed in. He answered that he believed in Allah, in what was revealed to them, in what was revealed to Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac) and Ya'qub (Jacob) and the tribes, in what Musa (Moses) and 'Isa (Jesus) received, and in what the prophets received from their Lord, making no distinction between any of them and submitting to Him (2:136).

When he mentioned 'Isa, they denied his prophethood. They then said that they knew of no adherents of any religion less fortunate in this world and the next, and no religion more evil than his. This verse was revealed in reply.

Another account describes the same exchange and adds that when 'Isa was mentioned they said they knew of no religion worse than his. The response turns their own words back on them, as the next verse develops.

### Is belief really a fault?

The Qur'an elsewhere describes a people whose sole fault was their faith in Allah, the Mighty One who deserves every praise (85:8). Another passage says that people could find no cause for resentment except that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ had enriched them from His bounty (9:74).

An agreed hadith asks what made Ibn Jamil refuse zakah, although he had been poor and Allah made him rich. The examples share one pattern: the objection is not based on any real defect in the faith but on resentment of a blessing.

That is what makes the question here so pointed. When the only alleged crime is belief, the accuser has nothing to accuse.

### Why does the verse say most rather than all?

The explanation notes that some among them remained believers in every condition. Before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ they followed the Torah and the Injil and believed in them. When he came and the Qur'an was revealed, they believed in him and followed its injunctions.

Saying most therefore excludes those people. It does not lump every member of a community into one moral verdict. The verse's charge is directed at rebelliousness, not at ancestry or at a whole people without exception.

### What method of invitation does this show?

The treatment of this passage notes a principle of da'wah, the call to the religion. When a charge had to be made against the very people being addressed, the wording shifted from direct accusation to a description of a comparable case.

That is explained as consideration for the addressee. Prophets did not speak in a way calculated to make people angry before they had heard the point. The reply here follows the same method: it asks a question rather than hurling an insult, and lets the answer convict the objection itself.

### In short

- The believers' only alleged fault is faith in Allah and in every revelation He sent.
- The reported occasion was a question about which messengers the Prophet ﷺ believed in, and the denial of 'Isa's prophethood.
- Similar passages show resentment of blessing rather than any real defect in the faith.
- Most, not all, are described as rebellious, which leaves room for those who believed.
- The reply is framed as a question, following a method of invitation that avoids needless provocation.

60.text:
The answer continues with a comparison: "Shall I inform you of those who deserve a worse punishment from Allah". The people described are those who earned Allah's curse and wrath, some of whom were transformed, and who worshipped false objects of devotion. Their rank is worse and their distance from the straight path greater.

The verse is a reply to a claim made against the believers, and its form is deliberate. The charge is presented as a description rather than a direct accusation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Shall I inform you of those who deserve a worse punishment from Allah"** answers their statement that they knew of no religious community more disfavoured than Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions. The question asks whether they want to know who really stands worse with Allah in recompense.

**"It is those who earned Allah’s condemnation and displeasure"** describes people expelled from His mercy and subjected to His anger, after which He is not pleased with them. One gloss explains the curse historically through the imposition of the capitation tax.

**"some being reduced to apes and pigs"** recalls the transformations mentioned in Al-Baqarah and later in Al-A'raf. One account places the transformation into apes in the time of Dawud (David) and that into swine in the time of 'Isa, after people ate from the table sent down from heaven.

**"and worshippers of false gods."** describes those who served taghut and became its servants. The term is explained as any being worshipped besides Allah with its own consent, and the glosses name Satan, idols and soothsayers.

**"These are far worse in rank and farther astray from the Right Way.”"** concludes the comparison. Their abode will be the Fire, and they are further from the path of truth. The wording of worse and further astray answers their claim that no religion was worse than the believers'.

### Does comparison imply that the believers were astray?

No. The explanation notes that the comparative does not mean the other party was less astray. It means that the People of the Scripture described here were far astray. A similar use of comparison appears where the dwellers of Paradise are said to have the best abode and the fairest place of repose on that Day.

The comparative is therefore a rhetorical answer to an insult, not a concession that the believers share the same road at a slightly better position.

### What did the Prophet ﷺ say about the transformed people?

Sufyan Ath-Thawri narrates that Ibn Mas'ud reported the Messenger ﷺ being asked whether the monkeys and pigs then existing were descendants of those transformed. He answered that Allah never destroyed a people by transformation and then gave them offspring or descendants, and that monkeys and pigs existed before that.

Muslim also records this. The answer closes a question about the present animals without denying the historical transformation described in the Qur'an. The two statements are kept distinct rather than merged.

The moral point of the transformation is explained elsewhere in this discussion. Delicate inner feelings such as modesty, breadth of mind and the desire for cleanliness act as guards within a person and restrain him from evil. When these are smothered, the last stage of decline follows.

A group that reaches that stage and is distanced from Allah's grace becomes a curse to itself and to others. Having drifted far from the right path of nature, it begins to live like animals. What restrains a person from his desires is his moral fibre, and when obstinacy and enmity dominate him, his capacity to think is suppressed and nothing remains to resist desire.

Such a person may look human while being inwardly no better than an animal. Someone of deep insight, it is said, can tell what animal is hidden inside the human exterior. This is the moral reading of the comparison, not a description of every individual in any community.

### Why is the charge put indirectly?

The explanation notes that the condition described actually applied to the addressees themselves, and the occasion called for charging them directly. The Qur'an instead turned direct address into a comparison.

That is presented as a distinctive method used by prophets in calling people to the religion: do not put things in a manner that makes the hearers angry before the point can reach them. The indirect form keeps the door open for reflection rather than provoking immediate defiance.

It also makes the argument harder to dodge. The listener is asked to judge a described case, and in judging it he judges himself.

### What does the reply establish about mockery?

Those who claim a monopoly of devotion on the basis of a self-made religion can develop such aversion to a call for pure faith that they lose all sense of proportion. They ridicule things treated as sacred by everyone.

Some people of Madinah did not hesitate to ridicule the adhan. Any relation with such people can be one of conveying the message, never of intimate friendship. Their lack of fear of Allah leads them to regard pure Muslims as criminals while insisting, despite their own crimes, that their dealings are entirely fair.

That insensitivity blunts the conscience where truth and falsehood are distinguished and prevents the state of affairs from being corrected. The verse's answer therefore does more than defend the believers. It identifies the real location of disgrace.

### In short

- The comparison answers the claim that no community was worse than the believers.
- The described people earned Allah's curse and wrath, some were transformed, and some worshipped false objects of devotion.
- The Prophet ﷺ denied that present monkeys and pigs descend from those transformed, while the historical transformation stands.
- The comparative does not imply the believers were astray to a lesser degree.
- The charge is put indirectly, following a method of invitation that avoids provoking anger before the point is heard.

61.text:
The verse exposes a pretence: "they say, “We believe.” But they are committed to disbelief when they enter and when they leave." What is said at the door is not what is carried in the heart. Allah knows what they hide, and He will deal with them according to reality rather than according to words.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When they come to you ˹believers˺ they say, “We believe.”"** describes people who present faith outwardly. One gloss identifies them as the lowly among the Jews, and another as the hypocrites among them. A further explanation says they professed belief in the Messenger's ﷺ traits and description as they found them in their own scripture.

**"But they are committed to disbelief when they enter and when they leave."** They come in with disbelief in their hearts and depart with the same. The profession changes nothing inward, and they leave as they arrived.

**"And Allah knows what they hide"** states that their concealment is not successful. Allah knows their secrets and what their hearts keep, even when they pretend otherwise before people. He will recompense them accordingly.

### Why does their hearing benefit them nothing?

Because they enter and leave in the same state, they do not benefit from the knowledge they hear, and advice and reminder do not move them. Listening becomes a formality rather than an opening toward change.

That is the practical danger of pretence. It is not only a lie told to others. It deadens the liar's own capacity to receive guidance, since the words he hears are never allowed to reach the place where decisions are made.

### What led some of them to this posture?

Certain Jews of Madinah were impressed by Islam and, seeing its increasing strength, did not want to incur its open enmity. In their hearts they remained steadfast in the religion of their forefathers, while their speech made a show of belief.

Such people forget that their dealing is not really with a human being but with Allah, who knows what is inside the heart. When He deals with anyone, it is on the basis of reality, not on the basis of words chosen to protect an interest.

The verse therefore answers a calculation. Managing appearances may work on people, and it may even appear prudent. It does not work on the One who knows the unseen and the seen, and who has more knowledge of the hypocrites than any of His creatures.

### In short

- The profession of belief is contradicted by the state in which they enter and leave.
- Pretence prevents the hearing of guidance from benefiting the person who makes it.
- The reported motive was impression of Islam combined with unwillingness to accept it.
- Allah knows what is hidden and deals with people according to reality, not words.

62.text:
The conduct behind the pretence is then described: "You see many of them racing towards sin, transgression, and consumption of forbidden gain." The verse does not speak of occasional lapses. It speaks of speed and eagerness, of people moving toward these things as though competing.

The conclusion is severe: "Evil indeed are their actions".

### Phrase by phrase

**"You see many of them"** addresses the Messenger ﷺ about what is visible. The word many is important, since it excludes the good people among them. The description is of a widespread condition, not of every individual.

**"racing towards sin"** describes competing in contraventions. The glosses include lying, calumny, enmity and idolatry. The racing image suggests that these are not reluctant acts but eagerly pursued ones.

**"transgression"** adds wrongdoing and violation against other people. Aggression and unlawful consumption are included within sin generally, but they are named separately to emphasise the ruin they bring.

**"and consumption of forbidden gain."** This is explained as devouring what is prohibited, including bribes, riba, interest, and unlawful payment received in return for changing legal rulings. People's property is consumed unjustly.

**"Evil indeed are their actions"** condemns what they used to do and the transgression they committed. The evil is horrible in itself, not merely unsuccessful.

### What does racing imply about habit?

Ruh al-Ma'ani is cited for the observation that describing these people as racing toward sin indicates a chronic condition. The evil deeds have become fixed habits, so ingrained that a person moves in that direction automatically, even without forming an intention.

A deed repeated many times becomes part of a person's inner make up, almost a skill or drive. After that there is no exertion or hesitation in doing it. That is the limit these people reached.

The same expression is used of good. Another passage describes people who race toward good deeds (3:114), including prophets and men of Allah. Habit therefore works in both directions. The question is which direction a person's repeated acts have trained him.

### What lesson is drawn for others?

The moral decline of a group is described so that people who know of it may take a lesson and keep away from such deeds and from the causes leading to them. The passage is not merely a description of other people.

The religion favoured by Allah is described as taqwa. A person should live in society uttering no sinful words, avoiding forbidden ways in his activities and behaving with complete fairness toward those with whom he deals.

Selfishness pulls a person toward worship of the world. He wants a life in which he is not troubled by distinguishing right from wrong and needs to consider only his own interests. The general run of the people described trod that path of self-centredness mindlessly.

### What made the condition worse?

It was the duty of the foremost among them to alert people to their wrongdoing and turn them away from it. Instead they reached a tacit understanding with the common people.

They disseminated a version of religion that guaranteed salvation and promised high status without requiring any change in actual living. They left current lives undisturbed and recited false stories of the community's supremacy, gave a religious colour to communal events and told people that repeating a number of ritual actions would build palaces for them in Paradise.

Before Allah, spreading such a religion is described as the most evil deed, because it deludes people into thinking that showy rites guarantee Paradise while no change of life is required. This failure of leadership is taken up in the next verse.

### In short

- Many, not all, are described, which leaves the good people among them outside the charge.
- Racing toward sin indicates habits so fixed that the person moves toward evil without deliberate intention.
- The same expression describes those who race toward good, showing that habit forms in either direction.
- Forbidden gain includes bribes, interest and payment for altering rulings.
- A religion that promises salvation without changing how a person lives is the most serious form of this corruption.

63.text:
The failure moves upward to those who should have stopped it: "Why do their rabbis and scholars not forbid them from saying what is sinful and consuming what is unlawful?" The question is not neutral. It is a rebuke, and the verse ends by calling their inaction evil.

Ibn Jarir records Ibn 'Abbas saying that no verse in the Qur'an carries a more severe admonition than this one. Ad-Dahhak described it as, in his view, the most frightening verse for religious leaders.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Why do their rabbis and scholars not forbid them"** names two groups. Rabbaniyyun are explained as men of Allah intensely devoted to worship and abstaining from worldly temptations, commonly called dervish, pir or shaykh, or as scholars holding positions of authority. Ahbar are the religious scholars and interpreters.

Another reading distinguishes them as scholars appointed and authorised by the government on one side and scholars generally on the other. On that reading the duty of stopping people from crime falls on officials and scholars together.

**"from saying what is sinful"** concerns utterance. The glosses describe sinful speech as calumny and lying, and one identifies it with idolatrous speech.

**"and consuming what is unlawful?"** concerns taking what is forbidden, explained as bribes and unlawful payment, including payment for changing legal rulings. The two named offences match those of the preceding verse.

**"Evil indeed is their inaction"** condemns the leaders' abstention from forbidding. In the report that 'Ali bin Abi Talhah gives from Ibn 'Abbas, this wording points to the rabbaniyyun, and their fault was abandoning the forbidding of evil.

### Why is the leaders' failing rated more gravely?

The two verses use different words for what is done. One term covers everything done, whether or not it is intended. Another applies specifically to what is done with intention and volition. A third adds that the act is repeated as a settled habit and considered purpose.

For the common people's evil, the verse uses the word indicating intentional action. For the leaders' failing, it uses the word indicating deliberate, repeated, purposeful conduct. The choice of terms marks a difference in gravity.

The hint drawn from this is that the leaders' attitude was false. They knew that their people would listen if they spoke and would probably abstain from evil. Yet greed for the offerings they received, or fear of losing their clients' confidence, kept their hearts from standing up for the truth.

The conclusion is stark. If a people fall into sin and their religious leaders know that an appeal would be heard, but do not act because of temptation, fear or apathy, their crime is graver than that of the actual criminals.

### When does the obligation apply?

The stern warning operates where the leaders are reasonably certain that their appeal will be heard and accepted. Where prevailing conditions or experience make it strongly likely that nobody will listen, or that speaking will bring harm, the obligation is described as falling away.

Even then, the better and higher conduct remains to continue the duty whether heard or opposed, without regard for blame or pain. That is the quality described in verse 54, of people striving in Allah's way who fear no blame from any blamer.

The wider rule is stated for all Muslims, not only leaders. Once a person knows something to be sinful or unlawful, he is bound to check it as far as he is able: with his hand, with his word, or at the least by dislike in his heart. That is subject to the same condition about the likelihood of being heard.

These details of the well known Qur'anic maxim, Al-Amr bil-Ma'ruf, commanding what is fair and forbidding what is wrong, are said to be drawn from authentic hadith. It keeps people on the path of obedience rather than leaving them to drift. By placing this responsibility on Muslims generally and on scholars and spiritual guides particularly, Islam is described as offering a priceless principle of peace, which could cleanse nation after nation of the evils afflicting them.

### How did the spiritual masters apply this insight?

Those most concerned with correcting deeds are described as the Sufis and men of Allah. From such Qur'anic statements they drew the principle that human deeds, good and bad, come from ingrained habits and traits that become a second nature. To change the deeds, they work on the habits.

Consider a person whose heart is filled with greed for worldly acquisition. From that greed he takes bribes, devours income from interest, and may go on to theft and robbery if given the opportunity. Rather than correcting each crime separately, the prescription given is the realisation that this world is mortal and that its luxuries are poisoned.

Similarly, someone suffering from excessive pride, arrogance or anger belittles and insults others and quarrels with friends and neighbours. The same prescription applies: keep the concern for the life to come and the fear of accountability before Allah actively in view, and those patterns die out.

The general principle is that ingrained traits tilted toward good produce good deeds on their own, and traits tilted toward evil produce evil deeds automatically. Total correction of behaviour therefore requires correction of the traits.

### What happens when a community abandons this duty?

As long as Muslims upheld this principle through the early and later centuries, they held a position of distinction in knowledge, deed, morals and character. When they neglected it and began treating the prevention of crime as the sole responsibility of government and its law enforcement agencies, the result became visible.

The description given is of a father, a mother and a whole family religiously observing and adhering to the Shariah, while their children and family circle are almost their reverse, thinking, feeling and acting differently. Personal observance alone did not carry the next generation.

That is why commanding good and forbidding wrong is stressed in the Qur'an and hadith as the surest method of collective reform in the Muslim ummah. It is identified as a unique distinction of this community, and contravening it is declared a grave sin and a certain cause of punishment.

A hadith says that when sins are committed among a people and someone living among them does not stop them, it is likely that Allah sends a punishment falling on all of them. This is cited in al-Bahr al-Muhit.

### Which reports illustrate the danger of silence?

Malik ibn Dinar relates that Allah commanded His angels to destroy a town. The angels noted that a devoted servant of His lived there, busy praying. The command came that he too should taste the punishment, because he never showed anger against people who openly disobeyed Allah and sinned, not even a sign of it on his face.

Another report concerns Yusha' ibn Nun, the Israelite prophet Joshua. Allah revealed to him that a hundred thousand of his people would be destroyed by punishment, forty thousand of them righteous and sixty thousand evil. He asked why the good would perish along with the evil.

The answer was that the good had friendly relations with the wicked, ate and drank with them and enjoyed life together, and never frowned upon people sinning and disobeying their Creator. Details of these narrations are given in al-Bahr al-Muhit.

These reports describe shared punishment reaching those who were personally upright but socially silent. They are warnings about the cost of indifference, not a claim that mere acquaintance with a sinner is itself a sin.

### What did 'Ali say about earlier communities?

Ibn Abi Hatim records Yahya bin Ya'mar reporting that 'Ali bin Abi Talib once gave a speech beginning with praise and thanks to Allah. He told the people that those before them were destroyed because they committed sins while the rabbaniyyun and ahbar did not forbid them from evil.

When those people persisted in sin, they were overcome by punishment. He therefore urged commanding good and forbidding evil before what struck them struck the listeners too.

He added that commanding good and forbidding evil does not reduce provision or shorten life. That statement answers a common fear, namely that speaking up costs a person his livelihood or safety.

Ahmad records Jarir reporting a saying of the Messenger ﷺ about a community in which sins are committed while the remaining members hold greater strength and power than the offenders and still do not restrain them. Allah will send punishment on such a people. Ahmad alone has this wording.

Abu Dawud records Jarir's account with a different formulation: whoever lives among people committing evil, and they do not stop him although able to do so, will find that Allah punishes them all before they die. Ibn Majah also records the hadith.

### In short

- The verse rebukes religious leaders and scholars for not forbidding sinful speech and unlawful gain.
- Ibn 'Abbas and Ad-Dahhak describe it as the severest admonition and the most frightening verse for such leaders.
- The differing words for action mark the leaders' failing as deliberate and habitual, and therefore graver.
- The duty binds all Muslims according to ability, and remains praiseworthy even when it is no longer obligatory because no one will listen.
- Reports of earlier communities warn that silence can bring shared punishment, while correction of ingrained habits is the way to change deeds.

64.text:
A blasphemous claim is quoted and answered: “Allah is tight-fisted.” May their fists be tied and they be condemned for what they said. The reply does not merely deny the statement. It affirms the opposite, that both of Allah's Hands are wide open and that He gives as He wills.

The verse then turns to the effect of revelation upon those who resent it, to the enmity placed among them and to their repeated attempts at war and corruption. Each statement answers something the claim implied.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Some among˺ the Jews said, “Allah is tight-fisted.”"** reports the words of particular people, not of every Jew. The statement is explained as meaning that Allah is a miser who does not spend from what He has, not that His Hand is literally bound.

**"May their fists be tied and they be condemned for what they said."** answers them in their own image. Their hands are described as restrained from good deeds and from spending in good causes, and they are cursed for the words they uttered.

**"Rather, He is open-handed, giving freely as He pleases."** affirms Allah's generosity. His favours are ample, His bounty unlimited and He owns the treasures of everything. The dual form of the word for hand is explained as indicating abundance, since the most a wealthy person can give freely is with both hands.

**"That which has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ from your Lord will only cause many of them to increase in wickedness and disbelief."** describes the effect of the Qur'an on those who reject it. The same revelation increases believers in faith, good works and beneficial knowledge.

**"We have stirred among them hostility and hatred until the Day of Judgment."** states that their hearts are never united. Their groups and sects remain opposed to one another.

**"Whenever they kindle the fire of war, Allah puts it out."** describes plots that fail and turn back on those who made them. One explanation says that whenever they unite to kill the Prophet ﷺ in disobedience, Allah causes them to split and oppose each other.

**"And they strive to spread corruption in the land. And Allah does not like corruptors"** names their persistent effort at mischief, described as preventing people from the Prophet ﷺ and calling to other than Allah. Allah's dislike of the corruptors means that He will punish them.

### What exactly did the claim assert?

'Ali bin Abi Talhah reports Ibn 'Abbas explaining that they did not mean a hand literally tied. They meant that Allah is a miser who does not spend from what He possesses, and Allah is far holier than what they attribute to Him. Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, As-Suddi and Ad-Dahhak are reported with the same explanation.

Another verse forbids tying the hand to the neck like a miser and stretching it to its utmost reach like a spendthrift, since both lead to blame and severe poverty (17:29). That wording describes stinginess through the image of a bound hand, which is why the phrase here is read as an accusation of miserliness.

The claim also included saying that Allah is poor while they are rich. 'Ikrimah reports that the verse was revealed about Finhas, one of the Jews, and the earlier statement of his that Allah is poor and we are rich is recalled, along with Abu Bakr striking him for it. Another account names Finhas Ibn 'Azura'.

A fuller report describes two people, Nabbash son of Qays and Finhas, chief of the Jewish tribe of Qaynuqa', uttering words of affront about Allah, with the opening verse revealed on that account. It is given in Al-Lubab from Ibn 'Abbas, narrated by Al-Tabarani and Abu Al-Shaykh. These differing identifications are preserved rather than merged.

### Why would people say such a thing?

One explanation places the words in a change of circumstances. The Jews of Madinah had been given wide means and wealth. When the Prophet ﷺ came and they heard the call of Islam, they remained unmoved, being more concerned with communal leadership and the offerings they received through their self-perpetuating customs.

As a consequence of that stance, their affluent condition was turned into material straitening and they faced poverty. Frustrated and off guard, they began to say that the divine treasure seemed to be running short or that Allah had chosen to be miserly. Another account describes their circumstances becoming straitened after their denial of the Prophet ﷺ, though they had been the wealthiest of people.

A further explanation adds a motive. When the Qur'an stressed spending in charity and giving a loan to Allah, they made that the object of ridicule, saying that God is a pauper whose subjects are rich and whose hands are empty these days. They knew well that Allah is above any shortage, so the words were aimed at the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an rather than at a literal claim about divine need.

On that reading the real argument was that he was not a true prophet and the Qur'an not a book from Allah, since a genuine revelation would have had different content. Such a claim shows an insensitivity to the spirit of religion rather than a reasoned objection.

Refusing the Qur'an's guidance was also not a simple refusal. It was effectively a claim that they already possessed salvation and needed no further guidance. A conceited mentality of that kind develops extreme egotism, and such people are unwilling to give up their ego even in ordinary dealings. The result is that society falls prey to mutual differences and enmity.

### What is the answer given?

The verse says that what they wished against Allah returns upon them. Their own hands are bound and they are cursed. The explanation adds that what Allah said occurred, describing them as miserly, envious, cowardly and greatly humiliated, and cites the statement that indignity has been put over them (3:112).

Another passage asks whether they have any share in dominion, in which case they would not give people even the slightest thing, and whether they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty, when He had already given the family of Ibrahim (Abraham) the Book and wisdom and a great kingdom. The reference is not numbered in the account and is therefore given without a citation.

The curse is explained in one gloss as punishment through the imposition of the capitation tax, and in another as punishment reaching them in the Hereafter and in this world in the form of disgrace.

### How is Allah's generosity described?

His bounty is unlimited and He owns the treasures of everything. Any good reaching His servants comes from Him alone, without partner. He has created what people need by night and day, while travelling and at home, in every situation.

Another passage says that He gave people of all that they asked for, and that if they tried to count Allah's blessings they could never do so, while man is an extreme wrongdoer and ungrateful. The statement is given without a verse number in the account.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal reports through 'Abdur-Razzaq from Ma'mar from Hammam bin Munabbih that Abu Hurayrah narrated the Messenger ﷺ saying that Allah's right Hand is perfectly full and that no amount of spending reduces what He has, though He spends by night and day. He asked how much Allah has spent since creating the heavens and the earth, and said that it has not decreased what is in His right Hand.

The same report describes His Throne as being over the water, and in His other Hand the hold by which He raises and lowers. It also gives Allah's words, spend and I will spend on you. The hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs.

Giving and withholding are both acts of wisdom. Allah is independent and free of need while being master of all means. He extends provision for whom He wills in His wisdom and narrows it for whom He wills in His wisdom, and no objection can be raised against that.

### Why does revelation increase some people in rejection?

The bounty given to the Prophet ﷺ is a calamity for his enemies. The more revelation increases believers in faith and knowledge, the more those disbelievers increase in envy toward him and his ummah, in exceeding ordained limits and in denial.

Two other verses make the same point. The Qur'an is described as a guide and healing for believers, while for those who disbelieve there is heaviness in their ears and blindness, and they are as though called from a distant place (41:44). Another says that Allah sends down in the Qur'an what is healing and mercy for believers, and that it increases wrongdoers in nothing but loss (17:82).

One explanation attributes the increase to envy, another to their disbelief in the revelation itself. Neither treats the Qur'an as the cause of rejection in the sense of compulsion. It is the response of a resentful heart to a truth it will not accept.

### What does the enmity among them mean?

Their various groups and sects remain in enmity and hatred because they do not agree upon the truth and because they opposed and denied the Messenger ﷺ. Every sect among them is opposed to the others, and the enmity is described as showing itself in killing and destruction.

The practical effect is explained as protection for the Muslims. Differences inside their own sects mean they would neither dare to wage open war nor succeed in a conspiracy. The failure of open war is described in the extinguishing of the fire of war, and the failure of sinister plotting in their running about the earth spreading mischief.

### What is the deeper disturbance they cause?

A prophet's call asks people to adopt the religion of obedience to Allah that everything else in the universe already follows. That is what keeps a peaceful balance in the world, and it is described as islah, setting things right.

Those who place obstacles in the way of the prophetic call therefore seek disturbance in Allah's world. Yet a person has freedom only over his own inner turmoil. Nobody has that right over another's fate, which is why the work of a messenger is to convey rather than to compel.

### In short

- The claim that Allah is stingy is explained as an accusation of miserliness, and particular speakers are named in differing reports.
- The answer affirms open-handed generosity, with giving and withholding both acts of wisdom.
- The words arose from lost wealth and lost leadership, and were aimed at discrediting the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an.
- Revelation increases the resentful in rejection while increasing believers in faith and knowledge.
- Enmity among their sects, the failure of their wars and their striving for corruption are described together with Allah's dislike of corrupters.

65.text:
The verse states what was withheld and what remains open: "We would have certainly absolved them of their sins and admitted them into the Gardens of Bliss." The condition is faith and taqwa. Had the People of the Book believed and guarded themselves, their past would have been wiped away and their end would have been delight.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Had the People of the Book only been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺"** sets the condition. Faith is explained as belief in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and mindfulness as avoiding the sins and prohibitions they had committed. One gloss describes believing in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an and repenting of the previous path.

**"We would have certainly absolved them of their sins"** promises removal of what they had done, even if those sins were many. Another explanation describes the dangers being removed from them and their objectives granted.

**"and admitted them into the Gardens of Bliss"** gives the end. The gardens are described as full of bliss in the Hereafter, with delights that never end.

### Why is this stated as a condition that was not met?

The admonition recalls that the people of the Torah and the Injil gained nothing from the direction those books gave or from what the honoured prophets taught. When worldly greed took hold, they set aside things that should never have been set aside, and ran into straitened circumstances in this world as well.

The verse then keeps the door open. If they turn to the ways of faith and godliness even now, Allah can forgive their past sins and admit them to gardens of bliss. The unfulfilled condition is a statement about their choice, not a closure of the offer.

### What does reverence for Allah do to a person?

The root of waywardness is described as reckless bravado. Once a person fears Allah, he immediately grasps the power coming from Him and that bravado vanishes. The same fear makes him understand what Allah's will is, and he accepts it there and then.

Impure impulses are then driven out. When a person makes himself wholly attentive to Allah, he becomes entitled to Allah's attention. Allah washes away his human weaknesses and, after his death, lodges him in the flourishing gardens of Paradise.

Psychological weaknesses are the evils that stop a person advancing toward Paradise, but with Allah's help they can be overcome and the goal of lasting bliss reached. That is the process this verse promises in summary form: belief, mindfulness, forgiveness and admission.

### In short

- Faith and taqwa are the stated condition for forgiveness and admission to the gardens of delight.
- The promise remains open to those who turn now, despite the earlier failure to benefit from guidance.
- Reverence for Allah removes bravado, clarifies His will and drives out impure impulses.
- Human weaknesses obstruct the way to Paradise, but divine help overcomes them.

66.text:
The promise is widened from the Hereafter to this life: "And had they observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to them from their Lord, they would have been overwhelmed with provisions from above and below." Obedience to revelation is connected with abundance rather than with loss.

The verse ends with a distinction that must not be flattened. Some among them are upright, while many do nothing but evil. Both statements are true of the same community.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And had they observed the Torah, the Gospel"** uses a word meaning to establish and make something stand upright, not merely to act in accordance with a book. Iqamah signifies carrying the teachings out fully and correctly, with no increase, decrease or shortcoming.

What is meant to stand straight must stand perfectly straight, established and not tilting. The explanation adds that this includes demonstrating the description of Muhammad ﷺ contained in those books, and implementing what is in them.

**"and what has been revealed to them from their Lord"** is read as the Qur'an revealed after them. Another reading takes it as setting out for others what Allah had already made plain to them in those two books. A third reading takes it as believing that every scripture and every messenger comes from their Lord.

**"they would have been overwhelmed with provisions from above and below."** describes provision descending from the sky and growing from the earth, that is rain from above and vegetation and fruit from beneath their feet. Above and beneath indicate sustenance available easily and constantly, pouring forth from every place.

A parallel verse says that if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful, Allah would have unlocked for them the blessings of sky and land (7:96).

**"Some among them are upright, yet many do nothing but evil"** distinguishes a moderate, just community from the majority. Their uprightness is described as implementing the Torah and believing in the Prophet ﷺ, and the evil of the many as concealing his description.

### Why is worldly provision promised here but not in the previous verse?

The earlier verse promised blessings in the Hereafter. This one extends the promise to worldly comfort as well. The reason suggested is the malpractice of altering and distorting scripture out of taste for the temporal and insatiable greed for money.

That greed was their main obstacle to obeying the Qur'an and the Prophet of Islam, despite clear signs of their truthfulness. They feared that becoming Muslim would end their leadership in the community and stop the offerings and gifts they received as religious high priests.

The promise removes that fear. If they truly believe and act righteously, nothing will be taken from their worldly wealth and comfort. It will instead be increased. The offer answers a specific anxiety rather than stating a general economic law.

### Is extended provision a rule for every believer?

No. The promise was made to the Jews present at the time of the Prophet ﷺ, who were its direct addressees. Those who accepted the message received these blessings in full, such as Najashi, the Negus, king of Abyssinia, that is Ethiopia, and 'Abdullah ibn Salam.

It does not follow that provision is always extended for faith and always narrowed for its absence. The purpose here is not to state a general rule but to make a promise to a particular group under particular conditions.

The general promise of a good and pure life is universal, but it may take the form of extended means or of means that are outwardly constricted. The blessed prophets and men of Allah did not all have extended sustenance at all times, yet they all had the purest of lives.

### Who are the upright among them?

The word used describes a moderate community on the middle course. The explanation identifies people who were first Jews or Christians and then believed in the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ and entered Islam.

One account names 'Abdullah Ibn Salam and his followers, the monk Bahira, the Negus with his followers, and Salman al-Farisi with his companions. Another names a just community implementing the Torah, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

Those described as evil are named in one account as Malik Ibn al-Sayf, Abu Yasir, Judayy Ibn Akhtab, Sa'id Ibn 'Amr and the two men called Ka'b, Ibn al-Ashraf and Ibn Asad, with their evil identified as concealing the description of Muhammad ﷺ. Naming individuals is part of the historical report and does not turn the verse into a verdict on every member of a community.

### Why did so few recognise the truth?

When a call to truth goes out, prominent people in the existing order feel disturbed. They fear that complying will jeopardise their economic interests and high positions. That attitude is described as narrow-mindedness.

They forget that what they fear has appeared only to test their entitlement to Allah's blessings. Worthiness is decided by receptiveness to the call, not by self-centred devices. Rejecting it in order to keep high status is itself the act that rules out meriting Allah's favour.

Communities carrying divine scriptures tend to form a self-made religion through additions and deletions. As years pass, its members grow so used to it that they take it for the genuine religion of Allah. When the plain and true religion is then presented, they find it unfamiliar and are disturbed by it.

That was the condition of Jews and Christians, and a large majority of them were not impressed by the truth of Islam. Only a few, such as the Negus, king of Abyssinia, and 'Abdullah ibn Salam, were already on the path of moderation and understood the truth immediately. They came forward as though they had already been moving in that direction and were simply joining the caravan of Muslims to continue their journey.

### Where does the middle course stand among the grades?

The explanation connects this community with the grades described elsewhere. Allah gave them the highest grade of the middle course, which is also given to this ummah, and above it stands the grade of those foremost in good deeds.

One passage describes the Book being given as an inheritance to chosen servants, of whom some wrong themselves, some follow a middle course and some are foremost in good deeds by Allah's permission, which is a great grace. They enter gardens of Eden, adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, wearing silk (35:32-33).

Two other passages are cited in the same connection. Among the people of Musa (Moses) there is a community leading with truth and establishing justice by it (7:159), and those among the followers of 'Isa (Jesus) who believed were given their due reward (57:27).

These references show that the upright group named here is part of a wider pattern in the scriptures. Upright minorities have existed within earlier communities, and their existence does not cancel the criticism of the majority.

### In short

- Establishing the Torah, the Gospel and the later revelation means carrying them out fully, without addition, subtraction or shortfall.
- Obedience is promised abundance from the sky and the earth, answering the fear that faith would cost them their livelihood.
- The promise was addressed to a particular group at a particular time, and is not a rule that every believer receives extended provision.
- Some among them were upright and believed, while many concealed the truth. Both statements stand together.
- Self-made religion makes the plain truth feel unfamiliar, which is why so few recognised it immediately.

67.text:
After the long account of hostility and distortion, the Messenger ﷺ is addressed directly: "O Messenger! Convey everything revealed to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not delivered His message." The command is complete, and so is the promise attached to it. Allah will protect him from the people.

The verse holds two things together. Nothing may be withheld because it is unwelcome or dangerous. Nothing need be feared from those who hate the message, because protection belongs to Allah rather than to guards.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O Messenger!"** addresses Allah's servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ by his title of office. The command is given to him as the one entrusted with revelation, and he fulfilled it in the best manner.

**"Convey everything revealed to you from your Lord."** One gloss lists what this included: speaking against their goddesses, denouncing their religion, fighting them and inviting people to Islam. Nothing was excluded because it was difficult or provocative.

**"If you do not, then you have not delivered His message."** makes the obligation indivisible. Ibn 'Abbas, in the report given by 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, explains that concealing even one revealed verse means the message has not been conveyed. A variant reading speaks of messages in the plural, and the explanation given is that concealing part of it is concealing all of it.

**"Allah will ˹certainly˺ protect you from the people."** promises protection, aid, support and victory over his enemies. He is told not to fear or grieve, since none of them will be able to touch him with harm. One gloss describes the protection as being from the Jews and others, and another as being from people who might try to kill him.

**"Indeed, Allah does not guide the people who disbelieve"** separates the Messenger's ﷺ duty from the outcome. He conveys, and Allah guides whom He wills.
