One explanation says He withholds that guidance from whoever is not suited to His religion, and another describes those not blessed with guidance as people who have no desire to be guided.

### Did the Prophet ﷺ conceal anything?

Al-Bukhari records 'A'ishah saying that whoever tells you Muhammad ﷺ hid any part of what Allah revealed to him is uttering a lie, and she cited this verse. Muslim collects it in the Book of Iman, and At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i collect it in the books of Qur'anic commentary in their Sunan.

Al-Bukhari gives the short form here and the full narration elsewhere in his book. In the Two Sahihs 'A'ishah also says that if Muhammad ﷺ had hidden anything of the Qur'an, he would have hidden the verse reproaching him for concealing in himself what Allah would bring to light and for fearing people when Allah had a better right to be feared. That reference is given without a number in the account and is therefore described rather than cited.

Al-Bukhari also records Az-Zuhri's summary of the arrangement: the message comes from Allah, its delivery belongs to the Messenger ﷺ, and submission to it belongs to us. Each party has a distinct role, and none of them may be transferred to another.

### How was the delivery publicly attested?

The ummah of Muhammad ﷺ bore witness that the message had reached them and that the trust had been discharged. He asked them for that witness at the largest gathering of his life, in his khutbah at the Farewell Hajj, where more than forty thousand Companions were present.

Muslim records Jabir bin 'Abdullah reporting the Messenger ﷺ saying on that day that the people would be asked about him, and asking what they would reply. They answered that they bore witness that he had conveyed, fulfilled and given sincere counsel. He kept raising his finger toward the sky and then pointing it at them, saying, O Allah, did I convey, twice.

That great khutbah is described as both a constitution for Islam and the parting will of a prophet more affectionate and caring than a father or mother. After his instructions he asked whether he had conveyed their religion to them. When the Companions confirmed it, he called on them to be witnesses.

He also told those present to carry his message to those absent. The absent include people then alive who were not in that gathering and those not yet born. The means of reaching them was the spread of knowledge of the religion, a duty discharged by the great efforts of the Companions and their successors.

### What effect did that charge have on the transmission of hadith?

Under the influence of that parting instruction, the Companions treated his words and deeds as a weighty trust from Allah. They took care that not one sentence spoken by him should remain unconveyed to his community, and this holds under normal conditions.

Where someone withheld a particular hadith for a special reason or compulsion, he made a point of narrating it before his death to at least some of those around him, so that the trust would not remain a burden on him. An example is reported about Mu'adh in the Sahih of Al-Bukhari, that he passed on a hadith while dying rather than meet his Lord having kept a trust to himself.

This explains why the verse matters for the whole tradition that follows it. The obligation of complete delivery did not end with the Prophet ﷺ. It shaped how his Companions understood narration itself.

### Why did the command need such emphasis?

The preceding sections had described at length the crookedness, obstinacy and plotting of Jews and Christians. Two effects on a human messenger were possible. He might feel disappointed or constrained, so that the work of conveying slowed or fell short somewhere.

Alternatively, if he devoted himself single-mindedly to his mission without regard for hostility, harm or injury, the worst hardships at the hands of his adversaries were likely. The verse answers both risks at once. He is commanded emphatically to convey everything revealed to him, all of it, without hesitation.

Whether someone likes or dislikes it, accepts or refuses it, is not to worry him in his mission. Along with the command comes the good news that those disbelievers will be unable to harm him, because Allah Himself will protect him.

### What did the Messenger ﷺ say about the weight of this charge?

Al-Hasan reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that when Allah sent him with the message he felt oppressed by it, because he knew some people would give him the lie. He was apprehensive of Quraysh, the Jews and the Christians, and this verse was revealed.

Another account through Al-Hasan describes the charge as appearing very frightening when he was given the duty of conveying Allah's message, since those around him were bound to falsify and oppose him. When the verse came down, he was at peace.

The fear named here is not doubt about the truth of the message. It is the natural apprehension of a person told to announce things that powerful people will hate, before any guarantee of protection has been given.

### How was he guarded before this verse?

Ahmad records 'A'ishah describing the Prophet ﷺ as vigilant one night while she was beside him. Asked what was the matter, he said he wished a righteous man from his Companions would guard him that night.

Suddenly they heard the clatter of arms. He asked who was there, and the newcomer answered that he was Sa'd bin Malik, that is Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas, and had come to guard him. 'A'ishah says the Prophet ﷺ then slept and she heard the sound of his sleep. The hadith is in the Two Sahihs.

Another narration begins with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ being vigilant one night after he came to Al-Madinah, that is after the Hijrah and after his marriage to 'A'ishah was consummated in the second year of the migration.

A further account through 'A'ishah says the Prophet ﷺ was guarded until this verse was revealed, after which he raised his head from the room and told the people to go away, since Allah would protect him. At-Tirmidhi records it and calls it gharib, singly transmitted. Ibn Jarir records it as well, and Al-Hakim in his Mustadrak says its chain is sahih, authentic, though the two leading collections did not record it.

Another report through 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas says the Messenger ﷺ used to be guarded, with Abu Talib sending men from Banu Hashim every day for that purpose until this verse was revealed. When his uncle then wanted to send protectors with him, he said that Allah had protected him from jinn and human beings.

A further narration names Sa'd and Hudhayfah coming together to keep watch, and describes the Prophet ﷺ sleeping so deeply that 'A'ishah heard his snoring, after which the verse came and he put his head out from the collar of his garment to tell the people they could leave.

### What changed after the revelation?

Reports say that before this verse some Companions used to stay around him for protection, in the city and on journeys. After its revelation he relieved them all, since no security arrangements were needed any longer. Allah had taken that responsibility Himself.

One account says that after the verse no one dared to harm the Prophet ﷺ during his efforts to spread Islam. It adds that casual injury received in jihad battles is not contrary to this. The promise concerns the completion of the mission, not the absence of every hardship in combat.

### Which occasion is reported for the revelation?

The reports differ. Some connect the verse with the night watch and the end of guarding, as described above. Others connect it with the general command to convey, including the difficult matters of denouncing false worship and inviting people to Islam.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri is also reported as saying that the verse was revealed on the day of Ghadir Khumm concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. That report is preserved here as one transmitted account of the occasion.

These differing reports do not change the command itself. Whether the immediate occasion was a particular announcement or the ending of the guard, the obligation stated is complete delivery of everything revealed, and the protection promised covers the one who delivers it.

### What does the verse teach a person who conveys the religion?

Arabian society at the time was not irreligious. It was founded on religion, and many people held positions of prominence and leadership in its name. High religious standing was a mark of social status and a source of pride.

The Prophet ﷺ nevertheless endured the worst opposition, because a self-made religion had taken the place of the real religion of Allah. Centuries of tradition had produced seats of power and centres of vested interest. A call for pure religion therefore felt like an attack on the status of those who held it, and they feared the destruction of the old order that gave them prominence.

That situation is hard on a preacher. Open religious activity becomes equivalent to a struggle against the established religious authorities of the day. If he makes no compromises, he expects severe reaction, ridicule, degradation, impoverishment, violent action and the loss of all support and assistance.

Two paths then appear. He can take worldly considerations into account, in which case successful communication of Allah's word becomes impossible. Or he can disregard those constraints, in which case Allah's promised help enables him to concentrate on the task.

The promise given is that if he devotes himself fully to conveying, divine help will be sufficient against whatever difficulties the addressed community creates. The one who carries Allah's will should simply trust in Allah.

Opposition is natural and must be faced, but its sphere is limited by Allah's law concerning the trial of human beings. It can never happen that opponents gain enough control to stop the work or prevent its completion. Achieving the goal of that work is Allah's plan, so it will be completed. Acceptance by those addressed is their own responsibility, and it takes effect only to the extent they desire it.

### How does the closing statement complete the argument?

Guidance is not the messenger's to produce. Two other verses are cited with this one: guidance is not upon him, but Allah guides whom He wills (2:272), and his duty is only to convey while the reckoning belongs to Allah (13:40).

That is why the verse can demand complete courage and complete honesty at the same time. The Messenger ﷺ is responsible for delivery, not for the outcome in other people's hearts. Refusing to guide those who disbelieve is a statement about their choice, and it releases him from measuring his success by their acceptance.

### In short

- Everything revealed must be conveyed, and concealing one verse means the message has not been delivered.
- 'A'ishah's reports and Az-Zuhri's summary establish that nothing was hidden and that each party has its own role.
- The Farewell Hajj gathering provides the public testimony of the community that he conveyed, fulfilled and advised sincerely.
- Before this verse he was guarded by Companions and by men sent from Banu Hashim. Afterward he dismissed the guards on the strength of Allah's protection.
- Reports differ on the immediate occasion, including one connecting it with Ghadir Khumm, while the command and the promise remain the same.
- Whoever conveys the religion faces vested interests and must trust Allah's help, since acceptance belongs to those addressed and guidance belongs to Allah.

68.text:
The People of the Book are told what their position actually rests on: “You have nothing to stand on unless you observe the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.” The claim to a religion is not established by ancestry, by possessing books or by spiritual reputation. It is established by acting on what those books require.

The verse then consoles the Messenger ﷺ. Revelation increases many of them in wickedness and disbelief, and that is not a reason for grief.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book!"** addresses Jews and Christians through the Messenger ﷺ. The instruction to say shows that the statement is to be delivered openly, not merely held.

**"You have nothing to stand on unless you observe the Torah, the Gospel"** means they have no real religion until they adhere to and implement those books. One gloss explains it as truly believing in what they contain, and another as having no basis in religion to rely upon.

**"and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.”"** is understood by the great majority, including the Companions and their successors, as the Qur'an. It was sent to the whole community invited to faith, including Jews and Christians, through the Prophet ﷺ.

The books they already hold command following Muhammad ﷺ and believing in his prophethood while adhering to his law. Observing the Torah and the Gospel therefore leads to the Qur'an rather than away from it. One gloss adds that what was revealed to him concerns all the scriptures given to all the messengers.

**"And your Lord’s revelation to you ˹O Prophet˺ will only cause many of them to increase in wickedness and disbelief."** repeats the effect described earlier in this chapter. Their disbelief and envy turn the blessing given to him into an increase of rebellion in them.

**"So do not grieve for the people who disbelieve"** consoles him. He is not to be saddened or taken aback by their disbelief, nor concerned with them if they refuse. One explanation adds that in the believers who follow him there is goodness enough.

### What would be wasted without obedience to the law?

They had been given high privileges. They were the descendants of prophets. They possessed the intellectual treasure of the Torah and the Injil. Many men of Allah among them had undergone severe spiritual exertion in searching for truth.

All of it depends on one binding condition, which is following the divine shariah. Without that, no superiority of lineage works, and neither intellectual excellence nor spiritual striving becomes a means of salvation. If they do not adhere, their achievements stand wasted.

### Does the same rule apply to Muslims?

The statement is read as crucial guidance for Muslims too. No way of the dervishes, no path of spiritual realisation, no repeated striving toward spiritual goals, no extra-sensory illumination and no visitation of inspiration becomes a source of spiritual achievement or salvation in Allah's sight without full adherence to the shariah.

Inward attainment is therefore not an alternative to the revealed law. It is a fruit of it. The verse's demand for implementation applies to whoever claims a religion, and the claim of inner experience does not excuse neglect of the commands.

### Why is the third item named at length?

The Torah and the Injil are named briefly, while the third is described as what has been revealed from your Lord. One explanation takes the longer wording as pointing to the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that he had been given the Qur'an and, along with it, other fields of knowledge like it.

He warned that in later times a sated man reclining on his couch would say that the Qur'an alone is enough for them, so that whatever they find halal in it they treat as halal and whatever they find haram in it they treat as haram. The answer given is that what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has declared unlawful is like what Allah has declared unlawful. Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and Ad-Darimi record the hadith.

On this reading the longer phrase indicates that following every injunction given in the Qur'an or given by the Prophet ﷺ is equally mandatory.

### How many kinds of ruling are included?

The discussion divides the rulings given to the ummah into three. First are those stated clearly in the Qur'an. Second are those not stated clearly in it but revealed to the Prophet ﷺ through a separate revelation that is not recited as scripture.

Third are commands he gave on the basis of his own ijtihad, fully deliberated judgment, and qiyas, analogical deduction, where no contrary guidance was subsequently revealed. Those also carry the force of a revealed injunction.

The Qur'an itself testifies to this arrangement by stating that he does not speak from himself, and that what he says is revealed to him. That passage is referred to without a verse number in the account, so no citation is added here.

All three kinds are obligatory to follow, and all fall within the phrase about what has been revealed from your Lord. The distinction matters because it explains why the verse does not simply name the Qur'an and stop there.

### How can three books be followed when some replace others?

The objection is obvious. The Injil replaced some injunctions of the Torah, and the Qur'an replaced many injunctions of both. How then can the sum of the three be acted upon?

The answer is that each incoming book changed certain rulings of the one before it, so following the later ruling is itself acting in accordance with both books. Both require that the replacement be followed. Acting on an abrogated ruling goes against the requirement of both.

Obedience to the earlier books is therefore not preserved by refusing the Qur'an. It is completed by it, since they themselves direct their readers to the messenger whose coming they announce.

### What does wishful thinking do to a community?

The Jewish community is described as thriving on stories of its own excellence and the supposed holiness of its elders, while not subjecting itself and its personal affairs to Allah's will. Wishful thinking convinced them of salvation before Allah, but that conviction had no value with Him because they were not ruled by His religion.

What carries weight with Allah is scrupulous obedience to His commandments and founding one's life on His religion. People given to false hopes react strongly when told that intentions and deeds carry weight rather than wishes. To them that call looks like the wrecking of every castle they had built in the air, and the imagined state of affairs becomes a trial.

Their self-centredness, hidden under showy devotion, then comes into the open. Instead of drawing divine nourishment from the call to truth, they are driven by it toward disbelief and arrogance. That is the mechanism behind the increase mentioned in this verse.

### In short

- Their standing depends on implementing the Torah, the Gospel and the revelation given to the Prophet ﷺ, not on lineage, learning or spiritual claims.
- The third item is understood as the Qur'an, and the longer wording is connected with the obligation of following what the Messenger ﷺ declared.
- Rulings stated in the Qur'an, revealed to him without recitation, and given through his deliberated judgment all bind the community.
- Following a later revealed ruling is obedience to the earlier books too, since they announce it.
- The Messenger ﷺ is consoled, because revelation increases the resentful in rejection while wishful thinking hardens them.

69.text:
Four communities are named together and one condition is stated: "whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve." The promise is wide, and its condition is precise. Lineage, homeland and communal name carry no weight beside it.

The explanation of this verse therefore has two parts. It establishes that distinctions of community do not save anyone by themselves, and it explains what belief in Allah actually requires after the final revelation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, the believers, Jews, Sabians and Christians"** addresses four traditional religious communities. The believers are the Muslims, the Jews were entrusted with the Torah, and the Christians were entrusted with the Injil and are known.

The Sabians are less clearly identified, since no community of that name exists today and scholarly opinion varies. Quoting Qatadah, one report describes them as people who worshipped angels, prayed in a direction other than the qiblah and recited the Zabur revealed to Dawud (David). The Qur'anic context is said to support this, because the four scriptures it names are the Torah, the Zabur, the Injil and the Qur'an, so the four groups here are the believers in those books.

Mujahid describes them as a group drawn from the Christians and the Magians who followed no particular religion. Another gloss calls them a Christian sect milder than other Christians, and a third treats them as a sect among the Jews. These differing identifications are preserved rather than settled by assertion. The Christians named include those of Najran as well as others.

**"whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good"** states the condition for each of them. Belief in the Last Day means belief in resurrection after death and in the Day of Judgment and reckoning.

Good action is not left undefined. The explanation says that deeds count as good only if they conform to the law of Muhammad ﷺ, after his being sent to all mankind and the jinn. Another gloss adds repentance from the previous path and doing right sincerely between a person and his Lord.

**"there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"** promises freedom from fear of what is coming and from sorrow over what was lost. One account describes believers in Musa (Moses) and in all the prophets and scriptures who die in that state. Other glosses say they will not fear when others fear, or will not grieve when death is slain and the Fire is closed.

### Where else does the Qur'an say this?

An almost identical statement appears in Al-Baqarah, promising such people their reward with their Lord, with no fear and no grief (2:62). Apart from a transposition of some words according to place, there is no difference between the two.

The repetition shows that this is not an isolated remark. It is a settled principle about who is acceptable to Allah.

### What does the principle establish?

Distinctions of lineage, homeland and nationality do not matter in Allah's sight. Anyone who takes complete obedience, faith and good deeds as his way of life, whatever he was before, will find himself acceptable to Allah, and his devotion will bring the best appreciation from his Creator.

That is why the verse can address four communities with one condition. It removes salvation from group membership and places it in belief and conduct.

### What does complete obedience mean after the Qur'an?

The explanation is explicit. Once the Qur'an had been revealed, obedience in the full sense is bound up with being a Muslim, because the past scriptures themselves contain instructions to that effect and the Qur'an was revealed for this purpose.

After the Qur'an and the appearance of the last of the prophets, it is not correct to follow the Torah, the Injil or the Zabur without believing in the Qur'an and having faith in the Prophet ﷺ. The verse therefore means that whoever from among these communities becomes a Muslim becomes deserving of salvation and reward in the Hereafter.

The doubt that naturally follows is answered at once. What happens to their past sins, disobedience, disbelief and plotting against Islam and Muslims? All past sins and shortcomings stand forgiven, and in the life to come they will have no fear and no grief.

### Why are Muslims mentioned when the aim is to invite others?

Someone might object that the occasion calls for mentioning only those who need persuading to enter Islam, since Muslims already stand where the verse points. The answer given is that this is a special mode of eloquence in the Qur'an.

It is compared with a law issued by the highest authority stating that it applies to everyone, whether in favour of it or opposed to it, bringing reward for the obedient and punishment for the disobedient. Those already in favour are obedient, and the purpose of naming them is to make the opposing camp hear.

The particular wisdom is that the obedient are told why they are appreciated. Their acceptance rests on no personal merit and no superiority of their group, but only on the fact that they obey their Creator. If the dissenter takes the path of obedience, he deserves the same grace and reward.

### What three things does the address require?

The instruction is divided into belief in Allah, belief in the Last Day and good deeds. The verse does not intend to give the entire detail of the articles of faith, and there is no occasion for it here.

By mentioning some basic beliefs, the aim is to point to all of them and invite people to them. It is not necessary that every verse mentioning faith should list its details at that point.

### Why does the absence of an explicit mention of prophethood not create a loophole?

The absence of an emphasised mention of belief in the Messenger ﷺ at this place should not have given anyone room for doubt. The whole Qur'an, and hundreds of its verses, are full of clear statements about belief in the message.

There are plain assertions in the Qur'an and the Sunnah that no salvation exists without believing in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and in what he said, completely, and that no belief or action is acceptable or valid without it. A group insisting on pushing its own ideas into the Qur'an has nevertheless produced a theory from the silence of this single verse.

That theory holds that any person, whatever his religion, whether Jew, Christian or even an idol worshipper, might earn salvation in the next life merely by holding belief in Allah and the Last Day together with good deeds, and that becoming a Muslim is not required for final salvation. The discussion answers it with a plea for Allah's protection from such a claim, and then with the Qur'an itself.

### What do the other verses say?

The place where the articles of faith are detailed is at the end of Al-Baqarah, where all are described as believing in Allah, His angels, His Books and His Messengers, making no distinction between any of His Messengers (2:285). Believing in only one or some of the messengers is therefore insufficient. Belief in all of them is a binding condition, and whoever disbelieves in even a single messenger has no valid or acceptable faith.

Another passage describes those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and want to separate Allah from His messengers, saying that they believe in some and disbelieve in some and want a way between the two. Those are the disbelievers in truth (4:150-151).

The Prophet ﷺ is also reported as saying that had Musa been alive, he would have had no option but to follow him. That statement removes the possibility of an independent continuing path for an earlier law after his coming.

### What would the theory make meaningless?

If the followers of every religion could keep acting according to their own religions and find Paradise without believing in the Prophet ﷺ and without becoming Muslims, the verses just cited would be disregarded outright.

More follows. If acting on any religion in any age were sufficient for ultimate success, the coming of the last of the prophets and the revelation of the Qur'an would become pointless, and sending one shariah after another would be redundant. The first messenger's book and law would have been enough.

At most it would have been necessary for people to preserve that law and book, practise them and persuade others to do the same, which has been the duty of the scholars of every community. In that situation the statement that Allah made a way and a method for each of them (5:48) would lose its meaning.

The discussion adds a further argument from history. The Prophet ﷺ carried out jihad against Jews, Christians and others who did not believe in him and in the Book revealed to him, and fought them on battlefields. What justification would remain for that if their own path were already sufficient for salvation?

### Why is Satan not saved by believing in Allah and the Last Day?

The argument is put as a question. If faith in Allah and the Last Day alone made a person a true believer acceptable to Allah, why is Iblis, Satan, cursed? Did he not believe in Allah? Was he a denier of the Last Day?

He was not. Even in his anger he confirmed the Last Day by asking for respite until the Day when the dead are raised (38:79). His ruin therefore cannot be explained by absence of those two beliefs. What he lacked was submission to the command.

That is the point the theory misses. Belief is not a list of propositions held while obedience is refused. It is acceptance of what Allah has said, including what He has said through His Messenger ﷺ.

### Does this verse itself point to belief in the Messenger ﷺ?

The discussion answers that it does. In Qur'anic usage, only that belief in Allah is valid which includes belief in everything Allah has told. The Qur'an makes its terminology clear where it says that if they believe in the like of what you believe in, they have certainly found the right path (2:137).

That means the faith of the Companions is the only faith deserving the name of belief in Allah. Belief in the Messenger ﷺ was a great pillar of their faith. The words whoever believes in Allah therefore include belief in His Messenger ﷺ.

### Where does the error come from?

The discussion traces it to a notion that religion can be handed over as a gift on a silver plate, as gifts are given at weddings. In a modern international setting, religion can be used to build bonds with other nations.

The Qur'an is described as saying openly that relations with non-Muslims should be based on tolerance, sympathy, favour, charity and mercy. That must be done while ensuring that the limits of the religion are not crossed and its frontiers remain guarded.

Courtesy and goodwill are therefore required. They are not a reason to redefine what salvation requires. The verse's own promise stands, and its condition is belief in Allah, belief in the Last Day and good action conforming to the law now in force.

### What does upholding the Book of Allah mean in practice?

Upholding Allah's Book is described as having full faith in Him, being overwhelmed by fear of the Hereafter and living with an upright character among other people. That is genuine religion, and every person has to take it up in the way he lives.

A community given the Book of Allah holds high standing in this world for as long as its members take up that true religion. On turning away from it they become wholly undeserving before Allah, described as even less meritorious than open deniers and polytheists.

The reason given is that generations succeeding the early followers of the ancient prophets gradually took the shape of a regular group. They no longer followed the examples set by the prophets but perpetuated legends praising past glories and supremacy. Each group came to regard itself as the best, certain of salvation and highest in status before Allah.

Such group religions have no value in Allah's eyes. Every individual's case will be presented separately, and the decision about his future will rest wholly on his own deeds and on no other basis. That is the sentence this verse pronounces, and it applies to whoever hears it.

### In short

- Four communities are addressed with one condition: belief in Allah and the Last Day, and good action.
- The Sabians are identified differently in the reports, and the differing views are preserved.
- After the Qur'an, complete obedience means becoming Muslim, and past sins are forgiven for those who do.
- Muslims are named so that the obedient learn why they are accepted and the opposed hear the same law.
- Other verses, the hadith about Musa, the meaning of successive laws, the record of jihad and the case of Satan all show that belief in Allah includes belief in His Messenger ﷺ.
- Every individual's case is judged on his own deeds, not on group membership or inherited legends.

70.text:
The chapter returns to a long history: "Indeed, We took a covenant from the Children of Israel and sent them messengers." Allah bound them to hear and obey, and He kept sending reminders. The verse then states what happened whenever a messenger brought something they did not want.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We took a covenant from the Children of Israel"** recalls pledges to hear and obey Allah and His messengers. One gloss describes the covenant taken in the Torah concerning Muhammad ﷺ, including the undertaking not to associate partners with Allah. Another describes it as a covenant to believe in Allah and His messengers.

**"and sent them messengers."** The sending was repeated. Allah raised reformers among them to remind them of their pledge as their conduct deteriorated.

**"Whenever a messenger came to them with what they did not desire"** gives the condition. The test was not whether the message was unfamiliar but whether it agreed with their hearts and their desires. They broke their pledges and followed their lusts instead of the law.

**"they denied some and killed others"** states the two responses. Whatever part of the law suited them they took, and whatever did not conform to their desires they abandoned.

### Who is named in these two responses?

The denial is explained as directed at 'Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad ﷺ, and the killing at Zakariyah (Zechariah) and Yahya (John). Firm promises to listen and follow were broken by ignoring what the messengers brought, by disbelieving some and murdering others.

One grammatical observation notes that a present tense is used for the killing in order to narrate past events as though occurring now and to match the verse endings. The form does not change the historical claim.

### What happened when their arrogance passed all limits?

The pledge was taken through Musa (Moses) and was kept for only a few days before their behaviour began to deteriorate. Their waywardness and arrogance increased until they silenced the admonishers themselves and killed many people.

Allah then subjected them to the rule of Nebuchadnezzar, ruler of Babylon, described as king of Babylonia from 605 to 562 before the common era. Their holy city of Jerusalem was attacked and destroyed in 586 before the common era, and they were taken to his country as bonded labour. The Old Testament book of Daniel is referred to in the account of their enslavement in Babylon.

The purpose of that subjugation is explained elsewhere as a testing period. Light punishment was meant to awaken moral sense, and where devotion to Allah was aroused the punishment ceased.

### In short

- The covenant required hearing and obeying Allah and His messengers, and reminders were sent repeatedly.
- Their response depended on desire rather than on truth, so some messengers were called liars and others were killed.
- Zakariyah and Yahya are named among those killed, and 'Isa and Muhammad ﷺ among those denied.
- Their arrogance brought subjugation under Nebuchadnezzar and the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 before the common era.

71.text:
The verse explains how such conduct becomes habitual: "They thought there would be no consequences, so they turned a blind eye and a deaf ear." Assuming that nothing would follow, they became unable to see or hear the truth. Allah then turned to them, and many of them returned to the same state.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They thought there would be no consequences"** describes the assumption behind the behaviour. They supposed no fitnah, that is no trial or punishment, would reach them for denying and killing the messengers. Another reading of their thought is that their hearts would not be corrupted by what they did.

**"so they turned a blind eye and a deaf ear."** They became wilfully blind and did not see guidance, and deaf so that they did not hear the truth deep in their hearts. Being unable to see or hear the truth meant they could not be guided by it.

**"Yet Allah turned to them in forgiveness ˹after their repentance˺"** records that they disbelieved, then believed and repented, and Allah forgave them. His turning toward them followed their turning toward Him.

**"but again many became blind and deaf."** The relapse came after a period of time. The wording says many of them, not all, and one gloss adds that some died in that state.

**"And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do"** closes the verse. He has perfect knowledge of what they do, of who among them deserves guidance and who deserves misguidance, and He will requite them for it.

### What historical sequence is described?

After the destruction and exile, their hearts were softened and they sought Allah's pardon. He helped them through Cyrus, king of Iran, who captured their region in 539 before the common era by attacking and defeating the Chaldeans. He freed them from exile and allowed them to return and settle in their own country.

Another account describes them being sent back to Jerusalem from Babylon after a long time through the help of some Persian kings who secured their release from the disgrace imposed by Nebuchadnezzar. They repented and turned to making amends, and Allah accepted their repentance.

They then received a new lease of life and progressed considerably. After a short time they fell back into recklessness and arrogance. Allah sent prophets and reformers to warn them once more, and still they would not come to their senses.

They went so far as to kill Yahya, that is John, and a man they understood to be 'Isa. They were also set on killing Zakariyah and 'Isa himself. Divine wrath then broke upon them. In the year 70 of the common era the Roman emperor Titus defeated them, attacking their land and destroying them, and after that they could never stand on their own.

### Why does the verse mention Allah's turning to them?

Because the mercy was real and was followed by a real relapse. The account does not present the forgiveness as a reason for confidence that consequences never arrive. It shows that a people given a second chance can waste it.

Their assumption that no harm would come of breaking covenants and killing prophets is what blinded them. The verse records that the assumption was false, first in exile and later in destruction.

### In short

- Assuming that nothing would follow their crimes made them blind and deaf to guidance.
- Allah turned to them after their repentance, and the historical account ties this to the release under Cyrus in 539 before the common era.
- Many relapsed, killed Yahya and sought to kill 'Isa, and were destroyed under Titus in the year 70 of the common era.
- Allah sees what they do and will requite them, and the wording says many rather than all.

72.text:
A claim is stated and answered with the words of the one it exalts: "Those who say, “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,” have certainly fallen into disbelief." The verse then gives the consequence of associating partners with Allah, and it answers the claim with what the Messiah himself told his people to worship.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who say, “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,” have certainly fallen into disbelief."** names particular Christian sects, described in one account as the Monarchites, Jacobites and Nestorians, and in another as the claim of the Nestorians. They said this even though 'Isa made known that he was Allah's servant and messenger.

**"The Messiah ˹himself˺ said"** introduces his own words to the Children of Israel, and those words are “Worship Allah—my Lord and your Lord.” That is his call to tawhid, affirming Allah's oneness. The first words he spoke as a baby in the cradle were that he is the servant of Allah. He did not say that he is Allah or that he is the son of Allah.

He said that he is a servant of Allah, that He gave him the Scripture and made him a prophet (19:30), and that Allah is his Lord and their Lord, so they should worship Him alone, which is the straight path (19:36). As a man, after being sent as a prophet, he commanded them to worship his Lord and their Lord alone without partners.

**"Whoever associates others with Allah ˹in worship˺ will surely be forbidden Paradise by Allah."** states the consequence for one who associates partners and dies in that state. Allah forbids Paradise to him and makes the Fire his abode.

**"Their home will be the Fire. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers"** adds that there is no help from Allah and no one to support or protect them from the state they will be in. Another verse says Allah does not forgive partners being set up with Him, but forgives anything short of that to whom He wills (4:48).

The dwellers of the Fire are described as calling to the dwellers of Paradise for water or anything Allah has provided, and being told that Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers. A report in the Sahih describes the Prophet ﷺ having someone proclaim that only a Muslim soul will enter Paradise, with another narration saying only a believing soul.

### How did miracles produce this error?

Allah granted 'Isa the power to perform extraordinary miracles so that people would recognise him as a prophet and have faith in him. The outcome was otherwise. He had been sent purely for guidance, but seeing his miracles, Christians came to hold that he was divine and that God had taken flesh in him.

The Jews, for their part, ignored him and relegated him to the position of a magician and conjurer. One group denied him, and the other was moved by him to establish polytheistic beliefs. The same person became the occasion of two opposite errors.

### What does the wider history of scripture-bearers show?

Communities carrying divine scriptures later developed the belief that they were Allah's special people and would face no reckoning whatever they did. Clear statements against such beliefs exist in Allah's teaching, but they became blind and deaf to them.

They built barriers of self-made beliefs and invented stories around themselves, so that divine warnings went unnoticed. The history of the Jews shows that subjugation by enemies was appointed as a testing period, and that light punishment was meant to awaken moral sense.

Where devotion to Allah was aroused, the punishment ceased. Where it was not, Allah cast them away and did not turn His attention to them again. The verse's warning about Paradise being forbidden belongs to this same pattern of consequence.

### In short

- The claim that Allah is the Messiah is contradicted by the Messiah's own call to worship Allah as his Lord and their Lord.
- His first words in the cradle named him a servant given the Scripture and made a prophet.
- Associating partners with Allah forbids Paradise and makes the Fire the abode, with no helper against it.
- Miracles intended to establish prophethood were misread into divinity, while another group reduced him to a magician.
- Scripture-bearing communities that assume immunity from reckoning build barriers that keep divine warnings out.

73.text:
A second claim is named: "Those who say, “Allah is one in a Trinity,” have certainly fallen into disbelief." The verse answers it in the shortest possible form. "There is only One God." It then warns that if they do not stop, a painful punishment will reach those among them who disbelieve.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who say, “Allah is one in a Trinity,” have certainly fallen into disbelief."** Mujahid and several others say the verse was revealed about the Christians in particular. As-Suddi and others say it concerns taking 'Isa and his mother as gods besides Allah, which makes Allah the third of a trinity.

One account names the claim as that of the Marqusiyyah, holding that there is a father, a son and a holy spirit. Another explains the phrase as referring to the Messiah, Ruh al-Quds, the Holy Spirit, and Allah, or to the Messiah, Maryam (Mary) and Allah, with all three taken as God.

The formulation is then described as making Allah a one third partner with them, so that all three become one and that one is three. This unity in trinity, three persons in one godhead, is identified as the common belief of Christians.

**"There is only One God."** There are not many worthy of worship. There is one God without partner, Lord of all creation and of everything that exists, the only God for the dwellers of the heavens and the earth, with no son and no partner.

**"If they do not stop saying this"** requires them to desist from what they say. One gloss describes it as repenting from the claim and professing His oneness.

**"those who disbelieve among them will be afflicted with a painful punishment"** warns of torment in the Hereafter, shackled and tormented, described as the Fire, with pain reaching their hearts. The wording says those among them who disbelieve, and one gloss identifies them as those fixed upon unbelief.

### How is the claim criticised?

The discussion says this belief is supported neither by reason nor by revelation, and that it is explained in circuitous and ambiguous language. When it is not understood, it is declared to be a reality beyond comprehension.

That is offered as the reason the verse answers with a plain sentence rather than an argument. Against three persons in one godhead, the reply is simply that there is no god but One God.

As-Suddi connects the claim with the question Allah will put at the end of the chapter, asking 'Isa son of Maryam whether he told people to worship him and his mother as two gods besides Allah, to which he answers, glory be to You (5:116). The link shows that taking him and his mother as divine is what makes Allah a third in the count.

### What is the relation to the preceding verse?

Both verses describe disbelief arising from an excess in reverence. The first names the claim that Allah is the Messiah, and this one names the claim of a third of three. The warnings that follow, including the call to repent in verse 74 and the description of the Messiah and his mother in verse 75, answer them together.

The two claims are therefore not treated as unrelated errors. They are two forms of the same departure from the worship the Messiah himself commanded.

### In short

- The claim of a third of three is named as disbelief by particular sects and formulations, including father, son and holy spirit.
- The answer is that there is one God without partner, son or equal.
- Desisting and professing oneness are required, and a painful punishment is warned for those fixed in unbelief.
- The claim is criticised as supported by neither reason nor revelation and explained in ambiguous language.
- It belongs with the preceding verse as two forms of the same excess in reverence.

74.text:
After such warnings the door is left open: "Will they not turn to Allah in repentance and seek His forgiveness?" The question is a rebuke and an invitation at once. Allah is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful, even toward people who have said what these verses have just described.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Will they not turn to Allah in repentance and seek His forgiveness?"** calls them to repent of the claims they have made and to ask forgiveness by affirming Allah's oneness. The interrogative form is intended as a rebuke, not as doubt about whether repentance is possible.

**"And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** describes Him as forgiving toward whoever repents and believes, whatever the sin may have been, even disbelief, and as merciful toward whoever dies repentant. He is compassionate toward the believers.

### What does this show about Allah's generosity?

The verse shows how generous, kind and merciful Allah is toward His creatures. They had committed a grave sin and invented a lie and a false allegation, yet He still calls them to turn back so that He may forgive them.

Allah forgives those who sincerely repent to Him. The invitation is not withdrawn because the offence was great. Its greatness is precisely why the offer of forgiveness matters.

### Why place the invitation between warning and argument?

It stands between the warning of painful punishment and the description of the Messiah and his mother that follows. The order keeps the reader from treating the preceding verses as a final sentence upon people still alive and still able to turn.

The argument that comes next is therefore given to people who can still act on it. Repentance is not a reward for having understood the argument. It is the response the argument invites.

### In short

- Repentance and seeking forgiveness are urged on those who made these claims.
- Allah forgives whoever repents and believes, even after disbelief, and is merciful to whoever dies repentant.
- The invitation shows generosity toward people who invented a grave falsehood.
- It is placed before the argument so that the reasoning reaches people who can still turn.

75.text:
The argument is drawn from the plainest facts about the two people exalted: "The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger." Messengers had come and gone before him. His mother was a woman of truth. Both of them ate food. The verse ends in wonder at how clear signs are made and how people are still deluded.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger."** He is like the prophets before him, one of Allah's servants and one of His honourable messengers. Another verse says he was nothing more than a servant upon whom Allah bestowed favour and made an example for the Children of Israel (43:59).

**"˹Many˺ messengers had ˹come and˺ gone before him."** Prophets came into the world, completed their mission and passed away. They were not eternal, and eternity is the mark of godhood. Being human like them, the Messiah was not eternal either, and so he cannot be what Allah is.

One gloss draws the inference directly. Prophets passed away ahead of him, and his own passing followed the same course. A god would not pass away, so the claim answered in verse 72 fails on that fact alone.

**"His mother was a woman of truth."** She believed in Allah with complete trust in Him. The word used means extremely truthful, and it is described as the highest rank given to her.

**"They both ate food."** They needed nourishment and the relief of bodily needs. They were therefore servants like other servants, not gods. The reasoning from eating is developed below.

**"See how We make the signs clear to them, yet see how they are deluded ˹from the truth˺"** expresses amazement. The signs are made unequivocal and plain, and they are the signs of Allah's oneness and of the falsehood of extremism in giving lordship to another. The delusion consists of the opinions, misguided ideas and claims they hold after that clarification.

### Why does eating disprove divinity?

Whoever needs to eat and drink depends on almost everything in the world. The earth, the air, the water, the sun and the animals cannot be described as things he does not need.

The reflection is directed inward. There is the grain of food outside a person, and then its journey begins at entry into the stomach and continues to digestion. Every factor involved, directly and indirectly, must be considered, and then there is a chain of effects generated by eating whose extent no one can precisely trace.

By pointing out that the Messiah and his pious mother used to eat, the Qur'an refers to that endless chain of needs. Neither of them was exempt from needing food and drink, a fact established by observation and by authentic narration that even Christians do not deny.

Whoever is not free of the need for food and drink is not free of dependence on anything in this world. How then could a human being, dependent like all human beings on a chain of causation for survival, be God? The argument is described as strong and clear, understandable by the educated and the uneducated alike, because eating and drinking are contrary to godhood.

A qualification is added. Not eating is not by itself proof of godhood, since otherwise the angels would all be gods. The argument from food shows dependence, and dependence is what excludes divinity.

Another gloss gives further reasons from the same fact: a being who eats is compound and fallible, and produces the waste a body produces. Such a being cannot be God.

### Was Maryam a prophet or a saint?

The question is debated. The complimentary use of the word meaning truthful indicates a godly person rather than a prophet, because on an occasion of compliment the higher rank is what gets mentioned. Had she held the station of prophethood, the word used for her here would have been the feminine form of prophet, but the word used is the one denoting truthfulness, which is the station of sainthood or godliness. This is abridged from a discussion in Ruh al-Ma'ani.

According to the majority of Muslim scholars, prophethood has never been given to women, that mission being particular to men. The verse cited for this, in Surah Yusuf, says that Allah sent before him only men to whom He revealed, from among the peoples of the towns (12:109).

The debate is reported rather than closed by assertion. What both readings agree on is that she was honoured, truthful and not divine.

### In short

- The Messiah was a messenger who passed away like the messengers before him, and eternity is not his attribute.
- His mother is described as extremely truthful, which is the highest rank given to her and not a claim of prophethood.
- Their need for food shows dependence on the whole chain of causes, which is incompatible with divinity.
- Not eating is not itself proof of godhood, since the angels do not eat.
- The signs are made plain, and the delusion lies in the claims held after that clarification.

76.text:
The question is put directly to the worshipper: “How can you worship besides Allah those who can neither harm nor benefit you?” The verse then contrasts that object of worship with Allah, who hears and knows. The comparison is between a thing without power and the One who has it all.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How can you worship besides Allah"** is addressed to the children of Adam who worship other than Allah, the Christians being one example among them. It admonishes people who set up rivals with Him and worship idols, monuments and false deities, which deserve no degree of divinity. It is a rebuke against shirk, associating partners with Allah, in the form this passage has discussed since verse 72.

**"those who can neither harm nor benefit you?"** describes what cannot ward off harm from you or bring you benefit, in this world or in the Hereafter. The question is meant as a disavowal rather than as a request for information.

**"And Allah ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”"** He hears what His servants say and knows all things. One gloss specifies that He hears their claims about 'Isa and knows their punishment, and another that He hears their sayings and knows their circumstances.

### Why is worship of anything else irrational?

How could anyone worship inanimate objects that do not hear, see or know anything, and have no power to bring harm or benefit even to themselves, let alone to others, instead of worshipping Allah? Such a god is in reality very weak, while Allah is high above any weakness.

Only a Being who is Himself dependent on nobody and who has power to benefit or harm can be worthy of worship. Food is the most significant symbol of human dependence, and whoever depends for his food depends for everything. Whoever takes food is a wholly dependent being, and such a being cannot be God.

The same reasoning applies to conferring benefit and inflicting harm. Someone receiving benefit or suffering harm is an event requiring the coordination of universal factors. No ordinary human being can organise such factors, so no human being can raise himself to a position where he is treated as worthy of worship.

### What lies behind venerating a created being?

When a person places someone at the heart of his reverence and affection, what he really feels is that this person enjoys high standing in Allah's world and will be of use to him before Allah. All such hopes are described as false.

In this world of test and trial, the fact that everything other than Allah is helpless is not absolutely clear, which is why people fall into that misapprehension. In the Hereafter, when the truth is disclosed, a person will see that every support he relied on besides Allah was wholly without value.

Nothing is hidden from Allah, and He will repay accordingly. The verse therefore ends where the argument ends, with hearing and knowledge belonging to Him alone. A related verse in Surah Yusuf recalls that those sent before the Prophet ﷺ were men given revelation from among the peoples of the towns (12:109), which is another way of placing 'Isa and Maryam among servants rather than among objects of worship.

### In short

- What cannot harm or benefit is not worthy of worship, and the question is a disavowal rather than an enquiry.
- Dependence for food shows dependence for everything, which excludes divinity.
- Benefit and harm require the coordination of universal factors that no human being controls.
- Hopes placed in a venerated created being are false, and their falsity becomes plain in the Hereafter.
- Allah alone hears what people say and knows what they do, and will repay them.

77.text:
The chapter now states the principle that explains both errors: "Do not go to extremes in your faith beyond the truth". Excess in religion is crossing the limits the religion itself has drawn, in belief and in action. The verse also forbids following the vain desires of people who went astray earlier and misled many.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, “O People of the Book!"** addresses Jews and Christians. One gloss identifies the addressees as the people of Najran, and another as the Christians in particular. The instruction is given to their generations as well, up to the Last Day.

**"Do not go to extremes in your faith beyond the truth"** uses a word meaning to cross limits. Ghuluww, excess in religion, is crossing the limits drawn by religion in matters of belief and deed.

The example given is homage to prophets. There is a limit to it, and the furthest one may go is to take them as the best among Allah's creation. Going past that limit and calling those same prophets God or a son of God is excess in belief.

**"nor follow the vain desires of those who went astray before ˹you˺."** names the cause of the error. They followed their teachers, the advocates of misguidance who came before their time. One gloss calls them their forefathers who went astray formerly on account of their extremism.

**"They misled many and strayed from the Right Way.”"** describes leaders who led others astray from guidance and themselves missed the plain road. Moving away from the right path, they lost it.

### What is the other form of excess?

The previous verses described the tyranny and injustice of Bani Isra'il toward the prophets sent to them, falsifying some and killing others. This verse exposes another aspect of the same crookedness. Not content with one extreme, they reached for another, committing excess in reverence by making Allah's messengers nothing short of God.

The section of Bani Isra'il who said that Allah is exactly 'Isa son of Maryam thereby became disbelievers. Elsewhere the Jews are censured for the same kind of excess, in the statement that the Jews said 'Uzayr (Ezra) is the son of Allah while the Christians said the Messiah is the son of Allah. That passage is described without a verse number here because the account gives none.

Their behaviour toward the prophets was therefore a mixture of opposites. They could be neglectful and irreverent enough to falsify or kill them, and they could push an exaggerated reverence so far as to name them God or a son of God.

A group behaviour swinging between excess and deficiency is read as a mark of ingrained brutality. A well known Arab saying is cited to the effect that an ignorant person never stays at moderation but goes either to excess or to deficiency. Excess means crossing the limit, and deficiency means falling short of one's duty.

The two extremes may have come from two different groups among them, or one group may have acted in both ways toward different prophets, falsifying and killing some while equating others with God.

### How does Allah make Himself known?

The most significant truth of life is that Allah alone created and owns every universe of existence together with all it holds, and rules over it. He is One. To Him belongs all that exists and to Him belongs command, and He alone must be obeyed.

Man, however, is a lump of clay come alive, still wrapped in layers of materialism. How can he reach the One so pure, and how can he learn what Allah wills and what He wants from him? In His grace Allah appointed two channels of knowledge through which a person can learn what Allah likes and dislikes and what he must do and avoid.

The first is divine scripture, standing as law and guidance for the whole of humanity. The second is those special and welcome servants chosen from among human beings and sent as practical models of Allah's likes and dislikes and as practical keys to His Books. In religious terminology they are called messenger or prophet.

The reason given for the second is that a book, however exhaustive, can never be sufficient for the complete grooming of a human being. It takes a person to be the natural groomer and nurturer of another person. Allah's practice has therefore been to allow two orders to flourish in the mission of reforming and training people in the art of living: the Book of Allah and the men of Allah, including the blessed prophets and then their deputies, the scholars and the spiritual guides.

### Where have people gone wrong about the men of Allah?

Concerning this second order, people have fallen into excess and deficiency since ancient times. The different sects that sprang up within religions are described as products of this error of approach.

In some places those men were inflated beyond the required limit, reaching the outer frontiers of worshipping them. In others they were wholly ignored and bypassed with the declaration that the Book of Allah is enough for us. That declaration is apparently true, but by misinterpreting it so as to negate the importance of the prophets they made it a slogan.

At one extreme a messenger of Allah, and even spiritual guides and ascetics, were taken to be knowers of the unknown and seers of the unseen, as though they possessed Allah's own attributes. People began by worshipping living guides and ended by worshipping their graves. At the other extreme even a messenger of Allah was given the status of a mere courier or postman.

The essential message is therefore that whoever insults the standing of the prophets is no less culpable in disbelief than whoever lifts them far past the bounds set for honouring them and calls them Allah's equal.

### What is religion in this light?

This verse, with its command not to be excessive in faith, is a preface to that subject, and it stands beside the prohibition of shirk discussed with the preceding verse. It makes clear that the religion is really a set of limits and restrictions. Falling short inside those bounds is a crime, and so is stepping over them.

As it is a grave sin to insult Allah's messengers and their deputies, so it is a far graver sin to take them to be owners of Allah's own attributes or equal sharers with Him. The guidance given here to the People of the Book and to their generations until the Last Day has the status of a basic principle, since the slightest deviation from it can lose a person forever.

### Is deep intellectual research a form of excess?

The word meaning unjustly appears alongside the command not to be excessive. Investigative scholars of Qur'anic commentary say it is used for emphasis, because excess in religion is always unjust and the possibility of its being just does not exist.

Al-Zamakhshari and others nevertheless identify two kinds of excess at this place. The first is the unjust and false kind prohibited here. The second is a just and permissible kind, for which he names deep intellectual research, such as the method of the scholastic theologians of Islam in matters of faith or of Muslim jurists in matters of rulings. On his view this too is excess, but excess that is just and permissible.

Most scholars, on the considered view, hold that such research does not come within the definition of excess at all. The practical conclusion given is that deep insight and detailed investigation into questions of the Qur'an and Sunnah should stay within the limits established from the Prophet ﷺ and from the Companions and their successors. If it does, it is not excess, and whatever does reach the limit of excess is blameworthy here as well.

### How did this excess arise historically?

To the early followers of 'Isa he was a man sent from Allah, human and a prophet. As that faith travelled out of Syria it met the philosophy of Egypt and Greece, and those who accepted it entered the fold while under the influence of the philosophical thought of the time.

From internal causes and external factors a new era began, in which efforts were made to describe the faith in the philosophical style then current. The philosophers of Egypt and Greece were dominant in the civilised world of those days, and their thinking greatly influenced its intelligentsia.

Greek philosophers had formed an imaginary concept of the universe and interpreted reality on three levels: existence, life and knowledge. Those ideas impressed the Christian theologians, who hoped to win over the intellectuals of the day and so set about reshaping their faith along contemporary lines.

They offered an interpretation relating the faith in essence to those three levels, hoping that people could equate it with their own way of thinking and so accept it. Religious reality was said to manifest itself in a trinity, with existence as the Father, life as the Son and knowledge as the Holy Spirit.

To complete the religion interpreted in this way, many ideas were imported into it, such as the belief that 'Isa was the embodied manifestation of the word, and that sin had come upon all humanity after Adam's descent, requiring God's son to make atonement by submitting to his own crucifixion. So it was that, by the fourth century of the common era and shaped around Egyptian, Greek and Roman ideas, the faith now known as Christianity took form.

This is the historical account supplied in the material. It is presented as an explanation of how an excess in reverence acquired a philosophical form, not as a survey of every Christian doctrine or community.

### What is the path the verse commands?

At the end of the verse they are told not to follow the desires and whims of a people who had already gone astray and had made others go astray. The reason is given at once: those people moved away from the right path and lost it.

That straight road lies in the middle, between going too far and falling short. Two things are therefore achieved. Verse 77 points out the fatal error of crossing over the norm or lagging far behind it, and it stresses the need to stay firm on the straight road of moderation.

### In short

- Excess in religion means crossing the limits drawn by religion in belief and action, and the limit in honouring prophets is to regard them as the best of creation.
- Bani Isra'il combined two extremes, killing and falsifying some prophets and elevating others to divinity, including the claim about 'Uzayr and about the Messiah.
- Allah makes Himself known through His Books and through the men He sent as practical keys to those Books, and both extremes concerning those men are condemned.
- Deep investigation within the limits established from the Prophet ﷺ, the Companions and their successors is not excess, and the majority do not class it as such.
- The historical account traces how reverence for 'Isa acquired a philosophical trinitarian form, and the verse commands the path of moderation.

78.text:
A long record is summarised in one sentence: "The disbelievers among the Children of Israel were condemned in the revelations of David and Jesus, son of Mary." The condemnation is not new. It was pronounced through two prophets and is repeated here so that later people will not imitate the conduct that earned it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The disbelievers among the Children of Israel were condemned"** describes a curse pronounced long ago and revealed through Dawud (David) and 'Isa (Jesus), son of Maryam. In the report 'Ali bin Abi Talhah gives from Ibn 'Abbas, they were cursed in the Torah, the Injil, the Zabur, that is the Psalms, and the Furqan, that is the Qur'an.

Another explanation says Allah distanced the disbelievers among them from His mercy in the scripture He gave Dawud, the Psalms, and in the scripture He gave 'Isa, the Gospel. The condemnation is therefore attested in more than one revelation, not only in this chapter.

**"in the revelations of David and Jesus, son of Mary."** is explained through their tongues and their supplications. One account says that through Dawud's supplication some became apes and through the supplication of 'Isa some became swine. Another identifies those transformed into apes as the people of Aylah and those turned into pigs as the people who ate at the table sent down from heaven.

A third account reverses the pairing, describing the curse through Dawud as producing swine and that through 'Isa as producing monkeys. These differing reports are preserved as they stand, since the material does not settle which prophet's supplication is connected with which transformation.

**"That was for their disobedience and violations"** gives the reason. They disobeyed Allah and transgressed against His creatures. Specific acts named include rebellion concerning the Sabbath and what followed eating from the table sent from heaven, killing the prophets, and declaring their own indulgence in sin lawful.

### Which prophets pronounced this condemnation?

Two are named here. Some scholars observe that the mention of two prophets follows from the context, while the fact is that the pronouncement began with Musa (Moses) and ended with the last of the prophets ﷺ. On that account four prophets in succession spoke this condemnation against those hostile to the prophets or guilty of making them sharers in divine attributes.

The naming of two therefore does not limit the history. It identifies the two revelations whose words are being recalled at this point.

### Why is the condemnation recalled here?

It describes the sad end of those among Bani Isra'il who fell into the excess and deficiency discussed in the preceding verses. Their conduct is recorded so that it will not be imitated.

The central failure named in the next verse is that they did not stop one another from evil. Many hadith command enjoining righteousness and forbidding evil, recorded by Ahmad, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah, and the principal ones are given with the following verse.

### In short

- The condemnation was pronounced through Dawud and 'Isa and is attested in the Torah, the Injil, the Psalms and the Qur'an.
- Reports differ over which supplication produced which transformation, and the differences are preserved.
- The causes named are disobedience, transgression, violation of the Sabbath, killing prophets and making sin lawful.
- The pronouncement began with Musa and continued to the last of the prophets ﷺ, even though two are named here.
- The record is given so that the conduct will not be imitated.

79.text:
The specific failure is named: "They did not forbid one another from doing evil." Sins were committed openly because nobody objected. The verse then passes judgment on that silence: "Evil indeed was what they did".

### Phrase by phrase

**"They did not forbid one another from doing evil."** They did not restrain each other from sins and prohibited acts. One gloss explains it as not restraining one another and not repenting from the wickedness they did. Another says one person would not forbid another from repeating an indecency already committed.

**"Evil indeed was what they did"** condemns both the sins and the silence. One explanation singles out the failure to forbid as itself the evil deed, since offenders acted openly because no one disapproved.

Allah chastised them for this behaviour so that it would not be imitated. The condemnation is therefore directed at a habit of a community, not only at individual crimes.

### What do the hadith say about forbidding evil?

Ahmad records Hudhayfah bin Al-Yaman reporting the Prophet ﷺ as swearing by the One in whose hand is his soul that they must enjoin righteousness and forbid evil, or Allah will send a punishment upon them from Himself. They would then supplicate to Him, and their supplication would not be accepted. At-Tirmidhi also records it and calls it hasan, good.

Muslim records Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri reporting the Messenger ﷺ as saying that whoever witnesses an evil should change it with his hand, and if he cannot, then with his tongue, and if he cannot even that, then with his heart, which is the weakest faith.

Abu Dawud records Al-'Urs, meaning Ibn 'Amirah, reporting that when sin is committed on the earth, whoever witnesses it and hates it, and in one wording forbids it, will be like one who did not witness it, and whoever was away from it yet approved of it stands with those who saw it. Only Abu Dawud records this hadith.

Abu Dawud also records a Companion reporting the Prophet ﷺ as saying that people will not perish until they leave, or have, no excuse for themselves.

Ibn Majah records Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri describing the Messenger ﷺ addressing the people and saying that fear of people must not prevent anyone from stating the truth he knows. Abu Sa'id then wept and said that by Allah they had seen errors and had been afraid of people.

Another report from Abu Sa'id gives the Messenger ﷺ as saying that the best jihad is a word of truth spoken before an unjust ruler. Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah record it, and At-Tirmidhi calls it hasan gharib, good and singly transmitted, through this route.

Ahmad records Hudhayfah reporting that a Muslim is not required to humiliate himself. Asked how a person humiliates himself, he said it is by taking on trials he is not capable of enduring. At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah record it, and At-Tirmidhi calls it hasan sahih gharib.

Taken together these reports set a graded duty, from action to speech to the heart, and at the same time forbid a person from loading himself with trials he cannot bear. The two limits belong to the same instruction.

### How does a community come to this silence?

One account explains deviation as arising when a people are impressed by the thinking of communities that have gone astray and try to imitate them. Accepting Allah's religion, they interpret it so that it appears consistent with current thinking, and in the name of Allah's religion they adopt an ungodly one.

Christians are described as adapting their religion to the ideas of polytheistic communities and presenting it as the religion Allah favours. A second type of deviation occurs when religion is cast in the mould of national aspirations, and the Jews are given as the example, interpreting Allah's religion so that it legitimised their worldliness.

Muslims have no scope for inserting such interpretations into the text of Allah's Book. Outside the text, however, they remain free to follow the example of earlier communities. The warning is therefore not only historical.

### What does faith do to a person's sensitivity?

Faith makes a person sensitive to transgression and evil. When he sees someone committing it, he is disturbed and immediately wants to stop him. He relates to evil people through separation rather than friendship.

When faith weakens, his sensitivity narrows to himself. Only what damages his own interests appears evil to him, and he stays neutral about evils directed at others. That narrowing is the beginning of the condition this verse condemns.

### In short

- The evil named is both the sins committed and the failure to forbid them.
- The hadith set a graded duty of hand, tongue and heart, and warn that silence can bring a punishment after which supplication is not accepted.
- Speaking truth before an unjust ruler is called the best jihad, while a Muslim must not take on trials he cannot bear.
- Deviation comes from reshaping religion to fit current thinking or national ambition.
- Weakening faith narrows a person's sense of evil to what touches his own interests.

80.text:
The next charge concerns alliances: "You see many of them taking the disbelievers as allies. Truly wicked are their misdeeds". The verse identifies what they sent ahead for themselves, the wrath it earned and the lasting torment that follows.

### Phrase by phrase

**"You see many of them taking the disbelievers as allies."** Mujahid says the verse refers to the hypocrites. One gloss describes many hypocrites seeking assistance and support from disbelievers, naming Ka'b and his followers, while another reading describes many Jews such as Ka'b and his followers befriending the disbelievers of Makkah, Abu Sufyan and his followers.

Another explanation says they affiliated with the disbelievers among the Makkans out of spite for the Prophet ﷺ. A further account describes disbelieving Jews allying with idolaters and opposing the Prophet ﷺ and those who believe in Allah's oneness.

**"Truly wicked are their misdeeds"** describes what their souls sent forward for the day of their inevitable return. The evil is that they gave loyalty and support to disbelievers instead of believers.

**"which have earned them Allah’s wrath."** That act produced hypocrisy in their hearts and brought Allah's anger, which remains with them until the Day of Return.

**"And they will be in everlasting torment"** states the end. They will abide in torment on the Day of Resurrection, described in one gloss as never dying and never being removed.

### Why is this alliance so damaging?

The cultivation of deep friendship with disbelievers is prohibited because its outcome is disastrous. The discussion suggests it may also indicate that the deviation of Bani Isra'il resulted from close friendly collaboration with disbelievers, which harmed their conduct and in the end brought them down into the abyss.

Alliance is therefore not treated as a neutral social arrangement. It shapes belief over time, and the shaping is what the verse warns against.

### What did their own prophets say about them?

The Children of Israel faced this downfall, yet they continued to make self-righteous statements, and their chosen speakers went on making fine speeches. They were not serious about rushing to intervene when they saw tyranny and evil, or about preventing it.

Dawud said of the Children of Israel of his own period that not one of them was righteous. From his discourses it is clear that they used to speak of peace with their neighbours, describing Allah's law and reaffirming their pledge to Him, while their hearts were full of ill intent.

'Isa likewise denounced the Jews of his time, calling them hypocritical scholars who had taken over the dwellings of widows while prolonging their prayers. He lamented that they paid tithes of mint, anise and cumin while neglecting the weighty provisions of the revealed law, namely justice, mercy and faith.
