He named them blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel, and scorned them for appearing righteous while being wholly hypocritical and faithless within. This is reported as recorded in the Gospel of Matthew.

They did what 'Isa described. They recounted Allah's law, offered long prayers and paid tithes from their crops, but all of it was lip service. They performed harmless commands with a show of piety, and when the question was treating others justly, showing mercy to a downtrodden person or crushing self-interest to carry out Allah's command, they turned back.

If anyone pointed out their mistakes, they became his enemy. It was such behaviour that brought upon them divine wrath and curses.

### In short

- The alliance described is with disbelievers, whether the hypocrites seeking support or Jews allying with the Makkans.
- What they sent forward earned wrath that lasts until the Day of Return and torment that does not end.
- Deep friendship with opponents of the faith is prohibited because it reshapes belief and led, in this account, to the fall of Bani Isra'il.
- Their own prophets described fine speech without intervention, tithes without justice, and enmity toward whoever corrected them.

81.text:
The verse states what sincere faith would have prevented: "Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what has been revealed to him, they would have never taken those ˹pagans˺ as allies." Belief and this alliance are presented as incompatible, not as two separate matters.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what has been revealed to him"** describes sincere belief in Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the Qur'an. One gloss explains it as genuine belief in Allah and in His oneness, in the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and in what was revealed to him.

**"they would have never taken those ˹pagans˺ as allies."** Such belief would have prevented the wrong of backing disbelievers in secret and treating as enemies the people who hold faith in Allah, in His Messenger ﷺ and in what came down to him. One reading describes the hypocrites not choosing the Jews as friends for assistance, and another describes the Jews not taking Abu Sufyan and his followers as friends.

**"But most of them are rebellious"** describes disobedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and defiance of the revealed verses. Some versions of the material read many rather than most, and many among the People of the Book are described as disbelievers or hypocrites, wicked and rebellious against faith. Another account says most of them do not obey Allah and do not side with Him and the believers.

### What does the conditional form show?

It connects inward belief with outward alignment. The verse does not treat alliance as a practical matter separate from faith. If the belief were genuine, the alliance would not exist.

That is why the preceding verses move from their misdeeds to their alliances. The alliance is the visible expression of the belief they actually hold, and the hypothetical statement exposes the contradiction they would rather not face.

### In short

- Sincere belief in Allah, the Prophet ﷺ and the revelation would have made this alliance impossible.
- The glosses differ over whether the hypocrites or the Jews are meant, and both readings are preserved.
- Most of them are described as rebellious, disobedient and defiant of the revealed verses.
- The conditional form ties inward faith to outward alignment rather than treating them separately.

82.text:
The verse compares two attitudes toward the believers. It names "the most gracious to be those who call themselves Christian" and sets that against the bitterness of others. The reason it gives is not ancestry or numbers. It is the presence of priests and monks, and the absence of arrogance.

That comparison is precise. It praises a described quality in a particular group. It does not turn praise into a general rule about alliances.

### Phrase by phrase

**"You will surely find the most bitter towards the believers to be the Jews and polytheists"** names the strongest enmity. One gloss adds that their hostility is the most vehement and their speech the vilest toward those who believe in Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions.

The Jews meant here include Banu Qurayzah and Banu An-Nadir, together with Fadak and Khaybar. The most vehement of the idolaters are the idolaters of Makkah.

Their disbelief is described as rebellion and defiance. It opposes the truth, belittles people and degrades scholars. Another account traces it to the intensity of their disbelief, to ignorance and to complete preoccupation with whims. A third names malice, jealousy and pride.

The history cited is grave. They killed many of their prophets. They tried several times to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They worked magic against him and poisoned him. They stirred up their like among the polytheists against him.

**"and the most gracious to be those who call themselves Christian."** refers to people who claim that name and follow the religion of the Messiah and the teaching of his Injil. They are described as more tolerant toward Islam and Muslims than the others.

The reason given is mercy and kindness. Their hearts acquired it through part of the Messiah's religion. Another verse recalls that Allah ordained compassion and mercy in the hearts of those who followed him, along with monasticism (57:27).

Their book contains the saying that whoever strikes the right cheek should be turned the left. Fighting was prohibited in their creed. One account describes them as nearest in affection and most lenient in speech.

That account identifies them as the Negus and his followers, thirty two men. Another count gives forty in all. On this reckoning thirty two came from Abyssinia and eight were monks from historic Syria. The Syrian group is named as the monk Bahira with Abrahah, Ashraf, Idris, Tamim, Tammam, Durayd and Ayman.

**"That is because there are priests and monks among them"** explains the cause. The word for priests is given in the text, and monks are described as people dedicated to worship.

One gloss describes the priests as ascetics whose heads are shaved in the middle. It describes the monks as secluded in monasteries and as the learned men of the group. Another calls the priests scholars and the monks devout worshippers.

**"and because they are not arrogant"** adds humility to knowledge and worship. They are described as following truth and fairness. They are not disdainful of the truth in the way the Jews and the people of Makkah were.

Pride is the obstacle named. One account states plainly that good does not enter a proud heart. Another says their lack of pride appeared in believing in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an.

### What was the occasion of revelation?

Sa'id bin Jubayr, As-Suddi and others connect these verses with a delegation. An-Najashi, king of Ethiopia, sent it to the Prophet ﷺ to hear his words and observe his qualities.

The delegation met him and he recited the Qur'an. They embraced Islam, wept and were humbled. They then returned and told An-Najashi what had happened.

'Ata' bin Abi Rabah says they were Ethiopians. They embraced Islam while the Muslims who had migrated to Ethiopia lived among them. Qatadah says they followed the religion of 'Isa son of Maryam. On seeing Muslims and hearing the Qur'an they accepted Islam without hesitation.

Ibn Jarir says the verses concern people matching that description, whether from Ethiopia or elsewhere.

Ibn 'Abbas gives a longer account. While the Messenger ﷺ was in Makkah he feared persecution of his Companions by the idolaters. He therefore sent 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Ja'far ibn Abi Talib to the Negus at the head of a group.

He described the Negus as a righteous man. He oppressed no one, and no one was oppressed in his dominion. The group was told to head there and remain until Allah granted the Muslims relief.

The Negus honoured them. He asked whether they had memorised anything of what had been revealed to them. They recited while monks and priests stood around him. At every verse tears ran down their cheeks, because of the truth they recognised.

Another report comes through Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, then Ibn Shihab, Yunus and al-Layth. The Messenger ﷺ sent 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri to the Negus with a message. The Negus read it.

He then called Ja'far ibn Abi Talib together with all the emigrants, and he brought priests and monks into the gathering as well. He ordered Ja'far to recite from the Qur'an, and Ja'far recited Surah Maryam. They believed, and their eyes flowed with tears.

### What happened during the migration to Abyssinia?

Among the People of the Book there were people free of malice toward Muslims. Their godliness and inclination toward truth explained it. 'Abdullah ibn Salam is given as an example.

Such people were very rare among the Jews, almost nonexistent. There were comparatively more among the Christians. Ethiopia held a large number of them in the Prophet's ﷺ time, including King Najashi and his officials.

The Muslims of Makkah al-Mukarramah were exhausted by the oppression of Quraysh. The Prophet ﷺ advised them to migrate to Ethiopia. He had heard that its king oppressed nobody and allowed no oppression, so they should stay there for a while.

A first group of eleven set out. It included 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ. A larger caravan followed, with eighty two men besides women, under the leadership of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib.

The king and his people received them gently, and they lived in peace. Quraysh could not bear that Muslims they had persecuted should be at peace elsewhere. They sent a delegation with the customary gifts, asking the king to expel the Muslims.

The king decided to investigate first. He spoke with Ja'far and his companions about Islam and its Prophet ﷺ. He heard of the Prophet's ﷺ life and of the teachings of Islam.

He found them true to the prophecy of 'Isa and to the Injil. That book carried glad tidings of the last of the prophets, Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ. It gave an outline of his teaching, his physical features and the features of his Companions for ready identification.

Convinced, he returned the gifts brought by the Quraysh delegation. He told them plainly that he could never order such people out of his country.

Ja'far's presentation was brief and comprehensive. The Muslims' conduct as role models also worked on the king, his officials and the common people. Genuine feeling for Islam and its Prophet ﷺ grew among them.

The Prophet ﷺ then migrated to Madinah al-Tayyibah. News reached Ethiopia that the Muslims were comfortable and at peace. The emigrants decided to go to Madinah.

Najashi sent a delegation with them. It was made up of leading scholars and missionaries from his own co-religionists, to present his compliments to the Prophet ﷺ. The group numbered seventy. Sixty were from Ethiopia and eight from Syria.

They wore the coarse robes of monks. The Prophet ﷺ recited Surah Yasin to them. Tears flowed as they listened, and they remarked how close it was to what had been revealed to 'Isa. All of them embraced Islam.

After their return, Najashi also embraced Islam. He sent his son to lead another delegation, carrying a letter. The boat that carried them sank at sea. The king, his officials and his people had treated Islam and Muslims gently and justly, and in the end they embraced it.

### Is the praise general or particular?

The majority of scholars say these verses were revealed about those honoured people. The wording is nevertheless general. Its legal force therefore reaches every Christian devoted to truth and justice as the people of Ethiopia were.

They followed the Injil before Islam and followed Islam after its coming. Any Christian who resembles them is counted with them.

Such people are described elsewhere in the Qur'an. They are people of the Scripture who hold faith in Allah together with what came to you and what came to them, and who humble themselves before Allah (3:199). They are those given the Scripture earlier who believe in this Book, and who say when it is recited to them that they were already Muslims before it (28:52-53). The description continues to the statement that they seek not the ignorant (28:55).

There were also Jews of this kind. They had adhered to the Torah since the time of Musa and entered Islam when it came. Their number was too small to be significant among communities and nations. The rest were foremost in hostility toward Muslims.

### What reading does the verse not support?

A particular group of Christians is praised here. They feared Allah and were upright in matters of truth. The group includes Najashi, his officials and his people, and other Christians who shared those qualities or will share them later.

It does not mean that Christians must be taken as friends however far they stray. Nor does it require friendship toward people aggressively hostile to Islam. That reading is described as false and contrary to the facts.

Abu Bakr Al-Jassas addresses it in his Ahkam al-Qur'an. He says some people take the praise of Christians here in an absolute sense. They then consider Christians better than the Jews in an absolute sense as well. He calls that open ignorance.

Comparing the beliefs of the two groups shows the Christians more pronounced in shirk, which is ascribing partners in Allah's divinity. In their dealings with Muslims, Christians of the modern age have not lagged behind Jews in activity against Islam.

What is correct is that many God-fearing and truth-loving people existed among them. That is why they were granted the ability to accept Islam and become Muslims. These verses were revealed to show that particular difference between the two groups.

The Qur'an gives the reason at the end of this verse. Among them are priests and monks, and they are not arrogant. Arrogance is what could make them unwilling to listen and think.

The contrast makes the position of the Jews at that time clear. God-fearing love of truth was absent from them. Their scholars and rabbis were nowhere near surrendering the pleasures of this life for the sake of knowledge and religion.

They harnessed learning as a means of gathering material benefit. Greed for the worldly gripped them so tightly that they stopped distinguishing truth from falsehood. They no longer separated the lawful from the unlawful.

### What does this say about a community's inner life?

The verse reveals something crucial about a believing community. Its scholars and spiritual guides are its real movers and makers. They are the spirit of its order.

Genuine scholars and guides must be present in a society. They should not follow worldly desires in matters of religion or in the public good of believers. Their motive should be the fear of Allah and answerability before Him alone.

Where such people remain, the community is never deprived of real good and real blessing. The difference drawn in this verse is therefore traced to the character of its learned people.

Where learning is joined to humility and worship, truth can still be recognised. Where learning is harnessed to material gain, a community loses the capacity to hear.

### In short

- The Jews and the idolaters of Makkah are named as most bitter toward the believers, for reasons of rebellion, defiance, ignorance, malice and pride.
- Those who call themselves Christians are named as nearest in affection, because of mercy in their religion, their priests and monks, and their lack of arrogance.
- The occasion is the delegation of Najashi and the earlier migration to Abyssinia, preserved with differing counts and lists.
- The praise describes a quality and extends to whoever shares it, and it is not a warrant for alliance with hostility toward Islam.
- Scholars and guides motivated by the fear of Allah are the moving spirit of a community, and their character explains the difference drawn here.

83.text:
The response of that group is described in detail: "When they listen to what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears for recognizing the truth." Their hearing produces a visible effect, and then words. They ask to be counted among the witnesses.

The tears are not sentimental. They mark recognition of something they already knew from their own scripture.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When they listen to what has been revealed to the Messenger"** describes them hearing the recitation. One gloss specifies that they heard Ja'far ibn Abi Talib reciting what had been revealed to the Messenger ﷺ. Another describes the Prophet ﷺ reciting Surah Yasin to the delegation of the Negus from Abyssinia.

**"you see their eyes overflowing with tears"** is the visible effect of hearing. The delegation wept and submitted to Islam, saying how close this was to what used to be revealed to 'Isa (Jesus).

**"for recognizing the truth"** gives the cause. They recognised the truth, and one gloss explains that recognition as finding the traits and description of Muhammad ﷺ in their own scripture. Their hearts were soft, and they wept in submission because they knew what 'Isa had brought.

**"They say, “Our Lord! We believe"** is their declaration, their shahadah. It is explained as belief in Allah, in His Book and in His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, and as accepting the truth of the Prophet ﷺ and the Book. Another gloss connects it with the good news they already held about the coming of Muhammad ﷺ.

**"so count us among the witnesses”** asks to be inscribed among the witnesses. One explanation says it means being made part of the community of Muhammad ﷺ that believes. Another describes the witnesses as those who affirm their acceptance of the truth and testify to it.

A further account explains the request as asking to be recorded among the people of this community who will stand as witnesses against others on the Day of Rising. These readings are not in conflict about the substance. All describe a request to be enrolled with those who attest the truth.

### What happened at that hearing?

The delegation came to the Prophet ﷺ and he recited the Qur'an to them. They wept, submitted and embraced Islam. The fuller account of the Negus, the migration to Abyssinia and the composition of the delegation is given with the preceding verse, and is not repeated here.

What this verse adds is the inner event. Hearing became recognition, recognition became tears, and tears became a spoken request to be counted with the believers.

### Why are such words rewarded?

Paradise is declared here as the reward for certain words. The question is what those words were that entitled their speakers to eternal Paradise.

What they said represented and expressed their whole being. It was the sound of their personality flowing out. They heard Allah's message in such a way that they found the entire truth enshrined in it, and it penetrated their hearts and minds.

It caused a revolution in them, changing the whole focus of their wishes and aspirations until every barrier of prejudice and interest broke down. They identified themselves with the truth so completely that they lost their separate identity and became its witnesses, and becoming a witness meant that truth took root inside them.

For them the Qur'an was never simply a book. It stood as a living sign of the Lord of the universe. That divine experience was expressed in words, but it was not simply a matter of words. It was a turmoil and an earthquake affecting their whole existence, so much so that tears flowed from their eyes.

### What is the significance of words here?

Words spoken about reality do more than make a statement. They are the highest form in which a person gives meaningful shape to his actions and feelings. In the known universe only human beings have the capacity to grasp the refinement and significance of words and to use them to best effect.

Words are therefore the best of what a person has, and a word is eloquent action. When a person demonstrates and voices his servitude to Allah in words, a certain claim to Paradise is established for him. That is why the reward in the verse that follows is given for what they said.

### What does the inward reading draw from this verse?

It notes that faith is to be heard, seen, recognised, spoken and done. Their hearing shows that it is heard. The overflowing eyes show that it is seen. Recognition of the truth shows that it is recognised. Their speaking shows that it is spoken.

The verse a little later describes the recompense of those who do good beautifully, and that shows faith is also to be acted upon. Hearing comes first in the order, because hearing is where it begins. A servant hears the truth and it gladdens him. He accepts it, enters into work and acts upon it. Allah, Lord of all worlds, is pleased with a group holding every one of these traits.

Three marks of recognition are named, and this group is said to hold all three perfectly: weeping, supplication and approval. The weeping is for disloyalty, the supplication is for bestowal, and the approval is of the decree.

Whoever claims recognition without these traits is not truthful in his claim. He is not counted among those who recognise Allah and has no standing among the knights of the path and the religious.

The Pir of the Tariqah is quoted distinguishing two kinds of recognition. That of common people comes by hearsay, and that of the elect by face-to-face vision. The recognition of common people arises out of Allah's munificence, while that of the elect arises from what they find.

Concerning the recognition of common people, Allah describes them hearing what was sent down to the Messenger (5:82-86). Concerning the recognition of the elect, He says that He will show them His signs (27:93). Hearing is praise of the people of the Shariah, and the showing of signs is a felicitation of the people of the Haqiqah.

A warning is attached to both. Whoever speaks of the Shariah and turns his back on it in any respect becomes a heretic. Whoever speaks of the Haqiqah and looks at himself in any respect becomes one who associates partners with Allah.

### What prevents people from this recognition?

The strongest reasons for not accepting the truth are ego and pride. People carrying hidden pride react most violently to the call toward truth. They refuse it whatever the cost, and can end up as its most dangerous opponents.

Those not filled with pride may be flawed by other evils, but they cannot oppose the truth to that extent. That is why the preceding verse named the absence of arrogance as the reason this group was nearest in love to the believers.

### In short

- Hearing the revelation produced tears, recognition and a spoken request to be enrolled among the witnesses.
- The recognition is explained as finding the description of Muhammad ﷺ in their own scripture.
- Their words expressed a change of the whole person, which is why Paradise is given for what they said.
- Faith is heard, seen, recognised, spoken and acted upon, with weeping, supplication and approval as the marks of recognition.
- Pride is what prevents this response, and its absence is what allowed it here.

84.text:
The believers' words continue as an answer to criticism: "Why should we not believe in Allah and the truth that has come to us?" The question is rhetorical. Nothing stands in the way of faith, and they add a hope to be admitted with the righteous.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Why should we not believe in Allah and the truth that has come to us?"** is their reply to those who blamed them for believing. One account says their own people reproached them, and another says Jews reviled them for their Islam.

The truth that came to them is explained as the Qur'an and as the truth reaching them from scripture and the Messenger ﷺ. Nothing prevents faith when its prerequisites are present, and that is the force of the question.

**"And we long for our Lord to include us in the company of the righteous.”"** adds hope to belief. The hoping is described as attached to their believing, and the company they ask for is the righteous among the community of Muhammad ﷺ, admitted with the believers into Paradise.

One explanation describes that hope as entering the Garden in the company of the prophets and of those who followed them in obeying Allah and dreading His punishment. Another states the wish as being admitted by their Lord along with the righteous people.

### Why is the reply phrased as a question?

They were being reproached for something that carries no rational obstacle. The question turns the reproach back on the reproachers. What reason is there not to believe, when the truth has come and its conditions are met, and when the shahadah they gave asks for nothing but the truth?

That form of answer also records their confidence. They do not defend themselves by minimising the truth or by claiming a private exception. They ask why belief should be surprising at all.

### What does the hope add to the belief?

Belief is not presented as complete without a direction. They believe, and they hope to be admitted with the righteous. The hope keeps their faith social rather than self-sufficient, since the company they want is the company of obedient people.

The same verse group describes such Christians elsewhere as among the People of the Scripture who believe in Allah and in what was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ and in what was revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah (3:199). Others are described as given the Scripture before this Book, believing in it and saying that they were already Muslims before it came (28:52-53), and as not seeking the company of the ignorant (28:55).

Those descriptions match the words here. The hope to be admitted with the righteous is the same posture as humbling themselves before Allah and refusing the company of the ignorant.

### In short

- The question answers reproach by asking what obstacle to faith could exist once truth has come.
- The truth named is the Qur'an and what reached them through scripture and the Messenger ﷺ.
- Their hope is admission with the righteous, described as the upright among the Prophet's ﷺ community.
- Parallel passages describe the same people as humbling themselves before Allah and refusing the company of the ignorant.

85.text:
The answer to those words is a reward: "So Allah will reward them for what they said with Gardens under which rivers flow". The reward corresponds to the declaration. It is permanent, and it is described as the reward of those who do good.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So Allah will reward them for what they said"** ties the reward to their statement. One gloss explains it as Allah decreeing this for them because they gave their shahadah, their declaration of faith, voluntarily. They were not compelled, and the declaration was their own.

The reward is given for embracing faith and for recognising and believing the truth. Their words were the outward form of that recognition, which is why the reward is expressed in terms of what they said.

**"with Gardens under which rivers flow"** describes the reward. The rivers are described in one account as flowing beneath its trees and dwellings, and as rivers of water, milk, wine and honey. Another describes gardens with palaces and trees overlooking flowing streams.

**"to stay there forever."** They will remain in Paradise forever, never dying and never being removed from it.

**"And that is the reward of the good-doers"** identifies who receives it. The good are explained as those who testify to Allah's oneness, and another explanation describes them as those who are kind in speech and action. A third describes them as virtuous through believing.

Another account describes the good-doers as people who pursue the truth and comply with it in every place, at every time and through whoever brings it. A further explanation describes doing good as following that truth and yielding to it with no restriction and no condition attached.

### Why is the reward tied to words?

The verse that follows the declaration describes Paradise as given for what they said. Their words were not empty formulas. They carried the whole weight of a changed allegiance, and the reward corresponds to that.

This does not make speech a substitute for action. The description of the good-doers includes obedience to the truth wherever it is found, and the inward reading of the preceding verse lists acting upon faith as its completion.

### What does following the truth wherever it is found mean?

It means accepting the truth without regard for the identity of the person who brings it or the community it comes from. The people rewarded here recognised the Qur'an as continuous with what they had received, and they submitted.

That is the quality the description stresses. Their reward is not for belonging to a particular group but for recognising and obeying the truth when it stood before them, without condition and without reservation.

### In short

- The reward answers their declaration and is given because they professed faith voluntarily.
- Gardens with flowing rivers and permanent dwelling are described, with rivers of water, milk, wine and honey in one account.
- The good-doers are explained as those who testify to Allah's oneness, who are kind in speech and action, and who obey the truth wherever they find it.
- The reward is tied to words that carried a real change of allegiance, not to speech in place of action.

86.text:
The contrast is stated in a single sentence: "As for those who disbelieve and reject Our signs, they will be the residents of the Hellfire." The verse that has just described a permanent reward now describes a permanent loss, and the difference between the two groups lies in their response to the same signs.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who disbelieve"** concerns disbelief in Allah. The group is set against those just rewarded, and no middle position is described between the two outcomes.

**"and reject Our signs"** adds denial of the revelations. One gloss identifies them as Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, and another describes the denial as defiance and opposition to the signs.

**"they will be the residents of the Hellfire"** states their end. They are described as the people of the Fire and its companions, entering it and remaining without leaving, and as its owners and folk.

### Why is this verse placed here?

It completes the comparison begun with the two groups described earlier in this passage. The delegation that wept and asked to be enrolled among the witnesses received gardens. Those who denied the signs receive the Fire.

The same signs were available to both. The difference was not in the evidence but in the response to it. That is why the preceding verses stress recognition, humility and the absence of pride.

### What does the permanence of both outcomes show?

The reward is described as dwelling forever, and the punishment as residence without exit. Neither outcome is provisional, and neither depends on communal identity.

The verse therefore closes the passage by removing any expectation that a religious label settles the matter. What settles it is belief in Allah, acceptance of His signs and the conduct that follows.

### In short

- Disbelief in Allah and denial of His signs lead to residence in the Fire.
- The signs denied are identified with Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, and the denial is described as defiance.
- The verse completes the comparison with the rewarded group, showing that both outcomes are permanent.
- The same signs were before both groups, so the difference lies in the response rather than in the evidence.

87.text:
A warning is given against a piety that oversteps: "Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress." The verse was revealed about Companions who wanted to abandon marriage, food and sleep, and even to mutilate themselves, in order to draw nearer to Allah.

Their intention was good. They said so themselves. The answer given to them defines the shape of Islamic devotion, and it closes with the statement that Allah does not like transgressors.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you"** prohibits declaring unlawful what Allah has permitted. One explanation specifies good food, drink and women, and forbids treating them as unlawful in an attempt to practise asceticism and devotion.

**"and do not transgress."** is explained in two directions. Do not exaggerate and make things hard for yourselves by prohibiting what is permitted. Do not exceed the limits by indulging excessively in permitted things either, but take what satisfies your need and avoid extravagance.

One gloss identifies the transgression meant here with cutting off the male organs, and describes the transgressors as those who move from the lawful to the unlawful by mutilating themselves.

**"Indeed, Allah does not like transgressors"** closes the warning. The explanation adds that Allah does not love those who overstep His limits, and rather hates that conduct.

Two other verses give the measure. People are told to eat and drink without wasting through extravagance (7:31), and the servants of the Merciful are described as neither extravagant nor miserly when they spend, holding a middle way between those extremes (25:67).

Allah legislated a middle way between those who go to extremes and those who fall short. It permits neither excessive application nor neglect.

### What did the Companions propose?

'Ali bin Abi Talhah reports Ibn 'Abbas saying the verse was revealed about some Companions of the Prophet ﷺ who said they should cut off their male organs, abandon the desires of this life and travel through the land as monks do. Ibn Abi Hatim also collected the report, and Ibn Marduwyah recorded a similar narration through Al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

When the Prophet ﷺ heard of it he summoned them and asked whether they had said so. They answered that they had. He then said that he fasts and breaks his fast, prays and sleeps, and marries women, and that whoever follows his Sunnah belongs to him while whoever abandons his Sunnah does not.

The Two Sahihs record 'A'ishah describing some Companions asking the wives of the Prophet ﷺ about his worship in private. One said he would not eat meat, another that he would not marry women, and a third that he would not sleep on a bed.

Hearing this, the Prophet ﷺ asked what was the matter with people saying such things. He said that he fasts and breaks the fast, sleeps and rises to pray, eats meat and marries women, and that whoever is not pleased with his Sunnah is not of him.

Another account describes a number of Companions resolving to keep fasting and night vigil without interruption and to abstain from women, perfume, meat and sleeping on beds.

### Who are named in the longer reports?

One account says the verse concerns ten Companions. It names 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Abu Dharr, Salman al-Farisi, Salim the client of Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad al-Kindi, 'Uthman ibn Maz'un al-Jumahi, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, 'Ali, 'Umar and Abu Bakr. They made their pledge in the house of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un.

The pledge was to eat and drink only enough to stay alive, to have no relations with their wives, never to eat meat or fat, and to cut off their male organs. Allah forbade such acts and revealed the verse about them.

A longer narrative sets the scene. The Messenger ﷺ sat one day and admonished the people, describing the Day of Judgment and mentioning only what would instil fear. Their hearts softened and they wept.

Ten Companions then gathered in the house of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un al-Jumahi. The names given are Ma'qil ibn Muqarrin, Salman al-Farisi, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, Salim the client of Abu Hudhayfah, Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

They agreed to fast by day and stand in prayer by night. They would take no meat and no fat. They would not lie with their wives or use perfume, and they would not sleep in beds. They would wear coarse wool, give up the worldly life, wander the land as monks and cut off their male organs.

When the Messenger ﷺ heard of it he gathered them and asked whether he had been informed correctly that they had agreed on such things. They said that it was so, but that they had intended nothing but good.

He answered that he had not been commanded to do those things, and that their own selves have a right over them. Fast and break the fast. Stand in prayer at night and sleep, for he stands at night and also sleeps. He sometimes fasts and sometimes does not, and he eats meat and fat.

The two lists differ in some names, and both are preserved as reported rather than merged into one roster.

### Is there another reported occasion?

Yes. A report through 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas describes a man who came to the Prophet ﷺ and said that he had forbidden meat to himself, because whenever he ate it he felt the urge for women. This verse and the one following are given as revealed on that account.

The reports therefore differ between a group pledge and an individual's vow. Both illustrate the same prohibition, and neither is cancelled by the other.

### How can a lawful thing be made unlawful?

The legal discussion identifies three forms. The first is in belief, that is, holding something to be haram, unlawful, when it is in fact halal. Where its lawfulness is established by decisive proof, a person who considers it unlawful becomes a kafir, a disbeliever, through that open contravention of the divinely ordained law.

The second is verbal. A person declares something unlawful for himself by an oath, for example swearing that he will never drink cold water, or will not eat a particular lawful food, or will not do something permitted. The detailed forms of oath are set out in books of fiqh.

In that case the oath takes effect. The rule given is that taking such oaths unnecessarily is a sin, and if one has been taken, the person must break it and make amends through the kaffarah, the expiation of an oath, whose details come later in this chapter.

The third form is practical. A person neither believes nor says anything, but decides in practice to abandon a lawful thing permanently.

If he treats that abandonment as an act of thawab, merit and reward, it is bid'ah, innovation in the established religion, and rahbaniyah, monasticism. That is a grave sin stated categorically in the Qur'an and Sunnah, acting against it is wajib, a binding obligation, and adhering to such a restriction is itself sinful.

If the restriction is not undertaken for merit but for another reason, such as a physical or spiritual illness that leads a person to give something up permanently, there is no sin in it. Reports of some Sufis and other pious elders abandoning certain lawful things are placed in this third category. They found those things harmful to their desiring selves, or a pious elder advised them to abstain as harmful in their case, so they gave them up as treatment and remedy.

### What is the right attitude toward lawful things?

Transgression here means abandoning something lawful as an act of merit without a valid excuse. An ignorant person takes that to be taqwa, the fear of Allah, while in Allah's sight it is transgression and is impermissible.

The following verse therefore commands eating of the good and pure provision Allah has given and fearing Him in whom they believe. Leaving good and pure things aside as a means of earning reward is not taqwa. Taqwa lies in using them as Allah's blessings and showing gratitude for them.

Abandoning something as a cure for a physical or spiritual illness does not fall under this rule.

### Why does the passage come here?

The subject returns to subsidiary rulings after the long discussion of the People of the Book. A particular link is also noted. Monasticism had been mentioned in a complimentary sense shortly before, in respect of one feature of it, which is the abandonment of worldly desires.

Since someone might infer that monasticism as a whole is praiseworthy, it was fitting at this point to forbid making unlawful what Allah has made lawful. Renunciation of worldly life and restraint of appetite are favourable within a certain limit, but transgressing the divinely ordained limits in this matter is blameworthy and unlawful.

### What is the deeper problem with renunciation?

The connection between a person and Allah is a living relationship established at the level of the heart and is inward in nature. When religion declines and that inward relationship weakens, a mentality develops that the relationship must be built up from outward means.

Among these means is the surrender of worldly comfort, which amounts to renunciation or the monastic life. The assumption behind it is that distancing oneself from material things draws a person closer to Allah. Some Companions were influenced by such thoughts and intended to stop eating meat and sleeping at night, to castrate themselves and to leave their homes to live as hermits, with some taking a vow or oath to that effect.

They were prohibited from this and told that nearness to Allah is not attained by treating permitted things as forbidden. Whatever a person achieves comes from remaining within natural limits, not from inventing stricter ones.

### In short

- Declaring lawful things unlawful, whether by belief, by oath or by settled practice for merit, is forbidden.
- The reports name a group pledge of ten Companions and an individual's vow about meat, and both are preserved.
- The Prophet ﷺ answered with his own practice of fasting and breaking fast, praying and sleeping, eating meat and marrying.
- Transgression runs in two directions, prohibiting the permitted and exceeding in its use, with a middle way legislated between them.
- Restraint for a genuine medical or spiritual reason is not the monasticism condemned here, and taqwa lies in gratitude for blessings rather than in refusing them.

88.text:
The prohibition is followed by a positive command: "Eat of the good, lawful things provided to you by Allah." The verse does not leave the believer between two refusals. It commands enjoyment of what is pure and lawful, and joins that enjoyment to mindfulness of Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Eat of the good, lawful things provided to you by Allah."** is a command to take what Allah has bestowed as food that is halal, lawful and good. One explanation describes eating items that are pure and permitted.

The command carries its own limit. Another explanation says to consume the halal and pure things from Allah's provision, and to keep away from the haram, such as what is taken wrongfully or what is impure.

**"And be mindful of Allah in Whom you believe"** joins the eating to faith. Mindfulness is explained as guarding against Allah in all affairs, obeying Him and seeking His pleasure while staying away from defiance and disobedience.

One gloss specifies fearing Allah concerning mutilation and forbidding what He has made lawful. Another describes mindfulness as doing what He instructs and leaving what He forbids, since the One they believe in is the One who lays that duty upon them.

### Why does the command to eat follow the prohibition?

Because the two verses form one instruction. The first removes a false piety, and the second establishes the right relation to provision. Eating what is lawful and good is not a concession to weakness. It is part of obedience.

Faith in Allah is named as the ground of mindfulness. The One who made these things lawful is the One to be feared, so gratitude and restraint belong together rather than competing.

### What does mindfulness look like in this matter?

It looks like using blessings as blessings. Taqwa here is described as taking what Allah has provided and showing gratitude for it, not as refusing it in order to earn merit.

It also looks like staying within limits. The prohibition of transgression in the preceding verse covers both making the lawful unlawful and exceeding in its use, so mindfulness governs the quantity as well as the intention.

### In short

- The command is to eat what Allah has provided that is lawful and good, and to avoid what is unlawful or impure.
- Mindfulness of Allah is tied to faith in Him, and covers obedience, seeking His pleasure and avoiding defiance.
- The two verses together remove a false piety and establish gratitude as the right relation to provision.
- Restraint is required in quantity as well as in intention, since transgression runs in both directions.

89.text:
The subject moves from declaring halal, that is lawful, things unlawful to the words used to do it: "Allah will not call you to account for your thoughtless oaths, but He will hold you accountable for deliberate oaths." Statements making lawful things forbidden are sometimes sworn, so the ruling on oaths follows.

The verse distinguishes oaths that carry no consequence from oaths that do, and then sets out the expiation in detail. It closes by telling believers to guard their oaths and by describing this clarification as a reason for gratitude.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah will not call you to account for your thoughtless oaths"** concerns laghw, what is not counted. It is explained as a word of oath slipping from the tongue without intention, such as saying no by Allah or yes by Allah, and as swearing about something assumed true that turns out to be false.

**"but He will hold you accountable for deliberate oaths."** concerns oaths intended in the heart. The accountability described here is worldly, taking the form of expiation, since the wording is set against the oaths a person has bound himself with.

**"The penalty for a broken oath is to feed ten poor people from what you normally feed your own family"** names the first option. The poor meant are those in need, unable to find the necessities of life. The measure is discussed below.

**"or to clothe them, or to free a bondsperson."** adds two further options. All three are expiations for a deliberate oath, and whichever a person chooses suffices by consensus.

**"But if none of this is affordable, then you must fast three days."** provides for the person who cannot bear the cost. He lacks the means to feed ten poor people, clothe them or free a slave, so his expiation is fasting.

**"This is the penalty for breaking your oaths."** identifies this as the legal way to atone for a deliberate oath that has been broken.

**"So be mindful of your oaths."** is explained in three ways, given below.

**"This is how Allah makes things clear to you, so perhaps you will be grateful"** describes Allah expounding His commands and prohibitions as He has expounded the expiation of oaths, so that people may be grateful for the clarification. Another explanation describes the laws as making clear what is lawful and what is unlawful, so that people may thank Allah for teaching them what they did not know.

### What are the three kinds of oath?

The first is yamin ghamus, the disastrous oath. It is swearing falsely about a past event with knowledge, as when a person did something, knows he did it, and then swears that he did not. Jurists call it a grave major sin whose curse falls in this life and the next.

No kaffarah, expiation, is required for it. Taubah, repentance, and istighfar, seeking Allah's forgiveness, are what it requires. Ghamus literally means that which drowns, and this oath drowns a person in sin and its curse, a disaster for his present and future life.

The second is yamin laghw, the ineffectual oath. A person declares on oath that a past event was true on the basis of his knowledge, while it was in fact false. He may have been told that someone had arrived and sworn to it in trust, only to learn that the opposite was the case.

The same category covers an oath word such as by, or I swear, said without intention. This kind of oath brings neither expiation nor sin.

The third is al-yamin al-mun'aqidah, the binding oath, in which a person swears that he will or will not do something in the future. If it is broken, expiation becomes necessary. In some situations breaking it also brings sin, and in others it does not.

### How do the two verses on oaths relate?

In Al-Baqarah the statement is that Allah does not hold people accountable for what is not countable among their oaths, but holds them accountable for what their hearts have designed (2:225). There, laghw means an oath slipping out without intention or volition, or an oath about something assumed true that turns out false.

Set against it is the oath containing an intentional lie, which is yamin ghamus. So laghw brings no sin, while the sin belongs to the intentional lie.

The sin mentioned in Al-Baqarah is therefore the sin incurred in the Hereafter for disobeying a divine injunction. The ruling in this verse concerns the present life, where expiation is required. Allah does not oblige amends for what is not countable, and He does oblige expiation for a binding oath about the future that is then broken.

The subject of unintentional oaths was treated in Al-Baqarah and is not repeated here at length.

### What measure of food is required?

The wording speaks of the awsat, the middle or average, of what people feed their families. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id bin Jubayr and 'Ikrimah explain it as the average scale of family food. 'Ata' Al-Khurasani reads it as the best of what people feed their families.

One explanation gives it as bread and the seasoning served at lunch and dinner. Another describes the midmost food a family consumes, neither better nor worse, at one mudd measure for each needy person. A third gives the average food of a person's city at half a sa' for each poor person.

The legal discussion develops two ways of discharging this duty, since the word used can mean either feeding someone or giving him food. The person paying expiation may choose either.

He may invite ten poor people and feed them. Then he must satisfy ten poor people with both of the day's meals, giving them to their fill from the middling food he and his family normally eat at home. One account describes this as two average meals for ten poor persons.

Or he may place the food in their ownership. In that case he gives each of the ten one fitrah amount per person, which is one and three quarter kilograms of wheat, or its value in cash. Fasting suffices only when a person cannot take any of the three options.

### What clothing is required?

Each of the ten is to be clothed with something suitable to pray in, whether the poor person is male or female. Al-'Awfi reports Ibn 'Abbas giving a robe or garment for each of the ten.

Mujahid says the least of clothing intended is a garment, and the most is whatever a person wishes. Abu Malik, Hammad bin Abi Sulayman, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i, Tawus, 'Ata', Abu Ja'far Al-Baqir and Al-Hasan give a garment for each.

Other explanations describe clothing that covers nakedness, such as a shawl, a gown or a loin cloth, and covering described as what genuinely counts as clothing, for instance a shirt, a turban or a waist wrap. One account specifies covering sufficient to clothe them properly, meaning a wrap for the lower body together with one for the upper. Another describes what society counts as a suit of clothing.

Al-Shafi'i is cited for the position that it is not sufficient to give all these items to a single needy person.

### Which slave is to be freed?

The freeing is explained as freeing a believing slave. A lengthy hadith appears in Malik's Muwatta', in the Sahih of Muslim and in the Musnad of Ash-Shafi'i. It reports that 'Umar bin Al-Hakam As-Sulami had to free a slave as atonement and brought a black slave girl before the Messenger ﷺ.

He asked her where Allah is, and she answered that He is above the heavens. He asked who he was, and she answered that he is the Messenger of Allah. He then told 'Umar to free her, because she is a believer.

One gloss restricts the general wording in the same way as in the expiation for killing or for repudiation through zihar, so that the slave freed must be a believer.

### Must the options be followed in order?

No. Allah mentioned the easiest option first and the harder ones after it, since feeding is easier than giving clothing and clothing is easier than freeing a slave. That ordering does not oblige a person to attempt them in sequence.

The position that following the order is not obligatory is attributed to al-Shāfi'ī, and the wider statement is that whichever option a person chooses suffices by consensus. The same jurist is also cited in the ruling on clothing given above.

### Must the three fasts be consecutive?

Ubayy bin Ka'b, Ibn Mas'ud and his students are reported as reading the verse with the addition of three consecutive days. Even if that wording is not transmitted as part of the Qur'an through mass narration, it stands as an explanation by Companions and carries the ruling of something related from the Prophet ﷺ.

On that basis Abu Hanifah and some other imams hold that the three fasts of the expiation of an oath must be consecutive. Another gloss likewise gives a three day fast consecutively.

### Can expiation be paid before the oath is broken?

No. Abu Hanifah and other imams explain the closing words as meaning that when a sworn statement about the future is violated, its expiation is what has been described. The expiation must be given after the oath is broken.

The reason is that the cause making expiation necessary lies in the breaking. As long as the oath is unbroken, no expiation is required. Just as there is no salah before its time and no Ramadan fast before the month of Ramadan, so the expiation of an oath cannot be given before the oath breaks.

One account puts the same point positively. If breaking the oath is the better course, a person should break it and then give the atonement.

### What does guarding one's oaths mean?

Three explanations are given. Ibn Jarir explains it as not leaving broken oaths without paying their expiation.

Another says that if a person has sworn to something, he should not break his oath without a legal or physical necessity. A third, given in Mazhari, says a person should not hasten to make a sworn statement at all. He should guard his oath as though keeping it in reserve and should not swear casually except under severe compulsion.

One gloss adds that oaths should not be broken unless it is for a righteous deed or to set right between people, as stated in the verse of Surat al-Baqara (2:225). Another warns against oaths taken falsely in Allah's name as well as against breaking them.

### What is the real renunciation this passage points to?

The discussion connects the verse with what preceded it. Real monasticism in Islam consists of the fear of Allah and gratitude to Him.

Fear of Allah makes a person abstain from what He has forbidden. When desire awakens for something haram, forbidden, that fear restrains him from satisfying it. When anger rises to the point of wanting to kill, it stays his hand. His heart may urge an unrestricted life, but fear of Allah's wrath keeps him inside the prescribed limits.

Gratitude works the same way from the other side. When a grateful person receives health, wealth, position, goods and a share of popularity, they do not lead him into self-importance or boasting. He takes everything as Allah's gift and concedes that all he enjoys is by grace, and he is overwhelmed by gratitude and humility.

These are the emotions that join a person to Allah. Through fearing Him and being grateful he comes close to Him. Keeping away from material things is certainly a virtue, but the distancing has to be a mental process and not merely a physical one.

### What does the inward reading make of oaths?

It observes that the chevaliers of the Tariqah, when ecstasy overpowers them, will at times take oaths that renew the covenant and confirm the compact. Their words take a form like this: by what is due to You, I shall look at nothing besides You, speak to nothing besides You, and never abandon Your covenant.

Measured against tawhid, the affirmation of Allah's oneness, oaths of that kind count as idle talk. They show negligence in the witnessing of unity. What standing has a servant to assign himself value, to imagine that he is somebody, or to treat his own words as weighty enough for swearing an oath to his Lord?

The servant's part is to receive Allah's rulings with a fine approval. If Allah calls him near or pushes him away, he neither objects nor withdraws. Talk of the realities of joining and parting is not for him. He takes whatever is given and accepts whatever arrives. In truth Allah is the One whose kindness reaches perfection, and He is the One who decides and disposes in every condition.

The Pir of the Tariqah is quoted praying to the One closer to us than ourselves and more lovingly kind to us than ourselves, who caresses us without us by His generosity rather than because of our worthiness or our works. The load exceeds what we can carry, the practice is not ours to perform and the favour lies past our power. Our own doing has only harmed us, while what You have done endures for us. Whatever You have done standing in our place, You did by Yourself and not on our account.

People of knowledge are familiar with expiation in the Shariah as the freeing of slaves and as feeding and clothing the poor. In the language of allusion the path has its own threefold expiation. The spirit is spent in ecstasy, the heart in sincerity of intention, and the soul in unceasing effort.

Whoever cannot do that should abstain and fast from what is forbidden and blameworthy. The inward reading therefore mirrors the three options and the fasting that replaces them, without cancelling the outward ruling.

### In short

- Oaths are of three kinds, and only the binding oath about the future requires expiation when broken.
- The expiation is feeding, clothing or freeing a believing slave, in any order, with three fasts for whoever cannot afford them.
- Measures differ in the explanations, from two filling meals to stated amounts of wheat, and the fasts are held by some to be consecutive.
- Expiation cannot be paid before the oath is broken, and guarding oaths includes not swearing casually and not leaving a broken oath unexpiated.
- True renunciation is fear of Allah and gratitude to Him, an inward distancing rather than a merely physical one.

90.text:
Four things are named together and given one description: "Intoxicants, gambling, idols, and drawing lots for decisions are all evil of Satan’s handiwork." The verse then commands avoidance and attaches a promise to it. Success depends on staying away.

The grouping matters. Intoxicants and gambling are placed beside idolatry and divination, which tells the reader how serious the first two are considered.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Intoxicants"** concerns khamr, what intoxicates and overcomes the mind. 'Umar bin Al-Khattab described it in a speech from the minbar of the Messenger ﷺ as extracted from five things: grapes, dates, honey, wheat and barley, and he defined it as whatever intoxicates the mind.

Al-Bukhari records Ibn 'Umar saying the prohibition came down when there were five kinds of intoxicant in Al-Madinah besides what was made from grapes. A report in Muslim gives the general rule that every intoxicant is khamr and every intoxicant is unlawful.

**"gambling"** is maysir. Ibn 'Umar says it means gambling, and Ad-Dahhak reports the same from Ibn 'Abbas, who added that people gambled during the period of ignorance until Islam came and Allah forbade that evil behaviour.

'Ali bin Abi Talib is reported as saying that chess is a kind of gambling. 'Ata', Mujahid and Tawus, or two of them, are reported as saying that every form of gambling counts, including children playing with a certain kind of nut.

**"idols"** concerns al-ansab. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', Sa'id bin Jubayr and Al-Hasan describe them as altar stones near which sacrifices were offered in the period of ignorance. Another explanation gives the singular as nusub and describes it as anything set up to be worshipped, whether an idol, a stone or a tree.

**"and drawing lots for decisions"** concerns al-azlam, the arrows used for divination and lotteries. The practice is described below.

**"are all evil of Satan’s handiwork."** Rijs is explained as abomination or filth by 'Ali bin Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, as sin by Sa'id bin Jubayr, and as evil handiwork of Satan by Zayd bin Aslam. One gloss says they are unlawful because they are instigated by the devil's order and whispering, and another that Satan adorns them.

The word is explained in Arabic usage as something foul and disgusting to human taste. All four are repulsive to anyone with common sense and good taste.

**"So shun them so you may be successful"** commands avoidance of all these abominations and is a statement of encouragement. Success in this world and the next is made to depend on abstaining, and one gloss describes it as escaping Allah's anger and punishment and being safe in the Hereafter.

### How was the prohibition revealed in stages?

Ahmad records Abu Hurayrah describing three stages. When the Messenger ﷺ migrated to Al-Madinah, people were drinking and gambling and asked him about both. Allah revealed that in them is great sin and some benefit for people (2:219).

The people said that they had not been forbidden, since Allah had only mentioned sin along with benefit, and they went on drinking. Then one of the emigrants led his companions in the Maghrib prayer and confused the verses in his recitation.

A tougher statement followed, forbidding believers to approach prayer in a drunken state until they know what they are saying (4:43). People then drank before the time of prayer so that they would attend it sober.

The firmer verse came later, in this chapter, describing these things as an abomination of Satan's handiwork and commanding avoidance (5:90-91). The people said that they had abstained, O Lord.

### What is reported about 'Umar?

Ahmad records 'Umar bin Al-Khattab praying that Allah would make the ruling on khamr clear to them. The verse in Al-Baqarah was revealed and recited to him, and he repeated his request.

The verse in An-Nisa' then came, and the Prophet ﷺ had someone announce at prayer time that those in a drunken state must not approach prayer. 'Umar was again summoned and again asked for clarity.

When the verse in Al-Ma'idah was revealed and recited to him, and he reached the words asking whether they would then abstain (5:91), he said that they had abstained, twice. Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i record the hadith, and 'Ali bin Al-Madini and At-Tirmidhi graded it sahih, authentic.

### What happened on the day of prohibition?

Ahmad records Anas saying that he was pouring an alcoholic drink in Abu Talhah's house for Suhayl bin Bayda', 'Ubayy bin Ka'b, Abu 'Ubaydah bin Al-Jarrah and several of their friends. When they were nearly intoxicated, some Muslims came and asked whether they did not know that khamr had been prohibited.

They said they would wait and ask, then told Anas to spill what remained in his container. By Allah, they never drank it again, and their drink at that time was made from unripe and ordinary dates. This is also in the Two Sahihs.

Another narration from Anas describes him as the cupbearer in Abu Talhah's house when the prohibition came. A caller announced it, Abu Talhah sent him to see what it was about, and he found a person proclaiming that alcoholic drinks were forbidden. Abu Talhah ordered him to go out and spill the wine, and it flowed in the streets of Al-Madinah.

Ibn Jarir records Anas bin Malik pouring for Suhayl bin Bayda', Mu'adh bin Jabal, Abu Dujanah, Abu 'Ubaydah bin Al-Jarrah and Abu Talhah until they were intoxicated by a drink of mixed unripe and ordinary dates. He then heard someone announce that khamr had been made unlawful.

Nobody went in or out until they had spilled the drink and broken its barrels. Some performed ablution and others washed, and they put on perfume. They then went out to the mosque while the Messenger ﷺ was reciting this verse and the one after it.

Another account records Anas describing wine made from unripe dates, split unripe dates and dates, and the crier's announcement, after which wine ran in the streets of Madinah. Muslim narrates it through Abu'l-Rabi and Al-Bukhari through Abu Nu'man, both from Hammad.

### What does the curse attached to khamr include?

Ahmad records Ibn 'Umar reporting the Messenger ﷺ as cursing ten matters connected with khamr: the drink itself, its drinker, its server, its seller, its buyer, its brewer, the one who asks for it to be brewed, its carrier, the one it is carried to and the one who consumes its price. Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah record the hadith.

Ahmad also records Ibn 'Umar describing the Messenger ﷺ going out with him. He walked on the Prophet's ﷺ right until Abu Bakr came and he gave way, and 'Umar then walked on the left. The Prophet ﷺ found a hanging leather skin containing alcohol, asked for a knife and ordered it cut open.

He then repeated the curse on khamr and on those who drink, serve, sell, buy, carry, have it carried, brew, have it brewed and consume its price. The prohibition therefore surrounds the trade and not merely the act of drinking.

Ash-Shafi'i narrates from Malik from Nafi' that Ibn 'Umar reported the Messenger ﷺ as saying that whoever drinks khamr in this life and does not repent will be deprived of it in the Hereafter. Al-Bukhari and Muslim record it. Muslim also records that whoever drinks and dies addicted to it without repenting will not drink it in the Hereafter.

### What incident prompted the revelation according to other reports?

Al-Bayhaqi records Sa'd describing four verses revealed about khamr. A man from the Ansar prepared food and invited them. They drank before the prohibition and became intoxicated, then began boasting of their status.

The Ansar claimed to be better, and Quraysh among the emigrants claimed the same. One of the Ansar picked up a bone, hit Sa'd on the nose and opened a flesh wound there. The scar stayed with him from that day. The verses on intoxicants and gambling up to the question about abstaining were then revealed. Muslim records the hadith.

### What did 'Uthman say about drink?

'Abdur-Rahman bin Al-Harith bin Hisham reports hearing 'Uthman bin 'Affan tell people to avoid khamr because it is the mother of all sins. He described a worshipper of earlier times who lived secluded from people.

An evil woman loved him and sent her servant to say they wanted him as a witness. He went, and each door was locked behind him until he reached a beautiful woman with a young boy and some alcohol. She told him she had not invited him to witness anything but to have intercourse with her, kill the boy or drink the alcohol.

She gave him drink and he kept asking for more until, intoxicated, he had intercourse with her and killed the boy. 'Uthman concluded that khamr should be avoided because it is never combined with faith, and one of the two must expel the other.

Al-Bayhaqi records the statement and its chain is authentic. Abu Bakr bin Abi Ad-Dunya also recorded it in his book on the prohibition of intoxicants but related it from the Prophet ﷺ. Relating it from 'Uthman is described as more authentic.

### Is this prohibition found in earlier revelation?

'Abdullah bin 'Amr is reported as saying that this verse was also in the Torah. The wording given describes Allah sending truth to erase falsehood, joyful play, wind instruments, dances, cabarets using the lute and bagpipe, tambourine, guitar, harp and amatory poetry, and describes khamr as bitter to whoever tastes it.

Allah is then reported as vowing by His grace and power that whoever drinks it after the prohibition will be made thirsty on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever leaves it after the prohibition will taste it in the residence of grace. The chain is described as sahih.

### Why are idols named with drink and gambling?

The main purpose of the verse, evident from its background and the verse that follows, is that drinking and gambling are agencies of corruption and therefore unlawful. Altar stones and idols are added so that listeners understand drinking and gambling to be as serious a crime as idol worship.

Ibn Majah records the Prophet ﷺ saying that a drinker is like an idol worshipper, with some narrations naming the idols Al-Laat and Al-'Uzza. The comparison explains the grouping rather than equating the legal categories.

### How did the divining arrows work?

Azlam is the plural of zalam and names the arrows used for drawing lots in gambling, an Arab practice of the time. Ten people would join as partners and slaughter a camel.

Instead of dividing the meat into ten equal shares, they turned the division into a gamble. Of ten arrows they marked seven with signs indicating one, two or three shares and left three blank. All were put in a quiver and shaken, and each participant drew one.

Whoever drew a marked arrow received that number of shares, and whoever drew a blank went without. The practice resembles the many lottery style games and ventures familiar today. Taking lots this way is qimar, gambling, and the Qur'an makes it haram.

### Is any drawing of lots permitted?

One form is permitted and established from the Prophet ﷺ. Where everyone's rights are equal and the shares have already been divided equally, lots may decide who receives which share.

The example given is a house to be divided among four sharers in four portions of equal value. If mutual agreement cannot settle who takes which, lots may decide it. Another example is a thousand people with equal claims to only a hundred items.

The pagan custom of distributing meat by divining arrows was already prohibited earlier in this chapter, in the wording about determining shares through the arrows (5:3). Maysir and azlam are therefore the same in outcome, while ansab belongs with idolatry.

### What is the inward warning about drink?

A prophetic saying describes wine as the gatherer of sin and the mother of loathsome things. It is described as the root of what is loathsome, the key that opens great sins, the ground misdeeds grow from, the seed of crooked acts and the wellspring of strife.

It dries the spring from which obedience flows, dams the water of remembrance and swings the door open to negligence. The soul grows drunk from wine and is kept from prayer, and the heart grows drunk from heedlessness and is kept from intimate whispering.

The Pir of the Tariqah is quoted admonishing such people. Drunkards full of appetite and sleepers in negligence are told to feel shame before the Lord acquainted with the eyes' betrayal and with everything the chest hides (40:19).

The admonition asks where there is a whip like 'Umar's or a sword like 'Ali's to give these discourteous drunkards the punishment of the Shariah in the world of justice and to rouse the sleeping and heedless. It asks whether the wretch who drinks does not know that when he raises the cup the Throne and the Footstool tremble, and that a call comes from the exalted presence swearing by Allah's majesty to make them taste His chastisement in boiling water and the tree of Zaqqum.

### What does the inward reading make of gambling?

Arrow shuffling is gambling. The passage observes that in a gambling house someone who stakes everything and loses all is considered great and recognised as one who goes ahead.

The passage turns this into an allusion to how the chevaliers travel. They cast themselves onto the road of what is already decreed, content to be abased before any scrap of straw, to slip out of bondage to every colour and to reckon themselves as nothing at all.

As long as a person remains bound to colour, nature, the spheres and the stars, he is not in a position to speak like a Qalandar. The comparison contrasts staking everything on chance with surrendering everything to Allah.

### What damage do these practices do to a society?

Intoxicants, gambling, frequenting places where beings other than Allah are worshipped or offered sacrifice, and drawing lots that seek help from other than Allah are all base and satanic acts. They lead a person to mental and physical downfall.

Intoxicants destroy the refined feelings in a person. Arrows and lots rest on superficial thought or superstitious belief. Islam wants a person to be a rememberer and worshipper of Allah, wholly obedient to Him and His Prophet ﷺ, and seriousness is absolutely necessary for that. These misdeeds are the greatest destroyers of seriousness.

Islam aims to form a person who recognises realities and rises above materialism. Intoxicants make a person forgetful of realities, arrows and lots plunge him into the dark depths of superstition, and gambling drives him into materialism to a criminal degree.

Intoxicants produce an excessive loss of awareness of what is proper, and gambling produces excessive selfishness. These are described as the two root causes of disturbance and riot. Whoever loses moral awareness also loses respect for the dignity and property of others, becoming brazen in tyranny and injustice and in harassing people.

Gambling is the worst form of exploitation and selfishness, since it enables a person to strip many people and enrich himself. A drunkard has no awareness of other people's trouble or grief, and for a gambler other people are only objects of exploitation. A society containing such people is spoiled by clashes and enmity, and its members live in mutual mistrust and recrimination.

### How do these verses fit the surrounding passage?

The preceding verses forbade treating lawful things as unlawful. These forbid particular unlawful things. Together they set the rule for using a created world that serves human beings.

Everything in the universe is described as appointed to serve people, with one restriction: do not transgress the limits Allah has set while benefiting from what He created. Refraining from good and lawful things made halal is bad manners and ingratitude, while contravening what is prohibited is disobedience and rebellion.

A servant of Allah must use what was created for him according to the instruction of its Creator. That is 'abdiyyah, the state of being Allah's servant, which requires total submission and is the highest achievement a human being can hope for.

The spiritual ills are mentioned first. Indulgence in these activities is disgusting and is a trap of Satan. Whoever walks in does not walk out but becomes the victim of many further vices. The command to refrain follows from their nature, and success in both worlds depends on it.

### In short

- Intoxicants, gambling, altar stones and divining arrows are named together as filth and Satan's handiwork, and avoidance is tied to success.
- The prohibition came in stages, from the verse on sin and benefit through the restriction at prayer time to this decisive command.
- The reports of 'Umar, Anas, Sa'd and the spilled wine in the streets of Madinah show how the community responded at once.
- The curse covers the whole trade in drink, not only the drinker, and reports describe its appearance in earlier revelation.
- Divining arrows are gambling, while lots used to divide equal shares are permitted, and the inward and social damage of both is described at length.

91.text:
The verse explains what Satan is after: "Satan’s plan is to stir up hostility and hatred between you with intoxicants and gambling and to prevent you from remembering Allah and praying." Two harms are named, one between people and one between a person and Allah.

It closes with a question that functions as a command: "Will you not then abstain".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Satan’s plan is to stir up hostility and hatred between you"** describes his single aim. One gloss explains it as precipitating enmity and hatred because of the evil and discord that follow drinking and gambling. Another ties it to becoming drunk and to losing money.

**"with intoxicants and gambling"** names the two instruments. The description concerns the effects that follow their use rather than the substances alone.

**"and to prevent you from remembering Allah and praying."** adds the spiritual harm. Intoxicants are described as driving a person from obedience to Allah and as preventing the five daily prayers. Prayer is mentioned separately in order to magnify it, since it is itself part of the remembrance of Allah.

**"Will you not then abstain"** is a threat and a warning in the form of a question. One gloss renders its force as a direct command to desist, and another as asking whether the believers will leave these evil acts, adding that leaving them is plainly the right thing.

### What background produced this statement?

The verses were revealed against events in which actions taken under the influence of strong drink caused mutual anger and aggression. Such things do not happen by chance. A drunk person loses reason and acts compulsively in that manner.

The incident of Sa'd's nose being struck with a bone during a gathering of Ansar and emigrants, described with the preceding verse, is an example of the enmity named here. Boasting about status while intoxicated turned into violence.

Gambling works the same way. The loser takes his loss at the counter, but malice and anger toward his adversary continue to shape his behaviour afterward. Qatadah says it was the habit of some Arabs to wager all their possessions and even their families, lose them, and then live a wretched life.

### Why is the spiritual harm mentioned last?

The worldly bad effects are described first, and then the harm of being barred from remembrance and prayer. That order may hint that the real harm is spiritual, because the real life is the eternal life of the Hereafter.

A wise person therefore takes the betterment of that life as real betterment and its suffering as real suffering. This worldly life has a very limited span, and within those limits neither good nor bad stands out as something to be proud of or to pine over, since both conditions pass quickly.

### How is neglect of remembrance and prayer harmful in this world too?

Neglect of the remembrance of Allah and of prayer harms both worlds and both body and soul. Its harm to the Hereafter and the soul is obvious, since whoever skips prayer while forgetting Allah ruins his future life and deadens his soul.

A person heedless of Allah makes his own life a curse for himself. Once he turns from Allah and sets his heart on gaining wealth and standing as the goal of his life, those pursuits drag in so many entanglements that sorrow and worry follow. Once inside them he is deprived of the very peace and comfort he sought through possessions.

People of the material are therefore never at peace, whether they have what they work for or not. The contrast is the person whose heart is lit by thought of his Creator and by the bliss of his prayer. Wealth, power and office come to him with whatever peace they carry, and if they leave, nothing happens to his heart.

Gains are no happiness and losses no sorrow to him, since both are visiting guests of those who do right. Reflection on neglect of remembrance and prayer therefore shows its effects to be equally bad for this world and the next.

### How do the three descriptions divide the harm?
