The animals offered were male and never female, and when they died both men and women shared the meat. A further gloss describes it as an animal released in the name of the idols, like a bull let loose in some rural areas today.

**"waṣîlah"** is the third. Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib describes it as a she camel set free for the idols because she bore a female at her first delivery and another female at the second. They freed such a camel when she produced two females with no male between them.

Through Az-Zuhri, Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib explains that they called her a wasilah because she had connected two females with no male between, and that they cut off her ears and let her roam to pasture for their idols. A similar explanation is reported from Malik bin Anas.

Ibn 'Abbas applies the term to sheep. He describes a ewe that gives birth seven times. If the seventh delivery was a stillborn male or female, the men ate from it and not the women. If she bore a female, or a female and a male, they set them free, saying of the male that his sister had connected him to being forbidden to them. Ibn Abi Hatim records the statement.

Muhammad bin Ishaq describes the wasilah sheep as a ewe bearing ten females in five deliveries, two females at each. She was called wasilah and set free. Whatever she bore afterward, male or female, was given to the men and not the women, but if it was stillborn, men and women shared it.

Another account describes checking the seventh birth. A male was sacrificed and its meat shared by men and women. A female could not be used by women until she died, after which both shared her meat. Twins, male and female, were spared for the men alone until death, and then both shared the meat. A further gloss describes a sheep that had borne six offspring and, at the seventh delivery, had its ears and horns cut with the announcement that it had connected the deliveries, after which it was not slaughtered, struck or barred from any watering place.

**"and ḥâm camels."** is the fourth. Al-'Awfi reports Ibn 'Abbas saying that when a man's camel had performed ten copulations they called it a ham and set it free. Abu Rawq and Qatadah report something similar.

In another report Ibn 'Abbas describes the ham as a male camel whose offspring had themselves produced offspring. They would announce that this camel had protected its back, so nothing might be carried on it, its wool might not be cut, and it might not be prevented from grazing where it liked or drinking from any pool, even a pool that did not belong to its owner.

Ibn Wahb reports hearing Malik say that the ham is a male camel assigned a set number of copulations, and that when it had completed them, peacock feathers were placed on it and it was set free. Other opinions are also mentioned, including a description of a stud male that mates and produces a given number of offspring, and an account of an animal left entirely alone, not ridden or used for carrying, not barred from any water or pasture or from any she camel that came its way, whose meat was shared by men and women when it grew old or died.

The word used for the fourth is also given in the form of one who is protected, and the explanations differ because these were customs rather than fixed legal terms. It is possible that each word was applied to a different situation.

### Who began these practices?

Abu Hurayrah reports the Messenger ﷺ saying that he saw 'Amr bin 'Amir al-Khuza'i dragging his intestines behind him in the Fire, and that he was the first to begin the practice of the sa'ibah. Ahmad records 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud reporting the same, naming Abu Khuza'ah, 'Amr bin 'Amir, as the first to begin the sa'ibah and the worship of idols.

The 'Amr named is the son of Luhay bin Qam'ah, one of the chiefs of Khuza'ah, the tribe that looked after the House of Allah between Jurhum and the Prophet's ﷺ own tribe of Quraysh. He was the first to alter the religion of Ibrahim, al-Khalil, in Makkah, and to bring idol worship into the Hijaz, the western region of Arabia.

He called simple people to worship idols and offer sacrifice to them, and he began these ignorant rituals concerning animals along with other practices of the period of ignorance. One gloss identifies those who invented lies against Allah as 'Amr ibn Luhayy and his followers. Allah speaks in Al-An'am of people assigning to Allah a share of the tillage and cattle He created (3:136).

### What was wrong with these customs?

Beyond the shirk involved, they challenged a right Allah had given. He had made the meat, milk and use of these animals halal, and they imposed restrictions of their own on what was halal and what was haram, as though the office of making divine law belonged to them.

The bitter irony is that they treated these polytheistic customs as the means of gaining Allah's pleasure and nearness. The answer given is that Allah never appointed them. Their elders invented lies against Him, and the ignorant masses accepted them.

Allah did not legislate these invented rituals and does not regard them as acts of obedience. The idolaters turned them into rituals and acts of worship by which to draw near to Allah, and they did not and will not help anyone draw near Him. Such innovations harm only those who adopt them.

Most of them are described as having no understanding, which one gloss extends to all of them, meaning that they had no sense of Allah's command, of what He made lawful and of what He made unlawful. Another says they did not grasp that this was a lie, since they were merely following the example of their forefathers. Another describes them as unable to tell truth from falsehood, or the lawful from the unlawful.

### What does the two-fold warning amount to?

The passage gives a paired warning. It is a crime to bring hardship into divine injunctions by asking pointless questions, which the following verses address. It is a far more serious crime to declare things lawful or unlawful on the basis of personal opinion and desire, without the will and command of the Lawgiver.

A brief gloss describes the four as categories of domestic animals which the pre-Islamic Arabs dedicated to their deities. The verse denies that Allah ordained any of them.

### What did the Prophet ﷺ say to a man practising it?

Ibn Abi Hatim records it through Abu Ishaq As-Subay'i, who gives it from Al-Ahwas al-Jushami on the authority of his father Malik bin Nadlah, and Malik said that he came to the Prophet ﷺ wearing old clothes. Asked whether he had property, he said yes, and named camels, sheep, horses and slaves.

He was told that if Allah gives a person wealth, its effect should be visible on him. The Prophet ﷺ then asked whether his camels delivered calves with entire ears, and he answered that they did, asking whether camels ever give birth to anything but whole calves.

He was then asked whether he took a knife and cut off the ears of some of them, calling one a bahirah, and tore the ears of others, declaring them sacred. He said that he did. He was told not to do that, since all the wealth Allah has given a person is permitted to him, and the verse was recited.

The explanations of the four terms appear as an addition in that narration. In another version, from Abu Ishaq through Abu Al-Ahwas, 'Awf bin Malik gives the explanations in his own words rather than as part of the hadith, and this is described as the sounder form. Ahmad records the hadith on a chain running up from Malik bin Nadlah through his son Abu Al-Ahwas 'Awf bin Malik, then Abu Az-Za'ra' 'Amr bin 'Amr, and so to Sufyan bin 'Uyaynah, and that narration does not contain the added explanations.

### In short

- Four customs are denied, and the reports explain each with differing details that are preserved rather than merged.
- The bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah and ham were animals dedicated to idols by condition of births, milk, ears or copulations.
- 'Amr ibn Luhayy is named as the first to begin the sa'ibah and idol worship, altering the religion of Ibrahim in Makkah.
- The wrong was twofold, shirk and the usurping of Allah's right to declare things lawful and unlawful.
- The Prophet ﷺ told a man practising it that all the wealth Allah gives is permitted to him.

104.text:
The reply of those addressed is quoted: “What we found our forefathers practicing is good enough for us.” The verse answers with a question rather than an insult, asking whether that would still be enough if their forefathers knew nothing and had no guidance.

The form of the answer is itself instructive. It states a principle about following anyone, and it does so without provoking the hearer.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When it is said to them, “Come to Allah’s revelations and to the Messenger,”"** describes being summoned to the religion, law and commands of Allah and to keeping away from what He forbade. One gloss sets the scene with the Prophet ﷺ addressing the idolaters of Makkah, calling them to treat as lawful what Allah clarified in the Qur'an and what the Messenger ﷺ showed them to be lawful. Another describes it as a call to the Qur'an and to the path of the Messenger ﷺ so that they may learn what is lawful and unlawful.

**"they reply, “What we found our forefathers practicing is good enough for us.”"** gives their only answer. The practices and ways they found their fathers and forefathers following are, they say, sufficient for them in religion and law. One gloss renders their words as claiming that the prohibition they inherited is enough for them.

**"˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had absolutely no knowledge or guidance"** supplies the answer's weakness. Their fathers did not understand or recognise the truth and did not find its way. One gloss specifies ignorance of Allah's oneness and religion, and absence of guidance to the practice of any prophet.

The interrogative is meant as a disavowal. Another reading puts it as a plain question: were their fathers not wholly ignorant of the religion and unguided to the practice of the Prophet ﷺ, and how then can their example be followed?

The conclusion drawn is sharp. Only someone more ignorant and more astray than those forefathers would follow them.

### What lay behind this answer?

Following forefathers was one of many customs of the period of ignorance that involved people in every kind of evil and deprived them of every kind of virtue. As reported in Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur from Ibn Abi Hatim, a fortunate person who listened to the truth and embraced Islam was shamed on the grounds that he had shown his forefathers to be worthless, since he chose another way at the cost of theirs.

That compounded error is what the verse answers. It is described as the master argument of Satan, which brought millions into error although they had at least average sense, knowledge and skill.

The Qur'an's one sentence gives a correct principle for following any person, group or party. It is a principle that gives eyes to the blind and the real shape of things to the ignorant and the inattentive.

### When does following make sense?

It makes sense for those who do not know to follow those who do, for the uninitiated to follow the experienced and for the ignorant to follow the learned. What makes no sense is to step aside from the measures of knowledge, reason and direction and settle on inherited practice as the thing to be preferred, without knowing where that leader stands or where he will lead, while feeling obliged to trail along behind him.

Some people take a crowd as the measure of right and wrong and move wherever they see many people going. That also makes no sense. The greater number of people anywhere is never made up of the wisest, the cleverest or the best in conduct. Following a crowd cannot be the test that separates truth from falsehood or good from bad.

### What are the two criteria of leadership?

The sentence gives two clear criteria for choosing a leader: knowledge and guidance. Knowledge means knowing the desired destination and the methods of reaching it. Guidance means actually travelling toward the chosen objective. Together they mean constant effort resting on sound knowledge.

Before choosing a leader a person must therefore establish whether he is fully acquainted with the objectives and methods to be followed. He must then see whether that person is himself travelling the same path in the same direction. He must also determine whether his conduct matches his knowledge.

A leader must be tried against reliable knowledge and consistent behaviour. None of the other options, whether ancestry and lineage, being followed by masses, wealth in money or property, or power and authority, deserves to be treated as a criterion of leadership in the real sense.

### Why is following an undeserving leader so dangerous?

The correct attitude is that a person first determines the aim of his life and the direction of his journey. He then looks for someone who knows that direction and is himself travelling along it. Following such a person can take him all the way to his destination.

This is the reality underlying the following of the mujtahid imams. They know the religion and they practise it, so those who do not know can, by following them, attain the main purpose of religion, which is obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and adherence to their commands.

As for someone already astray, who does not know the destination or who knowingly travels in the opposite direction, following him is a waste of effort and deeds in the sight of every wise person. It amounts to writing out one's own sentence of ruin.

It is regrettable that in this age of advertised knowledge and enlightenment, even people of education and foresight overlook the greatest single cause of turmoil in the world, which is unquestioning attachment to leaders who are unqualified, unworthy and false.

### How does the verse criticise without insulting?

The Qur'an points out the error of people who follow ancestral custom blindly, and at the same time shows an effective method for identifying another person's error without hurting or provoking him.

The remark in the text is not frontal. Nowhere does it state that those forefathers lacked knowledge or had gone astray. It uses a subtle interrogative style, asking whether following one's forefathers could be reasonable in a case where they had neither knowledge nor guidance.

That method leaves the hearer to draw the conclusion himself. It is the same method the verse uses, and it is why the answer is a question.

### What happens to elders over time?

The earlier leaders of a community acquire a holy status after a certain passage of time. Many wrong practices then take place in the name of those long dead people. If they had established a custom of venerating sheep and camels, their successors would continue it without giving it a thought.

Misguided behaviour resting on a tradition of holiness takes root so firmly and deeply that it is very hard to dissuade people from it. Rising above such psychological complications is possible only when a person acquires a firm belief, in the real sense, that he must finally appear before Allah.

Whoever holds that belief accepts today what he will be compelled to accept after death. Acceptance at that later time will be of no use to anyone.

### In short

- The call is to revelation and to the Messenger ﷺ, and the reply is that inherited practice is enough.
- The verse answers with a question about knowledge and guidance rather than with a direct insult.
- Following makes sense only when the followed person knows the way and is travelling it.
- Ancestry, crowds, wealth and power are not criteria of leadership, and following an undeserving leader is self-destruction.
- Elders acquire holiness with time, and only firm belief in appearing before Allah breaks that hold.

105.text:
The believers are addressed about the limits of their responsibility: "You are accountable only for yourselves. It will not harm you if someone chooses to deviate—as long as you are ˹rightly˺ guided." The condition matters as much as the promise, and the verse ends with the return to Allah.

The apparent sense has been misunderstood, and the reports that correct that misunderstanding belong to the explanation of this verse.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! You are accountable only for yourselves."** is a command to take care of themselves, to preserve their own souls and to do what serves their best interest. Allah directs His believing servants to set themselves right and to perform as much righteousness as they can.

**"It will not harm you if someone chooses to deviate—as long as you are ˹rightly˺ guided."** promises that whoever reforms himself will not be harmed by the wickedness of the wicked, whether they are his relatives or not. One gloss describes the error of one who errs as unable to injure a person who is rightly guided to faith and who further shows the erring person his error. Another restricts it to the misguided among the People of the Scripture.

**"To Allah you will all return, and He will inform you of what you used to do"** closes the verse. The return is after death, and Allah will tell people what they used to do and say, of good and evil, and will requite them for it.

### What was the occasion?

One account says the verse was revealed about the idolaters of Makkah, at the time the Prophet ﷺ took the capitation tax from the People of the Book and afterwards would not take it from them. That story is described as already mentioned in Al-Baqarah.

### Why did Abu Bakr correct the way people read it?

Ahmad records Qays saying that Abu Bakr As-Siddiq stood, thanked and praised Allah, and then told the people that they recite this verse and explain it in the wrong way.

He said that he had heard the Messenger ﷺ say that when people witness evil and do not change it, Allah is about to send a punishment that will encompass them. Qays also heard Abu Bakr tell the people to beware of lying, because lying contradicts faith.

Sensing the doubt produced by a surface reading, Abu Bakr said in a khutbah that people recite this verse and use it out of context, as though commanding what is fair were not required. He insisted that he had himself heard the Prophet ﷺ say that whoever watches a sin being done and makes no effort, so far as he is able, to prevent it is likely to be seized by divine punishment along with the actual sinners.

At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah carry that narration. In Abu Dawud the words are that those who see an oppressor oppressing and do not stop him, to the best of their ability, will find that Allah seizes everyone in punishment.

### How do the scholars read the condition?

When this verse was revealed some people had doubts, and the Prophet ﷺ clarified that it did not contradict the injunctions about commanding what is fair. If they abandoned that mission they would be answerable for it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr is reported in al-Bahr al-Muhit as saying that a person should keep doing what his religion obliges, which includes jihad and commanding what is fair, and that if, after doing all this, those who remain astray can bring no loss on him, the verse applies. Reflection on the words if you are rightly guided makes the point clearer, since the converse shows that whoever has abandoned the duty of commanding what is fair is plainly not rightly guided.

Being on the right path therefore includes encouraging good and forbidding evil. Only then does the deviation of others cease to harm a person.

A hadith of Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani, reported by al-Hakim and others, gives the same balance. He asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about this verse and was told to enjoin decency on one another and forbid indecency to one another, and that if a person then sees stinginess obeyed, whims followed, this world preferred and every clever man proud of his own opinion, he is still responsible for looking after his own soul.

### What practical advice is reported from Ibn 'Umar?

Al-Durr al-Manthur carries an account about 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar. In his presence someone described a grave quarrel between certain named people who were branding one another as polytheists.

Ibn 'Umar asked whether they thought he would tell them to go and fight those people. He said they should not. They should go and speak to them gently. If they listened, that was good. If not, they should stop worrying about them and busy themselves with their own souls. He then recited this verse as confirmation of his answer.

The advice distinguishes the duty of speaking from the duty of fighting, and it locates the point at which a person's responsibility is discharged.

### What do the terms commanding good and forbidding evil mean?

The word for what is fair comes from knowing, that is, understanding and recognising something after deliberation. Its antonym comes from not knowing and not recognising. The two are treated as opposites.

The Qur'an describes people who recognise Allah's blessings in the manifestations of His perfect power and then deny them as though they did not know them (16:83). Lexically, then, the fair is what is well recognised and its opposite is what is unrecognised.

Keeping that congruity in view, Raghib al-Isfahan gives their meanings in the terminology of the Shariah in his lexicon of the Holy Qur'an's vocabulary. Commanding the fair is known in that terminology as Al-Amr bil-Ma'ruf. The fair is what is known to be good in the light of reason and of revelation. Its opposite is what is unfamiliar and unrecognised, that is, what is taken to be bad. Commanding the fair therefore means bidding toward what is right, and forbidding its opposite means restraining from what is wrong.

### Why are these words used instead of obedience and disobedience?

The choice may indicate that in deep matters, and in problems requiring ijtihad because of brevity or ambiguity left in the Qur'an and Sunnah, two opinions can exist. That is the basis on which the sayings of Muslim jurists differ, and such matters are excluded from this scope.

The brilliance of the ijtihad of the great mujtahid imams is an accepted fact among the scholars and jurists of the Muslim ummah. Where two views differ on a religious problem, neither can be considered censurable in the Shariah. Both sides fall within what is fair.

In such problems a person who considers one opinion weightier has no right to censure the other in the way one censures sin. That is why, despite many differences in ijtihad and opposing opinions, it is nowhere reported that the Companions and their successors called one another sinners. They had debates, dialogues and polemics. They presented their views, explained the grounds of their preference and did not hesitate to question what others said, but nobody treated another as a sinner merely for a difference of opinion.

This refers to the views of competent mujtahids, equipped with deep knowledge of the Qur'an and Sunnah, who state a sincere view after doing their utmost to reach the truth. An incompetent person lacking the standard required for ijtihad, who declares a view out of whim and conjecture, cannot claim that his view rests on ijtihad and cannot claim immunity from being restrained.

Briefly, where an ijtihadi difference exists, every knowledgeable person with the requisite subject knowledge may take the side that seems weightier to him. He has no right to censure what another has done by treating it as evil and sinful. Writings that spread mutual hatred and hostility over ijtihadi questions therefore do not fall within commanding the fair or forbidding its opposite. Opening a front of war on the basis of such religious issues can arise only from unawareness or ignorance.

### What comfort does the verse give reformers?

Muslims who sacrificed greatly in their concern for reforming people are comforted here. They did their best to spread the call of truth and discharged the duty of conveying what was good for people.

If others then chose to hold on to their error, that was not for them to worry about, since the straying of others brings no loss on them. The comfort is real, but it is given to those who have already done their part.

### What does the inward reading say?

Beyond the plain explanation, the tongue of allusion addresses those who taste what the people of desire describe. The faithful are told to beware and to subdue their own soul before it subdues them, and to busy it with obedience before it busies them with disobedience.

Abu 'Uthman was asked about this verse and answered that a person's own soul is against him. If he occupies himself with making its corruption wholesome and concealing its shameful parts, he will be too busy to gaze at the creatures or occupy himself with them.

Husayn Mansur al-Hallaj advised his disciple that your own soul is against you, and that a soul left without work will find work for you. Muhammad ibn 'Ali said that your own soul is against you, and if you spare the creatures its evil you will have discharged most of what it is owed.

The soul is described as forever settled in this world and quick toward disobedience. It reckons disobedience a trifle and drags its feet over obedience. It is vain and acts for the sight of other people, and inside it sit associationism, show and duplicity. A saying describes it as two-faced in every condition, false in most of them and an associator in a few.

Abu Yazīd Basṭāmī is quoted saying that if the Lord told him in that world to make a wish, he would ask permission to enter the Fire to punish this soul, because in this world it had always made him writhe and suffer.

Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ said that your worst enemy is your soul between your two sides. The reason given is that when you come to terms with an enemy you become safe from his evil, but when you come to terms with your own soul you perish.

The contrast is drawn sharply. If you treat someone well he will thank you at the resurrection, and if you treat him badly he will complain. The soul behaves in the opposite way. Treat it well in this house and it becomes your antagonist in that house. Treat it badly here and it will thank you there.

### In short

- A person is accountable for himself, and the deviation of others does not harm whoever is rightly guided.
- The rightly guided are those who have discharged the duty of commanding the fair and forbidding its opposite, as Abu Bakr's correction makes plain.
- Ibn 'Umar's advice shows the duty as gentle speech rather than fighting, and the hadith of Abu Tha'laba locates the point where self-reform remains the responsibility.
- Differences requiring ijtihad are not censurable, and both sides fall within what is fair, provided the views come from competent mujtahids.
- The inward reading turns the verse on the soul, which must be subdued and kept busy with obedience before it does the reverse.

106.text:
A precise legal procedure is given for a traveller facing death: "When death approaches any of you, call upon two just Muslim men to witness as you make a bequest". The verse allows two others from outside the community when no Muslim is available, and it sets a solemn oath after prayer if their word is doubted.

The ruling is narrow in its conditions and careful in its safeguards, and the reports about its occasion explain why each condition exists.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! When death approaches any of you"** concerns the time of making a will, when the signs of death appear. One gloss describes it as death drawing near with one of its causes.

**"call upon two just Muslim men to witness as you make a bequest"** requires two witnesses, described as just, from your own people, meaning Muslims. The wording shows a preference for Muslim witnesses.

**"otherwise, two non-Muslims if you are afflicted with death while on a journey."** permits two others from outside, understood by Ibn 'Abbas as the People of the Book, in a report given by Ibn Abi Hatim. Two conditions permit this: being on a journey and needing to write a will, as Sharih al-Qadi states.

Ibn Jarir records Sharih saying that the testimony of Jews and Christians is not accepted except while travelling, and even then only to witness the dictation of the will. One gloss describes the two others as people from another tribe or from outside your own community, and another as two free men.

**"If you doubt ˹their testimony˺, keep them after prayer"** addresses the case where the heirs suspect treachery or theft. The prayer meant is 'Asr, according to Al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muhammad bin Sirin, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i and Sa'id bin Jubayr are reported with the same explanation.

Az-Zuhri says they are detained after the Muslim prayer, that is, after prayer in congregation. The two witnesses are therefore held after a congregational prayer.

One explanation gives the reason for that time. The People of the Book held 'Asr in esteem, and lying at that hour was particularly forbidden among them. This shows that restricting a solemn oath to a special time or place is permissible.

**"and let them testify under oath ˹saying˺, “By Allah! We would never sell our testimony for any price"** is their oath. One gloss explains the wording as not exchanging the oath for a paltry portion of this soon-ending world, whether by swearing falsely or by testifying falsely for that price. Another explains it as not seeking worldly gain in what they vow.

**"even in favour of a close relative"** adds that even if the beneficiary, or the person for whose sake testimony is given, is a near kinsman, they will not compromise the truth. One gloss reads it as applying even if the deceased is one of their own kin.

**"nor withhold the testimony of Allah."** describes the testimony as Allah's, out of respect for it and recognition of its weight. It is the testimony Allah commanded them to give, and they will not conceal it if asked.

**"Otherwise, we would surely be sinful.”"** states the consequence of distorting, altering or wholly concealing it. One gloss renders the sinful as the wrongdoers.

### What happened to produce this ruling?

A Muslim named Budayl travelled to Syria on business with Tamim and 'Adiyy, who were then Christians. On reaching Syria he fell ill. He wrote a list of his belongings and put it in his baggage without telling his companions.

When his illness grew serious he called his Christian companions and made a will before them, instructing them to deliver everything to his heirs. On their return they handed over the belongings, but they removed a silver bowl inlaid or plated with gold.

When the heirs found the written list in the baggage, they asked whether the deceased had sold anything or had been so ill that unusual expenses were needed. The answer was no. The matter was finally brought for hearing before the Prophet ﷺ.

The heirs could produce no witnesses, so the two Christians were put to oath. They swore that they had committed no breach of trust concerning the deceased's property and had hidden nothing of it, and the verdict went in their favour on the strength of that oath.

Some time later it emerged that the two had sold the bowl to a goldsmith in Makkah. Asked about it, they said they had bought it from the deceased, and explained that they had no witnesses to the purchase, so they had not mentioned it earlier for fear of being contradicted.

The heirs appealed to the Prophet ﷺ. The position had now reversed, with the executors claiming a purchase and the heirs denying it. In the absence of evidence, the two closest to the deceased gave a sworn statement that the bowl had belonged to him and that the two Christians had lied in their oath. The price for which it had been sold, a thousand dirhams, was then handed over to the heirs.

Another account names the deceased as Budayl ibn Abi Maryam, a client of 'Amr ibn al-'As, who died on the road while travelling with 'Adiyy ibn Bida' and Tamim ibn Aws al-Dari. A third, from Ibn 'Abbas, describes Tamim al-Dari and 'Adiyy ibn Badda' travelling to Makkah with a man of Quraysh from Banu Sahm who died in a land where there was not one Muslim, so that he had to entrust his belongings to them for his family.

These differing accounts agree on the substance and differ in names, and they are preserved as reported.

### How does the procedure work in legal terms?

The person with whom the deceased leaves property in trust, to be handed to someone, is called a wasiyy, an executor or trustee, and there may be one or more. That a trustee should be Muslim and just is better but not required, whether the will is made on a journey or at home.

In a dispute the complainant is the plaintiff and the other party is the respondent. Witnesses are taken from the plaintiff first. If he produces witnesses recognised under the norms of Islamic law, the case is decided for him. If he cannot, the respondent is put to oath and the case is decided for him, unless he denies the claim, in which case the plaintiff prevails.

In the case of Budayl the heirs were the plaintiffs, since they claimed that a silver bowl had been given to the executors. Failing witnesses, the defendants were required to swear that they had committed no breach of trust. That is why the Qur'an advises the judge to detain them after prayer and have them swear.

Taking an oath at a particular time or place to make it more emphatic depends on the judge's opinion and is not compulsory. Its compulsory nature is not established by this verse, and the opposite is established by other verses and hadith reports. It is nevertheless advised here so that the sanctity of the time and place may further move people to speak truly.

### What is deduced about testimony between non-Muslims?

Abu Hanifah deduces from the permission of two others from outside that testimony given by unbelievers for one another is acceptable. Since their testimony has been made acceptable even in the case of Muslims here, its acceptance between themselves is more fitting.

Later, testimony by unbelievers for Muslims was abrogated on the authority of the verse requiring two witnesses from among your own men (2:282). The testimony of unbelievers for one another remains as it was. This is set out in Al-Ahkam, the legal work on the rulings of the Holy Qur'an, and the same discussion asks whether the testimony of a kafir, an unbeliever, may be accepted at all.

Support for Abu Hanifah's position is also drawn from a hadith about a Jew who had committed unlawful intercourse. His people blackened his face with soot and brought him to the Prophet ﷺ, who asked the reason and was told what had happened. After hearing the witnesses he ordered the prescribed stoning.

### What does the word about detention imply?

The wording about detaining the two shows that a person who genuinely owes something to another, who holds a right of return, may be detained by that other for the recovery of his right when needed.

### How does the verse read as a practical instruction?

A man on a journey who senses that his death is approaching should find two Muslims and hand over his possessions to them with clear instructions about passing them to his heirs. If he cannot find two Muslims in time, he should do the same with two non-Muslims.

Those two should bring the possessions and hand them to the heirs. If the heirs then doubt the witnesses' account, the witnesses should be detained in a mosque and made to swear before the general body of Muslims, who will attest that what they said on the deceased's behalf was correct.

If the heirs are still not satisfied with the sworn statement, two of the heirs should swear to that effect, and a decision should then be taken in accordance with their declaration. Giving this right to the heirs establishes a check, so that nobody will dare commit a breach of trust.

### In short

- Two just Muslim witnesses are preferred for a bequest, and two others from outside are permitted on a journey when no Muslim is present.
- If their word is doubted they are detained after a congregational prayer, 'Asr being named, and swear an oath whose wording covers price, kinship and concealment.
- The occasion was the case of Budayl and the silver bowl, preserved with differing names in the reports.
- The plaintiff brings witnesses, and failing them the respondent is sworn, with the oath's time and place left to the judge.
- Abu Hanifah deduces from the verse that testimony between unbelievers remains acceptable, while testimony for Muslims was later abrogated.

107.text:
The procedure continues into the case of dishonesty: "If they are found guilty ˹of false testimony˺, let the deceased’s two closest heirs affected by the bequest replace the witnesses". The heirs then swear, and their oath is preferred. The verse explains why that preference is just.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If they are found guilty ˹of false testimony˺"** describes the two witnesses being found to have sinned, whether through breach of trust or through perjury in their testimony. One gloss gives the example of the accused item being found in their possession, after which they claim to have bought it from the deceased or to have received it as a bequest.

Another explains it as their being found to have cheated or stolen from the money the will concerns. A third says that after their oath it was established that they had lied in their testimony or in their oath.

**"let the deceased’s two closest heirs affected by the bequest replace the witnesses"** puts two others in their place, nearest in kin among those who claim a lawful right. One gloss names them as those most concerned with the bequest, that is the inheritors, and describes them as standing in the place of the two Christians. Another account names 'Amr ibn al-'As and Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah as the two who took their place representing the deceased.

**"and testify under oath ˹saying˺, “By Allah! Our testimony is truer than theirs."** is the heirs' oath. It is explained as their testimony that the two cheated being more truthful than the testimony the two offered, and as an oath to the breach of faith of the two witnesses and to the truth of what the heirs suspected.

**"We have not transgressed."** means that they did not exceed the truth when they accused the two of treachery, and did not overstep the bounds in their claim.

**"Otherwise, we would surely be wrongdoers.”"** states the consequence if they had lied about them. One gloss describes the wrongdoers as liars who harm others, and another as those who overstep Allah's limits.

### Why is the heirs' oath preferred?

This is the oath of the heirs, and preference is given to what they say. The comparison offered is the oath of a murdered person's relative when someone tries to tarnish the victim's case, so that the family swears in defence of his honour. The subject is treated in the discussions of oaths in Al-Ahkam and the other books of legal rulings on the Holy Qur'an, where the testimony of a kafir is weighed against that of a believer.

In the case described with the preceding verse, the two Christians claimed to have purchased the bowl from the deceased. They should have substantiated that claim with witnesses and failed to do so, so the oath was given to the legal heirs that no such sale had taken place to the best of their knowledge.

### What does the oath accomplish?

One account describes the heirs swearing that the property the deceased carried was more than what the two returned, and that the testimony of the Muslims is truer than the testimony of the Christians. The reversal is exact: those who first swore are now contradicted by those whose right was affected.

A gloss adds that this stipulation stands for a pair of trustees, while for a pair of witnesses it has been abrogated, and that testimony from people outside the community has likewise been abrogated. The distinction between a trustee and a witness therefore matters for how far the ruling still applies.

### What lesson does the procedure teach beyond the case?

In Islamic law such instructions about everyday life carry lessons in a wider sphere. Once a person dies, dividing his estate is a domestic and financial affair. It has nevertheless been turned into training in two important respects.

The first is that people should adopt the attitude of giving no weight in their dealings to connections and relations, taking account only of rights and truth. They should look at what the truth is and not ask who is favoured by it and who is not.

The second is that every procedure should be treated as giving evidence before Allah. Whatever is in a person's custody is in Allah's trust, because he saw it given by Allah with his own eyes, preserved it in the memory Allah gave him, and now has to declare it with the tongue Allah gave him.

In those circumstances it is a breach of trust not to state the facts as one saw them or committed them to memory. The oath of the heirs exists because the first oath failed that standard.

### In short

- Where the two are found guilty of breach of trust or perjury, the two nearest heirs take their place and swear.
- Their oath states that their testimony is truer and that they have not transgressed, with the consequence of wrongdoing if they lied.
- Preference is given to the heirs' oath, as in the defence of a murdered person's honour.
- The stipulation is described as holding for trustees and abrogated for witnesses, and the testimony of outsiders as abrogated.
- The procedure trains people to weigh rights rather than relationships and to treat every statement as evidence before Allah.

108.text:
The verse explains the purpose of the arrangement: "In this way it is more likely that witnesses will give true testimony or else fear that their oaths could be refuted by those of the heirs." Two motives are built into the procedure, and both aim at the truth.

It closes with a command to mindfulness and obedience, and a warning about guidance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"In this way it is more likely that witnesses will give true testimony"** describes the ruling as bringing them nearer to giving testimony in its true form, the form in which they were charged to give it, without distortion or breach of faith.

The requirement that two witnesses from outside the community swear, when their truthfulness is doubted, may compel them to admit the testimony in its true shape. Requiring them to swear by Allah may encourage that admission, because they respect swearing by Allah and glorify and revere Him.

**"or else fear that their oaths could be refuted by those of the heirs."** adds the second motive. They also dread being exposed should the deceased's heirs be called on to swear in their place, for then those heirs would take the oath and recover the inheritance the two had failed to disclose.

One gloss describes them as fearing that after their oath the oath of others will be taken, so that they should not withhold their testimony. Another describes the fear as being disgraced if the heirs give conflicting testimony, since they would then incur penalties, and so they will not lie.

**"Be mindful of Allah and obey."** calls for taqwa in all their affairs, and for listening and obeying. One gloss describes fearing Allah concerning what is entrusted to them, and hearkening to what they are commanded with a listening that accepts.

**"For Allah does not guide the rebellious people"** warns those who do not obey Him or follow His law. One gloss describes them as lying, transgressing unbelievers, and adds that Allah does not guide to His religion or clear proof those who are not fit for His guidance. Another describes the wicked as those rebelling against obedience to Him, whom He does not guide to the way of goodness.

### Why are these oaths and refusals effective?

The several oaths taken by the witnesses after prayer, when their testimony is doubted, together with the possibility of their testimony being overturned, increase the likelihood that they will testify as the sacred law requires, without deceitfully distorting the facts.

The procedure works on two levels at once. Reverence for the oath itself moves a person to speak truly, and the prospect of a contradicting oath by the heirs deters him from lying. Neither motive is a substitute for honesty, but together they make dishonesty harder to sustain.

That is why the ruling gives the heirs a right rather than leaving them without remedy. The check established by that right is what makes a breach of trust a risky undertaking. The same legal discussion in Al-Ahkam and the other books of rulings on the Holy Qur'an asks whether the testimony of a kafir may be accepted at all, and answers that question from this verse.

### What does mindfulness add to the procedure?

The verse does not end with the mechanism. It commands mindfulness of Allah and obedience, and warns that guidance is withheld from the rebellious.

The legal device therefore rests on a religious disposition. A person who fears Allah concerning a trust will not betray it, and the oaths exist for those whose fear needs reinforcing at a moment of temptation.

The warning about guidance also explains the stakes. Obedience is not merely a procedural requirement in a court. It is connected with being guided at all, and rebellion cuts a person off from that guidance.

### In short

- The arrangement makes truthful testimony likelier by working on reverence for the oath and on fear of a contradicting oath by the heirs.
- Witnesses would otherwise face disgrace and penalties if the heirs swore against them.
- Mindfulness of Allah concerning trusts, and listening that accepts, are commanded alongside the procedure.
- Allah does not guide the rebellious, who are described as lying and transgressing, and the warning sets the stakes beyond the courtroom.

109.text:
The chapter turns to the Day of Gathering: “What response did you receive?” The messengers are assembled and asked how their communities answered them. Their reply is extraordinary: “We have no knowledge ˹compared to You˺! You ˹alone˺ are indeed the Knower of all unseen.”

The verse opens a window onto that Day. It also explains why the answer takes this form, and what it shows about the messengers' feeling for their people.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Consider˺ the Day Allah will gather the messengers"** recalls the Day of Resurrection, when Allah will gather the messengers together. One gloss describes this as happening at a moment of bewilderment, and another notes that the whole world will be assembled on that day.

The particular mention of the prophets carries a meaning. Everyone will be gathered, but the first question will be put to the prophets, so that all creation may see that nobody is exempt from reckoning on that Day.

**"and say, “What response did you receive?”"** is the question. Allah will ask the messengers how the nations to whom He sent them answered and responded to their teaching. When they invited their communities to Allah and His true religion, how did people react? Did they act as commanded, or did they refuse the call and oppose it?

One gloss specifies that they were summoned to proclaim Allah's oneness. Other verses state the same reckoning, that Allah will question those to whom the message was sent and will question the messengers (7:6), and that by His Lord all of them will certainly be called to account for everything they used to do (15:92-93).

**"They will reply, “We have no knowledge ˹compared to You˺!"** is the answer. Mujahid, Al-Hasan Al-Basri and As-Suddi explain it as the result of the terror of that Day. 'Abdur-Razzaq narrates through Ath-Thawri from Al-A'mash that Mujahid gave this explanation, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim record it.

Another gloss attributes the answer to the intensity of the situation, and a third to the great terror and fright of the Day, which makes them forget what they knew.

**"You ˹alone˺ are indeed the Knower of all unseen.”"** assigns knowledge to Allah alone. He is the Knower of what is hidden, including what is hidden from the messengers of how people responded. One account describes them as assigning the answer to Allah and saying that He alone knows all things, present and absent.

### What did Ibn 'Abbas say the answer means?

In the report given by 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, Ibn 'Abbas explains that the messengers will say to the Lord most honoured that they have no knowledge beyond what they know, and that even of that, Allah knows those people better than they do.

The response is made out of respect before the Lord most honoured. It means that they have no knowledge compared with His encompassing knowledge. Their knowledge grasped only the outward behaviour of those people, not the secrets of their hearts.

Allah is the Knower of everything, whose knowledge encompasses all things, and their knowledge set beside His resembles having no knowledge at all, because He alone is the Knower of everything hidden.

### How can this answer be correct about people they knew?

A doubt arises. For those born in a community after its prophet had died, the answer is plainly correct, since nobody knows the unseen except Allah. But what of the great majority who professed belief at their prophet's hands, and who kept following before his eyes what they were told to follow, and of the disbelievers who would not listen and even treated the prophets with hostility? How can it be correct to say that there is no knowledge of their faith and deeds?

Al-Bahr al-Muhit records that Imam Razi answered the doubt by distinguishing two things. One is perfect certitude, and the other is conjecture or weighty likelihood. If a person can testify about the faith and deeds of someone sitting beside him, it is on no other basis than likelihood.

Real faith, iman, is a secret of the heart that nobody can ascertain with certainty without divine revelation. Every religious community had groups of hypocrites who professed faith and followed what they were commanded, while their hearts held neither faith nor the real feeling and drive to carry out those commands. All they had was hypocrisy.

Religious laws, like all laws, were applied to what appeared outwardly. Whoever called himself a believer, followed the divinely ordained laws, and against whom no word or deed was proved contrary to faith, stood as a sound believer before the prophets and the communities that believed with them. Whether he was a true believer at heart or merely a hypocrite did not count, since they had no means of knowing.

The Prophet ﷺ therefore said that we judge by outward deeds while Allah is the custodian of the secrets of hearts.

### What changes on the Day of Gathering?

Under that rule the prophets, their deputies and the learned could confirm, at least in this mortal world, that someone was a true believer on the basis of a favourable opinion drawn from his outward deeds. That mortal world, in which everything turned on opinion and conjecture, has passed.

This is Yawm al-Hashr, the day of gathering, the fateful day of Resurrection when the dead rise, things are sorted out and realities unfold. Offenders will be put on trial and people will give evidence about them. Where they will not confess, a further set of witnesses is produced, of a very particular and very formal kind.

With mouths and tongues silenced, the wrongdoer's hands, legs and skin will be asked to testify, and they will tell everything. On that Day their mouths are sealed, their hands speak to Allah and their feet give evidence of everything they did (36:65). People will then discover that parts of their own bodies can act as informants when summoned by the Lord of the universes, and after testimony of that kind no denial remains possible.

That will be a state in which no judgment rests on opinion, estimate or conjecture. Certitude will be the order of the day. Since nobody has real knowledge of another's faith except Allah, the messengers will recognise what the question amounts to. It is not being asked in the world of their experience, where conjecture could answer it, but in the terrifying scene of the Resurrection, where nothing but certitude will serve.

Their answer, that they have no knowledge, means that they lack the certain knowledge required to answer, and it is right and correct.

### What does the answer show about the messengers' affection?

The prophets did hold opinions about whether their communities accepted or refused their call, and they knew facts about their obedience and disobedience. On that basis they could at least have mentioned the apparent attitude as part of their answer, referring certainty of knowledge to Allah alone.

What we see instead is that they said nothing about what they knew and mentioned none of the events that had passed before them. They resigned all of it to divine knowledge and chose silence.

That was a great demonstration of consideration. The prophets are deeply affectionate toward their people and toward Allah's creation generally. They would not choose to make an adverse comment about their community on their own initiative, for fear of bringing their people into trouble. If they had to say it, they would, but here they had the excuse of lacking certain knowledge, and using that legitimate excuse they avoided saying anything against their communities.

One gloss adds that afterwards they respond and give evidence that the message reached their people. Another says that when their fright has settled they go on to give evidence concerning their communities. The first response of bewilderment is therefore not the whole of their testimony.

### What will be exposed about communities and their prophets?

Those who embraced faith on the strength of their prophets' teaching later fell away from the true religion and contrived one of their own in the prophet's name. Every group nevertheless treated itself as the community of its prophet, although after deviating from his real teaching it had ceased to have any connection with him.

Jews claim a connection with Musa (Moses) and Christians with 'Isa (Jesus), although their present religions are unconnected with those prophets. That fact has become obscure in this world of trial, and on the Day of Judgment it will all be made clear.

On that Day Allah will bring every prophet together and, with their communities standing by, will ask what instruction each gave his people and what use those people made of it. It will then be shown to every community, before its own prophet, how far its members contravened his teaching about the religion of Allah, and how they falsely attached their self-made religion to him.

The question addressed to the prophets is therefore really directed at their communities. The prophets will be the first to testify about the good and bad deeds of their people, and it will be a trying moment for those people. They will have been hoping for their prophets' intercession to rescue them from that shattering experience, and instead the question requires the prophets to explain the conduct of the community.

Since the prophets will say nothing but the truth, wrongdoers will fear that the prophets themselves will bear witness against them. Who then, they will wonder, is left to intercede for them?

### What should a person do with this?

Verse 109 opens a window onto the Day of Doom. Posted at the viewing places of that reckoning stand those nearest and most beloved to Allah, His honoured messengers and prophets, every one of them in awe and reverence. If that is their state, what will be happening to everyone else?

People should therefore begin to worry about that Day from this day. This short span of life is a blessing in hand and should be devoted to preparing for the ultimate accounting.

At-Tirmidhi records a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ says that no son of Adam will move a step on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked five questions. He will be asked about his life and what he used it up in, about his youth and what he spent it in, about his wealth and where he earned it and where he spent it, and about what he did with the knowledge he had.

Allah's mercy and affection are great. He tests people and Himself tells them the questions of the test. The Prophet ﷺ discharged that task by telling his ummah how to appear in it. What remains is to work out the answers and keep them ready for the day of trial. Whoever still fails after being told in advance what the test contains could hardly be more deprived.

### In short

- The messengers are gathered and asked how their communities responded, and the question is really aimed at those communities.
- Their first answer disclaims knowledge, explained as the effect of the Day's terror and as respect before Allah's encompassing knowledge.
- Outward judgment in this world rests on likelihood, while real faith is a secret of the heart known only to Allah.
- On the Day of Gathering certitude replaces conjecture, and bodies testify when mouths are sealed.
- The silence of the messengers shows their affection, and the exposure of self-made religions claimed in their names is part of what that Day will make clear.

110.text:
On the Day of Gathering a particular address is given: “O Jesus, son of Mary! Remember My favour upon you and your mother”. A long list of favours follows, and each miracle is tied to Allah's permission. The verse ends with the response of the disbelievers among the Children of Israel, who called clear proofs plain magic.

The listing is not merely honour for 'Isa. It answers two opposite errors, one that abused him and one that exalted him beyond his place.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹on Judgment Day˺ Allah will say"** places the address on the Day of Resurrection. The past tense used throughout indicates a matter already settled that will certainly occur, and the verse carries some of the hidden matters Allah disclosed to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ.

**"“O Jesus, son of Mary! Remember My favour upon you"** recalls the blessing given to him when Allah created him from his mother without male intervention and made him a sign and clear proof of His perfect power over all things. One gloss describes the favour as the bestowal of prophethood, and another as creating him without a father.

**"and your mother:"** recalls the favour to Maryam. Allah made him testify to her chastity, and so he cleared her of the charge brought by unjust and ignorant liars. Another gloss describes the favour to her as being graced with complete surrender to Allah and with worship, and another as being chosen above the women of her time.

**"how I supported you with the holy spirit"** names Ruh al-Qudus, the pure Ruh, that is the angel Jibra'il, the pure Gabriel. He taught and helped 'Isa to speak to people, and Allah made him a prophet calling to Allah in the cradle and in manhood.

**"so you spoke to people in ˹your˺ infancy and adulthood."** means that he called people to Allah in childhood and in maturity. The word used is explained as meaning invited, since his speaking as a child is not remarkable in itself as mere speech. In his mother's lap and in his cot he said that he is Allah's servant and His anointed one, and Gabriel helped him after his thirtieth year when he said that he is Allah's Messenger.

**"How I taught you writing, wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel."** The Book and wisdom are explained as the power of writing and understanding. Another gloss describes the Scripture as the scriptures of the earlier prophets, or writing with the pen, and wisdom as the wisdom of earlier sages, or as the lawful and the unlawful. One account says the Torah, revealed to Musa son of 'Imran who spoke with Allah directly, was taught to him in his mother's womb and the Gospel after his birth. Another describes being taught the secrets of the sacred law, its benefits and its wisdom.

**"How you moulded a bird from clay—by My Will—and breathed into it and it became a ˹real˺ bird—by My Will."** describes shaping the figure of a bird from clay by Allah's permission, breathing into it, and its becoming a bird with a soul, flying in the air, by Allah's permission, command and will. One gloss names the bird as a bat, and describes the breathing as like the breath of a sleeping person.

**"How you healed the blind and the lepers—by My Will."** concerns healing the person born blind and the leper by Allah's command, will and power. The subject was explained earlier in Surah Āl-'Imrān and is not repeated here. One account describes curing the person born blind and treating the leper and healing his skin.

**"How you brought the dead to life—by My Will."** means that he summoned them and they came up out of their graves by the leave, power, intent and will of Allah. Another describes raising the dead by Allah's will and through Him giving life to them, and a third describes bringing them to life by praying to Allah to give them life.

**"How I prevented the Children of Israel from harming you when you came to them with clear proofs"** recalls Allah stopping them from harming him when he brought clear proofs and evidence testifying to his prophethood and message. They refused him, accused him of magic and tried to kill him by crucifixion, but Allah saved him, raised him to Himself, purified him from their vulgarity and protected him from their harm.

One gloss specifies that they were restrained when they had decided to kill him, and that the clear proofs were commands, prohibitions and the wondrous things he showed them.

**"and the disbelievers among them said, “This is nothing but pure magic.”"** gives their response. What he was showing them was, they said, nothing but evident sorcery. A variant reading gives the word as sorcerer, so that the sense is that he is nothing but a manifest sorcerer.

### Why are the favours listed at this point?

The verse before spoke of prophets in general, with a question asked and answered. From here to the end of the chapter the text speaks of 'Isa, the last prophet of Bani Isra'il, and mentions Allah's blessings on him, together with a particular question put to him on the Day of Gathering and its answer in the verses that follow.

The purpose is to display a disturbing sight to Bani Isra'il and to all creation. When the one called Ruhullah, the Spirit of Allah, and the Word of Allah is asked on the plain of al-Mahshar why his people made him a partner with Allah, he will be distressed, despite being a great prophet, and will hasten to plead that he is free of what his followers did.

He does so in more than one way. First he declares that Allah is pure and that it does not befit him to say what is not right for him. Then he pleads his innocence from another angle, calling Allah to witness that had he said such a thing Allah would have known it, since Allah knows what is in his heart and he does not know what is in Allah's, and Allah alone has full knowledge of the unseen.

Only after that does he answer the main question. He taught his people precisely what he was commanded to teach, namely to worship Allah, his Lord and their Lord. As long as he lived among them he was a witness to what they said and did, and none of them said such things about him at that time. After his Lord raised him to Himself they remained under Allah's watch, and it is He who knows their words and deeds fully and truly.

### How does the listing admonish two groups at once?

By placing the bestowal of blessings alongside the scene of answerability, both groups among Bani Isra'il are admonished. One group insulted, accused and harassed him, and the other took him for God or a son of God.

The description of the blessings admonishes the first group, and the mention of the questions and answers warns the second. The juxtaposition is deliberate, and neither half of the passage can be read alone.

### What is significant about speaking in infancy and in middle age?

One sentence in the long description deserves particular attention, the statement that he spoke to people in the cradle and while middle aged. A special miracle given to 'Isa was that he talked to people as a child and also talks to them in middle age.

The first is obviously a miracle and a particular blessing, since children cannot speak meaningfully in the early period after birth. A child who begins to talk in the cradle or on his mother's lap has been given a distinction.

Speaking while middle aged does not appear worth mentioning, because everyone speaks at that age. Consider the circumstances of 'Isa, however, and this too appears as a miracle. He was raised from the earth before reaching middle age, so his speaking to people on earth after reaching it becomes possible only if he returns to this world.

That is the collective belief of Muslims, established on clear statements of the Qur'an and Sunnah. Just as his speech as a child was a miracle, his speech in middle age because of his return to this world is nothing other than a miracle. One gloss draws the same inference, namely that his coming down before the Hour is implied, because Allah took him up before middle age, a point already made in Surah Āl-'Imrān.

### Where does 'Isa stand among the prophets?

Among the prophets he stands as a middle link, joining those who came earlier to the last of them. He was given very special miracles to perform. Those who embraced faith through him were very few in number, and his opponents among the Jews held worldly power.

Despite that, they could not inflict harm on him and did not succeed in destroying his companions. The result of those miracles should have been that people accepted the religion he brought. What happened instead was that his opponents dismissed him, saying that his miracles were merely feats of magic.

Those who embraced his faith later gave him the status of a god. On the Day of Judgment it will be made clear to those claiming to follow him that every feat he performed was done at Allah's behest, and that it was Allah who saved him from the dangers his opponents presented.

When this was the true state of affairs, and 'Isa himself testifies to it while standing before them, his people will have to explain who gave them the religion they wrongly attributed to him.

### In short

- The favours recalled cover his creation without a father, his mother's vindication, support through Gabriel, speech in infancy and maturity, and being taught writing, wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel.
- Every miracle is tied to Allah's permission, command and will, from the clay bird to healing and raising the dead.
- Allah restrained the Children of Israel from killing him after they called his clear proofs evident sorcery.
- The listing admonishes both those who abused him and those who deified him, and the questions that follow answer the second group.
- His speech in middle age is read as pointing to his return before the Hour, since he was raised before reaching it.

111.text:
Another favour is recalled: "And how I inspired the disciples, “Believe in Me and My messenger!”" The inspiration came from Allah, and the response was immediate. They believed and asked to be witnesses that they had submitted.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And how I inspired the disciples"** is also a reminder of Allah's favour to 'Isa, in making disciples and companions for him. The word used is explained as inspired, and Allah inspired them just as He inspired the mother of Musa to suckle him (28:7), and just as the Lord inspired the bee to take habitations in the mountains, the trees and what people erect, then to eat of all fruits and follow the ways of its Lord made easy for it (16:68-69).

Al-Hasan Al-Basri says of the al-hawariyyin that Allah inspired them, and As-Suddi says that He put it in their hearts. One gloss describes the inspiration as a command given to them through the tongue of 'Isa.

The disciples, who will stand with him on the Day of al-Mahshar, are described as twelve in number. Their inspiration is another of the favours recalled to the one supported by the pure Ruh.

**"“Believe in Me and My messenger!”"** calls them to faith in Allah and in His messenger 'Isa. The command joins belief in the sender with belief in the one sent, and does not separate them.

**"They declared, “We believe"** is their answer. They believed in Allah and in His messenger 'Isa. One account renders the reply in the singular, as a believer saying that he believes and asking his Lord to witness that he submits in devotion.

**"and bear witness that we fully submit ˹to Allah˺.”"** asks for testimony to their submission. 'Isa is addressed as a witness, and they also bore witness for one another, being sincere in worship and in declaring Allah's oneness.

### What does the inspiration of the disciples show?

The one who calls people to truth performs the duty of invitation, but a positive response to that call cannot be given unless it is inspired by Allah. Even after being convinced that a call is true, a person does not necessarily go on to accept it, because many obstacles remain.

The caller appears as an ordinary man. Acceptance seems likely to crumble the structure of a life already built. And if this is the truth, the person wonders, were certain great men strangers to it?

That is a critical point at which a person cannot decide, even having reached the stage of decision. It is the point at which Allah helps him. He takes by the hand someone in whom He sees some good, leads him across the borders of doubt and brings him into the region of certainty.

The disciples' answer is therefore presented as a favour to 'Isa as much as to them. A messenger's success is not produced by his own eloquence, and the response of twelve men is itself a gift.

### In short

- Allah inspired the disciples, twelve in number, to believe in Him and in His messenger 'Isa.
- The inspiration is compared with Allah's inspiration of the mother of Musa and of the bee.
- They answered with belief and asked to be witnesses that they had submitted, being sincere in worship and in Allah's oneness.
- Acceptance of a call is itself a gift, since a convinced person may still be held back by obstacles that only divine help removes.

112.text:
The chapter takes its name from this request: “O Jesus, son of Mary! Would your Lord be willing to send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?” The disciples asked for a table from the sky, and 'Isa answered with a command rather than a promise.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Remember˺ when the disciples asked"** introduces the story of the ma'idah, the table with food on it, from which this chapter takes its name. The hawariyyun are the disciples of 'Isa, described in one gloss as the chosen among them, and Simon the Pure is named as the one who spoke.

**"“O Jesus, son of Mary! Would your Lord be willing to send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?”"** is the request. One reading of the wording asks whether his Lord is able, and a variant reading asks whether he is able to request it of his Lord. Another gloss explains it as asking whether he would pray to his Lord to send it down.

Some scholars say the disciples asked because they were poor and deprived, and wanted a table of food sent down that they could eat from every day and so be better able to perform acts of worship.

**"Jesus answered, “Fear Allah if you are ˹truly˺ believers.”"** is his reply. He told them to have taqwa and not to ask for this, because it might become a trial for them, and to trust Allah for their provision if they were truly believers.

One gloss adds the reason for the caution. It may happen that they would not give gratitude for it and would be punished as a result, and 'Isa told Simon to convey that to them. Another explains it as fearing Allah when requesting signs, if they are believers.

### Why is asking for a sign discouraged?

A servant who bears faith should not test Allah by making such requests. Rather than demanding something supernatural, he should seek things like sustenance through the means naturally appointed for him.

People are constantly provided with what they need, and the whole earth has become a table laid with provision for them. The request of the believers in 'Isa nevertheless drew a severe warning, because provision received under normal conditions comes through a veil of cause and effect, while their demand involved removing that veil.

That is Allah's way, since if the veil is removed, how can the conditions of human trial continue?

### In short

- The disciples asked for a table from heaven, and the chapter takes its name from that request.
- Some explain the request by their poverty and their wish to be freer for worship.
- 'Isa answered with a command to fear Allah and trust Him for provision, warning that the request could become a trial.
- Provision normally comes through a veil of causes, and removing it would end the conditions of trial.

113.text:
The disciples explain themselves: “We ˹only˺ wish to eat from it to reassure our hearts, to verify you are indeed truthful to us, and to become its witnesses.” Their answer states three purposes, and each is about certainty rather than about food.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They said, “We ˹only˺ wish to eat from it"** states the immediate need. They need to eat from it, and one gloss explains the request as wanting to eat so that their hearts are satisfied about Allah's perfect power and about his being His Messenger.

**"to reassure our hearts"** is explained as becoming stronger in faith when they witness the table descending from heaven as sustenance for them, and as satisfying their hearts concerning the marvels he shows them, reaching certainty. Another describes the reassurance as increased certainty.

**"to verify you are indeed truthful to us"** concerns his message. Their faith in him and their knowledge would increase, and one gloss describes it as knowing and being certain that he spoke truth to them about everything he said.

**"and to become its witnesses.”"** means testifying that it is a sign from Allah, as proof and evidence that he is a prophet and as attestation of the truth of what he brought. Another gloss describes them as witnesses when they return to their people, and a third as witnesses to it for those not present.

### What kind of request is this?

The three purposes are connected. Eating is not the goal but the occasion, and the goal is a settled heart, verified truth and testimony to others. That is why 'Isa's caution and their explanation can stand together, since their aim was certainty rather than curiosity.

### In short

- The disciples name three purposes: eating, reassurance of heart and verification of his truthfulness, and bearing witness.
- The reassurance is described as stronger faith and increased certainty on seeing the table descend.
- Their witnessing is for those absent and for their own people when they return.
- Eating is the occasion rather than the goal, which is settled certainty and testimony.

114.text:
'Isa then makes the request himself, in words of worship: “O Allah, our Lord! Send us from heaven a table spread with food as a feast for us—the first and last of us—and as a sign from You.” The prayer asks for a festival, a sign and provision, and it ends by naming Allah the best of providers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Jesus, son of Mary, prayed, “O Allah, our Lord!"** He takes the request upon himself after cautioning them. One gloss notes that he gave way to their request and prayed.

**"Send us from heaven a table spread with food"** asks for the table. Another reading takes it as asking for the grace of food, since they already had some food with them.

**"as a feast for us—the first and last of us—"** asks that the day of its descent be a festival. As-Suddi explains that they would take the day on which the table was sent down as a day of celebration, held sacred by them and by those after them. Sufyan Ath-Thawri explains it as a day of prayer.

One gloss describes the first as the people of their own time and the last as those who come after, so that they would worship Allah on that day, which happened to be a Sunday. Another describes the day as one they would consecrate and honour. A further account says they would hold a festival on the day it came down in order to honour Allah out of gratitude.

**"and as a sign from You."** asks for proof that Allah is able to do all things and to accept his supplication, so that people would accept what he conveys from Him. One gloss describes it as a sign for whoever believes and an argument against whoever disbelieves, and another as a sign of Allah's power and of his prophethood. A third describes it as a sign and proof of Allah's oneness and of the truth of what he was sent with.

**"Provide for us! You are indeed the Best Provider.”"** asks for provision. It is explained as delicious food from Allah requiring no effort or hardship, and as giving them what they asked for, since He is the best of those who feed others. Another describes it as provision that would help them worship Allah.

### What does the prayer show?

'Isa began by warning that the request could become a trial, and he ends by praying for it. The difference lies in who asks and how. A demand addressed to Allah as a test is one thing, and a supplication that asks for a festival, a sign and provision while naming Allah the best of providers is another.

The prayer also frames the sign correctly. Everything asked for is tied to worship, gratitude and the acceptance of the message, not to satisfying curiosity.

### In short

- 'Isa prays for the table after cautioning the disciples, taking the request upon himself.
- The day of descent is to be a festival, explained as a day of celebration, of prayer and of consecration by the first and the last of them.
- The sign is asked for as proof of Allah's power, of His accepting supplication and of 'Isa's prophethood and oneness of Allah.
- Provision is requested as food needing no effort, and Allah is named the best of providers.
- The prayer ties every request to worship and gratitude rather than to curiosity.

115.text:
The answer comes with a condition: "Allah answered, “I am sending it down to you. But whoever among you denies afterwards will be subjected to a torment I have never inflicted on anyone of My creation.”" The table will be sent, and disbelief after it will be punished as nothing else has been punished.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah answered, “I am sending it down to you."** grants the supplication. Allah tells 'Isa to inform them that He is sending down what they asked for, and He fulfilled His promise and sent the table to them.

**"But whoever among you denies afterwards"** concerns whoever disbelieves after it has been sent down and eaten from, by denying the sign and defying what it implies. One gloss describes the denial as coming after they had seen an overwhelming proof, so that any denial is the result of stubbornness, and says they should blame only themselves.

**"will be subjected to a torment I have never inflicted on anyone of My creation.”"** describes a punishment unlike any other, and one gloss limits it to the people of his time.

Similar verses are cited: on the Day when the Hour is established the angels will be told to cause the people of Fir'awn to enter the severest torment (40:46), and the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire (4:145).

Ibn Jarir reports 'Abdullah bin 'Amr saying that three groups will receive the severest torment on the Day of Resurrection: the hypocrites, those among the people of the table who disbelieved in it, and the people of Fir'awn.
